Sizing GPU Memory for a RAG Service: KV Cache, Context and Concurrency

According to recent reports, A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) app is usually drawn as a language model plus a vector database. When it goes live, the part that fails first is rarely the retrieval. It is GPU memory on the generation model, because a model that loads fine for one request can run out of memory when several people send long questions at once.

This article highlights how to estimate that limit before you deploy, with a short script you can run, and then covers what else in the pipeline can slow responses down.

Recent findings suggest that serving a model takes more than its weights. The GPU also holds:.

the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with the length of every active request.

activations and batching overhead.

memory used by the inference runtime itself.

SitePoint's guide to running a local LLM on 10GB of VRAM makes the same point for a single desktop GPU: the usable budget is the total VRAM minus overhead, and the KV cache grows with the context window, so the real model budget is smaller than the number on the box.

It has been revealed that for a RAG service, the KV cache matters even more. Retrieved passages are pasted into the prompt, so every request carries a long context, and every concurrent request holds its own cache.

The cache size per token depends on the model's architecture: two tensors (keys and values) for every layer, for every KV head. This script turns those numbers into a rough limit on concurrent requests:.

def kv_bytes_per_token(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes=2):.

# Keys and values, for every layer, for one token.

return 2 *layers *kv_heads *head_dim *dtype_bytes.

def max_concurrent(vram_gb, weights_gb, ctx_tokens, per_token, reserve_gb=2.0):.

budget = (vram_gb - weights_gb - reserve_gb) * GIB.

return int(budget // (ctx_tokens * per_token)).

per_token = kv_bytes_per_token(32, 8, 128).

print(per_token // 1024, "KiB per token").

for ctx in (4096, 8192, 16384):.

n = max_concurrent(24, 16, ctx, per_token).

print(ctx, "tokens ->", n, "concurrent requests").

For a 24 GB GPU holding about 16 GB of fp16 weights with 2 GB kept in reserve, it prints:.

4096 tokens -> 12 concurrent requests.

8192 tokens -> 6 concurrent requests.

16384 tokens -> 3 concurrent requests.

Industry observers note that the numbers are estimates. Real runtimes add their own overhead, and the architecture values come from the model's configuration file, so read them from the model you actually use. The pattern is what matters: doubling the context length halves the number of requests that fit. A RAG prompt that stuffs in ten retrieved chunks costs real capacity.

According to recent reports, serving runtimes do not simply crash when the cache is full. The vLLM documentation on optimization and tuning explains that when KV cache space is insufficient for all batched requests, the engine preempts some of them and recomputes them later, which can hurt end-to-end latency. Its suggested remedies include giving the cache more memory, reducing the number of concurrent sequences or batched tokens, or sharding the model across GPUs.

Recent findings suggest that so the symptom of undersizing is often not an error. It is slow, uneven responses under load. Test with realistic prompt lengths and several simultaneous users, not a single request.

Embedding and ingestion have a different profile from generation. Embedding is often lighter than serving a large language model, and some teams run it on CPU. Document parsing, chunking and tokenization also run on CPU, so a fast GPU cannot make up for a slow CPU upstream. SitePoint's tutorial on a local RAG system for private documents walks through chunking, embeddings, vector storage and reranking, and is a good map of which stages run where.

RAM: vector indexes, document loaders and caches all live in system memory, so large collections need more of it.

Recent findings suggest that storage: model files, indexes, logs and backups add up. Fast storage shortens model loading and re-indexing.

Network: if the vector database, application server and model server sit in different places, latency adds to every request.

Two layouts are common. A single instance runs everything and is simplest for prototypes and internal tools. Separated services put ingestion and retrieval on smaller machines and keep the GPU for generation, which scales better as traffic grows.

Memory estimates only hold if the GPU memory is really yours. On a shared or time-sliced GPU, other workloads can take memory and compute away from your service, which makes capacity hard to proposal. Hosting providers describe this in different terms, such as passthrough, vGPU, MIG and time-slicing. For a view of how one GPU hosting provider explains those allocation methods, GPU Mart's GPU virtualization guide compares them. It is a hosting company's page, so confirm any provider's claims about isolation and performance with your own load test.

Whatever provider you choose, ask these questions:.

Is the physical GPU assigned to you exclusively, or partitioned or time-sliced?

Do you have root access to install your own drivers, CUDA libraries and containers?

Which minimum commitments, regions and support terms apply?

A small stack can run as a handful of containers: an API service for request handling and prompt assembly, an ingestion worker, a vector database and a model server. Keeping them separate lets you monitor each one's memory and CPU use and move the heavy one to bigger hardware without rewriting the rest.

For a service that stays up all month, a fixed monthly term is easier to forecast than hourly capacity. Hourly capacity suits testing quantization settings or processing a one-off document batch.

Is GPU memory always the bottleneck for RAG?

In a recent development, not always. Generation usually hits memory first, but slow parsing, a small CPU or a distant vector database can dominate response time.

Does quantization solve the memory problem?

Sources indicate that it shrinks the weights, but the KV cache still grows with context length and concurrency. Test with your real prompt sizes.

Should embeddings run on the GPU?

Recent findings suggest that it depends on volume. Small workloads can run on CPU, while a large ingestion job may benefit from a GPU for a limited time.

Size a RAG service for the worst realistic moment, not the single-request demo. Estimate the KV cache from the model's architecture, remember that long retrieved contexts reduce how many requests fit, watch for preemption under load, keep CPU, RAM, storage and network in the plan, and find out whether the GPU is exclusive or shared. The script above is small, but it turns a vague worry about memory into numbers you can check.

We’re back! Don’t worry, this isn’t a trick (despite what our name suggests!). However, due to the hiatus, we’re also a little behind. That’s why this problem of What’s !vital is absolutely stacked. All killer, no filler. Here’s what you missed.

Preethi Sam demonstrated how to create background image refraction effects with CSS. The effects are stunning, can be animated, don’t need very much CSS (no JavaScript), and we don’t need to duplicate the image either.

Brecht De Ruyte demonstrated how to build customizable components using container style queries and advanced attr(), showcasing some incredible interactive demos, including the two below:.

Recent findings suggest that dan Holloran showed us how to use the different scroll-state() queries (scrollable, scrolled, snapped, and stuck). It’s not a long read, which is exactly what you want for a fresh but simple feature like this.

A quick, no-context CSS snippet to entice you:.

Declan Chidlow shared some of the craziest CSS to ever exist, and I mean craziest. Most of it comes from Internet Explorer, but let’s face it, you knew that already. Thankfully, they don’t build them like they used to.

According to recent reports, bramus demonstrated how to animate CSS grids using anchor positioning. The idea is that we anchor content to its corresponding cell, and then as the grid reflows, it’s the content (not the cell) that animates with it.

(But it doesn’t work in Firefox due to what sounds like a bug.).

According to recent reports, chris Coyier talked about a bunch of new HTML features, and honestly, there’s a whole lot in there that you definitely haven’t heard of. Like, I’m certain of it.

In a recent development, victor Ayomipo contemplated why container query adoption has been so terrible despite them topping CSS wishlists for years. Victor thinks that we’re using them wrong, so he’s here to set the record straight.

Cory LaViska demonstrated how to use @custom-media in addition to container style queries as a fallback.

Also, don’t forget that Declan has an extremely thorough @custom-media deep-dive in our Almanac.

Industry observers note that ahmad Shadeed tackled an interesting topic — detecting overlapping elements (with CSS, of course). If you’re keen on anchor positioning, scroll-driven animations, and again (!), container style queries, then this walkthrough is for you.

It has been revealed that I want to know when the decorative element hits the section from the left edge, taking into consideration that the element might have a fluid position or size that changes with the viewport size or container size. Basically, it’s a dynamic problem. It’s not about using a media query to hide the decorative element, I want to hide it upon overlapping.

Maybe container queries are finally picking up?

Patrick Brosset walked us through a proposal for the previewsrc HTML attribute, which would enable us to supply preview images for images that haven’t yet loaded using only HTML. For example, we could supply a blurry preview image. However, I’d rather have something like :loaded/:not(:loaded) so that we can style/transition unloaded images with CSS rather than needing to create extra images.

Temani Afif shared a custom borders demo, where the trick is to declare a transparent border, use border-shape to define its shape, then declare a background in addition to background-clip: border-area so that it only demonstrates up within the border, like this (requires Chrome at the moment):.

In a similar manner, Leon Arnott shared this awesome trick for animating the background color of ::selection, something that’s actually forbidden (or so we thought, anyway…):.

Recent findings suggest that today in CSS: We all know you can change the highlight colour of selected text, but it's impossible to animate that colour. Unless… the colour was just a variable inherited from the parent element, using @​property to make it animatable… Hahahahaha… [image or embed].

In a recent development, and that’s it, really. Simply use var(--bg-color) on ::selection or some other visually restrictive element.

Industry observers note that chris Coyier demonstrated how to random()ly animate an element along the edge of another element. There’s a cute doggo, by the way. Probably should’ve led with that.

Polypane explained how we might disable the root scroller accidentally (which is surprisingly easy to do — I’ve definitely done it), what we lose in doing so, and what to do instead.

According to recent reports, also, have you ever completely misunderstood how the root (:root/html) works? This is a solid explainer for that, too.

Speaking of accidents, have you ever tapped on a target twice, apparently in quick succession, and ended up zooming in? Andy Bell revealed that touch-action: manipulation disables the double-tap-to-zoom-in functionality. It isn’t new, but I don’t see many web developers using it. One for the CSS reset, I think?

It has been revealed that chrome and Firefox now ship every two weeks. The inaugural releases were fairly exciting (not smaller, as I assumed they’d be). In addition, Safari 27 (along with iOS, iPadOS, and macOS 27) shipped with some of the same features as Firefox, making them Baseline in the same release window. High fives all around!

And, as always, thanks for tuning in!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • MotorCity Casino was the only Detroit property to grow table games and slot revenue in October from a year earlier.
  • In a recent development, across the three casinos, tables and slots generated $108.1 million.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that growth at MotorCity Casino outweighed declines at MGM Grand Detroit and Hollywood Casino at Greektown, lifting Detroit's October table and slot revenue from a year earlier. Retail sports betting also rebounded sharply from September, adding to the month's gains.

MotorCity Casino was the only Detroit property to grow table games and slot revenue in October from a year earlier. Its rivals both lost ground. MGM Grand Detroit slipped 2.7% to $51.3 million. Hollywood Casino at Greektown fell 5.0% to $21.6 million.

In a recent development, across the three casinos, tables and slots generated $108.1 million. That was up 2.1% from October 2025 and 5.2% from September 2026. Year-to-date revenue from January through October was up 2.3%.

CDC Gaming Reports put October 2025 table and slot revenue at $105.9 million.

MGM still holds the largest piece of the market. It took 47% of Detroit’s October revenue. MotorCity held 33%, and Hollywood Casino at Greektown held 20%.

According to recent reports, the October split continues a pattern from late summer. In August, MotorCity rose 8.3% to $33.8 million and MGM grew 2.3% to $52.9 million, while Greektown fell 2.6% to $22.2 million, InterGame reported. Detroit’s August total was $109.7 million.

Greektown’s slide deepened in September, when its revenue fell 8.8% year over year to $21.34 million. October’s decline was smaller. MGM, by contrast, moved from growth in August to a decline in October.

Recent findings suggest that the citywide trend has been uneven. September table and slot revenue was 4.7% higher than a year earlier but 5.6% lower than in August. October’s rebound lifted aggregate revenue above September’s $103.55 million.

Retail sports betting produced $2.4 million in October. That compares with $769,771 in retail QAGR in September. Handle at the Detroit casinos was $12.87 million for the month.

MotorCity also led the sportsbook results. It posted $928,607 in retail receipts. MGM followed at $746,215, with Hollywood Casino at Greektown close behind at $729,350.

Industry observers note that the sportsbook activity generated $90,878 in state taxes. The casinos also sent $111,073 in sports wagering taxes to Detroit.

Sources indicate that the city’s take from the casinos goes well beyond sports betting. In October, Detroit collected $13.4 million from the three properties, combining its share of gaming taxes with sums owed under each casino’s agreement with the city.

A grand total of $9,985,482+ in jackpots hit at MotorCity Casino in October! 💰🎰.

Sources indicate that congratulations to all the guests who took home a win! Here’s to an exciting November! pic.twitter.com/bHIJGmc0jM.

— MotorCity Casino (@MotorCityCasino) November 8, 2026.

Fantasy contests remain a small part of the picture. Operators reported $837,938 in adjusted revenues for September 2026 and paid $70,387 in taxes.

Industry observers note that detroit’s land-based results now set a baseline for Michigan’s October online casino and sports betting figures, which come next. In September, the state’s commercial and tribal online operators took in $355.7 million in combined iGaming and online sports betting gross receipts, 5.4% more than in August.

The Frankenstein Table

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was naivety, but when I first came across Flexbox, and then CSS Grid, I had this feeling all those positioning properties (align-self, justify-content…) would be available to use on block and inline elements; things like tables, lists, fixed elements, everything.
  • Although that didn’t happen, what if I made something of that sort?
  • For example, I could take out the soul of an HTML table and stitch it back together with CSS Grid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Something wicked this way comes.”.

It was naivety, but when I first came across Flexbox, and then CSS Grid, I had this feeling all those positioning properties (align-self, justify-content…) would be available to use on block and inline elements; things like tables, lists, fixed elements, everything. The workings might be different under the hood, depending on the reference boxes, but the syntax and expected outcomes would be same: push to one edge, keep at the center, spread around evenly, etc.

Although that didn’t happen, what if I made something of that sort?

For example, I could take out the soul of an HTML table and stitch it back together with CSS Grid. In other words, it reads like a table, but acts like a grid, allowing me to use grid properties. Believe it or not, some form of this was used in the past to make tables responsive.

Industry observers note that before I kill off a table in this article though: there are a lot of advantages to straight-up tables. They provide a clean semantic layout that browsers perfectly understand and translate for assistive technology when needed. There’s even a element.

Recent findings suggest that on the CSS side of things, there are indeed circumstances where CSS Grid is necessary for its intrinsic responsiveness, source order independence, and positioning. That’s why it’s an indispensable tool for layouts. Use that and let HTML tables to do the work of actually displaying tabular data!

But there’s the presentational benefit of table we should consider. Technically, is not a presentational element like a . It’s semantic: the browser and I share a common meaning for it. But whether the browser understands it as such or not, if I read I believe it’s a heading followed by data. Let’s say that’s pseudo-semantic to me, if presentation is not the right term.

That pseudo-semanticism is still useful. It’s the difference between me having to read this:.

Despite there being semantic elements for titles, like and , they don’t bring in the connection that and have, and it’s better to reserve and for textual structuring like glossaries rather than layouts.

So, is it okay if I use this way? I mean, the table itself merely used as pseudo-semantic markup skin:.

Then, this CSS and its outcome (for the first markup):.

…changes to this (for the table markup):.

In a recent development, to me, the latter markup example — a pseudo-semantic table — is easier to scan than a handful of generic divs. I get the pseudo-semantics of table, and the ease of using CSS Grid for the layout. As for browsers, none of them have shunned this sort of Frankenstein creation, at least yet. The VoiceOver and keyboard navigation works as if it’s a real table.

But it’s understandable why it looks more than a little gross and against the grain of what we should be able to. We’re encouraged to maintain a separation of concerns between content and presentation and this does exactly that without affecting the tables semantics, such as its role. But maybe it should? There are plenty of other HTML elements that CSS is capable of busting.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, good news first? Or bad news first?

This is the final concern of What’s !crucial on CSS-Tricks.com. The good news is that it’s coming back in an expanded form as the CSS-Tricks newsletter. I had ya there for a second, didn’t I? Sorry, I couldn’t decide whether to trick or treat, so I went for both. Happy Halloween!

In a recent development, the newsletter officially kicks off on November 10th. That’s after a way-too-long four-year hiatus. What the heck, right? It’s not only high time for it to come back, but for you to get on the list. You’ll get hand-written and hand-curated news, links, and editorials that you can only find there. Join the party with me!

Recent findings suggest that so, let’s go out with a major bang for our “final” problem. It’s packed with some stuff that I’ve been holding onto since before the site came back to life earlier this week, but also some newly introduced stuff, and I can’t wait to finally get it out to you.

#11248. From Script to Screen: A Developer's Workflow for Long-Form AI Video

From Script to Screen: A Developer's Workflow for Long-Form AI Video

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Recent findings suggest that generating a single AI video clip is easy now.
  • In a recent development, most guides stop at the clip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Recent findings suggest that generating a single AI video clip is easy now. You send a prompt and get a few seconds of footage back. The trouble starts when the goal is three, five, or ten minutes of video where the same character looks the same in every scene, the style does not drift, and the captions line up with the picture.

In a recent development, most guides stop at the clip. This one covers the part after it, treating a video as a small build pipeline: a storyboard that is data, prompts generated from that data, clips normalised and stitched with ffmpeg, and captions derived from the same source. If you want to wire a generation model into your own application first, SitePoint's guide to integrating generative video APIs into web applications covers the request and webhook side. If the finished video is headed to a YouTube channel, how to get a YouTube API key and use the Data API is a good starting point for the publishing side. Everything between those two is below.

Long-form AI video fails at the seams between clips, not inside them. Plan for continuity before you generate anything.

A storyboard stored as JSON can be validated, versioned, diffed, and turned into prompts by code, which a pile of loose prompts cannot.

Repeat the full character description in every prompt. Models do not remember the previous clip.

Clips from different generations rarely share resolution, frame rate, or codec settings. Normalise them before joining.

Captions are cheapest when generated from the script and measured clip durations, not transcribed afterwards.

It has been revealed that current video models generate short clips, commonly a handful of seconds each. A longer video is therefore many clips, and every clip is an independent generation. The model has no memory of what the character wore in the previous one.

That produces three kinds of failure. The character drifts, so hair, clothing, or proportions change between scenes. The style drifts, so lighting and colour grade shift from cut to cut. And the technical specs drift, so one clip is 24 frames per second at one resolution and the next is something else. Each of these is fixable, but only if the project is organised so the fixes can be applied consistently.

Start with a structured storyboard instead of a document full of prompts. One file holds the style, a "character bible", and an ordered list of scenes.

"project": "rainy-day-lantern",.

"style": "soft watercolor picture book illustration, warm evening light, 16:9",.

"mira": "a nine year old girl with short curly black hair, a yellow raincoat and red rubber boots",.

"lantern": "a small round paper lantern with a gentle orange glow and a tiny smiling face".

"setting": "a narrow cobblestone street in light rain",.

"action": "walks slowly past closed shops, looking up at the sky",.

"camera": "slow push in from a medium shot",.

"narration": "It had rained all afternoon, and the street was quiet.".

"characters": ["mira", "lantern"],.

"setting": "under a bakery awning",.

"action": "finds the lantern glowing on a wooden crate and kneels beside it",.

"camera": "static medium close up",.

"narration": "Then she noticed something glowing under the awning.".

Sources indicate that because it is data, a script can check it before you spend any generation credits. Two checks pay for themselves swiftly: every character named in a scene must exist in the bible, and no scene may be longer than the clip limit of the model you use.

function validateStoryboard(board) {.

const known = newly introduced Set(Object.keys(board.characters));.

for (const scene of board.scenes) {.

for (const name of scene.characters) {.

errors.push${scene.id}: unknown character "${name}");.

if (scene.duration > MAX_CLIP_SECONDS) {.

${scene.id}: ${scene.duration}s is over the ${MAX_CLIP_SECONDS}s clip limit, split it into shots.

Treat MAX_CLIP_SECONDS as a setting. Limits differ between models and change over time, so check the one you are using rather than trusting the number in this example.

It has been revealed that never write the per-scene prompt by hand. Generate it, so the style line and the character descriptions are identical every time.

function buildPrompt(board, scene) {.

.map((name) => board.characters[name]).

The character description appears word for word in every scene that includes that character. This is the single most effective consistency tactic that needs no special tooling. Changing a detail, say the colour of the boots, becomes one edit in the bible instead of a search through twenty prompts, and the diff reveals exactly what changed between versions.

Put the style line first and keep it identical across all scenes.

Describe one action per clip. Two sequential actions in one prompt often produce a blend of both.

In a recent development, keep camera directions simple. A single move per clip is more reliable than a combination.

Avoid naming real people, brands, or existing characters in prompts. Beyond the rights problem, it makes results harder to reproduce.

Sources indicate that clips from separate generations often disagree on resolution, frame rate, pixel format, or codec parameters. Joining them directly can produce stutters, green frames, or an outright error. Convert every clip to one agreed format first.

-vf "scale=1280:720:force_original_aspect_ratio=decrease,pad=1280:720:(ow-iw)/2:(oh-ih)/2,fps=24,format=yuv420p" \.

-an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 "norm/$(basename "$f")".

Sources indicate that the filter scales each clip to fit a 1280 by 720 frame, adds padding if the aspect ratio differs, sets 24 frames per second, and forces a widely compatible pixel format. The -an flag drops any audio the model generated, since narration will be added as one track later. Name clips with zero padded numbers such as s01.mp4 and s02.mp4, so a shell glob sorts them in story order.

Once every file shares the same parameters, the concat demuxer can join them without re-encoding:.

for f in norm/*.mp4; do echo "file '$PWD/$f'"; done > list.txt.

ffmpeg -y -f concat -safe 0 -i list.txt -c copy stitched.mp4.

In a recent development, hard cuts are the safe default. Crossfades are possible with ffmpeg's xfade filter, but they require careful offset arithmetic and a re-encode, so add them only when a cut genuinely looks wrong.

Captions are easiest when they come from the script, not from a speech recognition pass over the finished video. The storyboard already holds the narration text and each scene's length, so an SRT file is a few lines of code. Use measured durations rather than planned ones, because a generated clip is often a little shorter or longer than requested.

const { execFileSync } = require('node:child_process');.

function measureSeconds(file) {.

const out = execFileSync('ffprobe', [.

'-show_entries', 'format=duration',.

return Number(out.toString().trim());.

function toTimestamp(totalSeconds) {.

const ms = Math.round(totalSeconds * 1000);.

const h = String(Math.floor(ms / 3600000)).padStart(2, '0');.

const m = String(Math.floor((ms % 3600000) / 60000)).padStart(2, '0');.

const s = String(Math.floor((ms % 60000) / 1000)).padStart(2, '0');.

const rest = String(ms % 1000).padStart(3, '0');.

const end = cursor + scene.duration; // set from measureSeconds() after generation.

if (!scene.narration) continue;.

${blocks.length + 1}\n${toTimestamp(start)} --> ${toTimestamp(end)}\n${scene.narration}\n.

In a recent development, patch each scene's duration from measureSeconds on the normalised clip before calling buildSrt. If a narration line is long, split it across two caption blocks so it stays readable. Then combine picture, voiceover, and captions in one final step:.

ffmpeg -y -i stitched.mp4 -i narration.mp3 -i captions.srt \.

-c:v copy -c:a aac -c:s mov_text -shortest final.mp4.

Industry observers note that soft captions like these can be switched off by the viewer and read by assistive technology, which is better than burning text into the picture. Keep the .srt file as well, since most platforms accept it as a separate upload.

Sources indicate that everything above is a good fit when you need repeatability: many videos from templates, versioned storyboards, automated publishing, or tight control over the model. The price is that you own the glue code, the ffmpeg settings, and the failures.

For one off projects, or when the people making the video are not developers, a managed platform is often the more sensible choice. Tools such as magiclight.ai bundle story to video generation, character handling, voice, and an editor in one interface, and advertise videos of up to 50 minutes. Check the specifics yourself, because claims like that are marketing, and results depend on your content. One point matters for developers in particular: if you need to automate generation from your own code, confirm that the platform you pick offers an API or export route before you build a workflow around it. A tool with a good editor and no programmatic access suits a different job than the pipeline in this article.

A short manual pass catches what automation does not. Watch the whole video once at normal speed, looking only at continuity. Read the captions against the audio. Check that no real person's likeness, brand mark, or protected character slipped into the footage. Finally, check the disclosure rules of the platform you publish on, since many now ask creators to label realistic synthetic media, and the rules change.

The model is only one component of a long-form AI video. The reliability comes from the structure around it: a validated storyboard, prompts generated from it, clips forced into one format, and captions derived from measured data. Each of those is ordinary software engineering, and none of it depends on which generation model you choose, so the pipeline survives when the model changes.

Start with a two minute video and four or five scenes. Fix the seams there before scaling up, because every continuity problem you find at that size is one you will not have to hunt for in a ten minute project.

In a recent development, west Virginia's online casinos posted record monthly revenue in October 2026, the second full month with bet365 live in the state. The result pushed 2026 revenue past the total for all of 2025, while a bill to raise the iGaming tax remains pending.

The revenue measure is adjusted gross interactive wagering receipts. State law defines it as an operator’s gross online wagering receipts minus winnings paid to players. Under 2019’s House Bill 2934, the privilege tax on those receipts goes into the Interactive Wagering Fund each week, and every licensed racetrack and historic resort pays it.

Recent findings suggest that bet365 rolled out online sports betting and casino in the state on Aug. 27, 2026. West Virginia is its fourth U.S. online casino state. In its other 14 states, bet365 offers sports betting only.

Lottery licensing documents show bet365 received an interim license in January 2026. It was approved for a full annual license on July 29. West Virginia was the firm’s sixth North American launch in 13 months, Yogonet reported. The earlier launches were Kansas and Maryland in August 2025, Missouri in December 2025, Michigan in April 2026 and Alberta in July 2026.

West Virginia’s market has a fixed structure. The Interactive Wagering Act allows no more than five gaming facility licenses with online wagering. Every online game counts as a state-owned lottery game. October’s record is consistent with bet365 adding to that market, but the operator split has yet to be shown.

Two months of 2026 remain to be reported. The comparison months set a high bar. Adjusted gross interactive gaming receipts were $37,198,210 in November 2025. Receipts for the fiscal year to date through Nov. 30, 2025, were $169,425,990.

According to recent reports, the broader lottery picture also shows growth. The Lottery took in more than $1.33 billion in gross revenue in fiscal 2026, which ended June 30. It sent $582.9 million to the state. Revenue was $58 million higher than in fiscal 2025. In its fiscal 2026 wrap-up, the Lottery named iLottery and iGaming as its biggest growth areas, and said iGaming was following national gaming trends.

In a recent development, higher revenue also raises the stakes of a pending tax change. Introduced on Jan. 16, 2026, House Bill 4397 would increase the iGaming privilege tax. The bill is still listed as pending in the House Local Governments Committee.

In a recent development, the next detail to watch is the operator breakdown. The Lottery publishes a file that splits interactive wagering data by skin and casino. That file will show how much of October’s record came from bet365.

#11243. Industry News: Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1427 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Css-tricks ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1427 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset.
  • I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.
  • Use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset. text-wrap: pretty can prevent a stranded word, container query units can scale a heading to the column it occupies, and text-box can trim the half-leading built into a line box. Some of these features are experimental and browser support is uneven, so they need guardrails rather than blind inclusion.

I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.

Use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you. I’ll walk you through all the details in this article and give you the full code at the end.

font-synthesis: none stops a browser from inventing bold or italic when the family lacks that face. The smoothing and text-rendering declarations are rendering hints, mainly for WebKit; results still vary by platform.

text-size-adjust disables mobile font inflation that can make a deliberately sized layout jump on rotation. font-size-adjust: from-font uses font metrics to reduce the apparent size change while a fallback swaps for a webfont.

(As with other snippets in this article, this ⁠:root block is a partial excerpt the final stylesheet combines it with additional custom properties defined later on.).

According to recent reports, viewport-based fluid type does not know how wide its element is. A heading in a narrow sidebar can therefore scale as though it fills the viewport.

According to recent reports, container-type: inline-size makes the wrapper a container query, so its children can use cqi: a unit based on the container rather than the viewport. Replacing vw in clamp() lets the same heading scale appropriately in an article column or a 300px sidebar without component-specific media queries.

line-height includes space above the cap-height and below the baseline: half-leading. It becomes obvious when text must align tightly with another element. text-box-trim removes it, while text-box-edge measures from capital-letter caps to the alphabetic baseline. This is a metrics-aware alternative to font-specific negative-margin nudges.

Sources indicate that selectors Level 5 proposes :heading, matching h1 to h6 and [role="heading"]. It has not landed in browsers, so keep it behind an @supports selector() check.

Default heading wrapping can leave one short final line. text-wrap: balance distributes text across its lines and works best for blocks of up to about six lines. For paragraphs, text-wrap: pretty avoids a stranded final word without balancing the whole block. Both replace JavaScript orphan fixers. Editable text needs text-wrap: stable, which prevents each newly introduced word from reshuffling the paragraph.

In a recent development, hyphens: auto relies on the browser’s language dictionaries, so the document needs a correct lang attribute (for example ). Without one the browser has no dictionary to use and won’t be able to hyphenate text. Even with the correct lang, the defaults can leave tiny word fragments or several hyphenated lines in a row.

hyphenate-limit-chars controls the smallest breakable word and fragments; hyphenate-limit-lines prevents a ladder effect. hyphenate-limit-zone makes breaks less frequent, while hyphenate-limit-last protects the final word. Safari needs the prefixed equivalents, so declare both sets together.

Set code, variables, and headings to hyphens: manual: a broken code word can change meaning, and a hyphenated heading usually reads as an error.

Punctuation marks don’t carry the same visual weight as letters, so a quotation mark sitting at the start of a line can look slightly indented against the text below it. hanging-punctuation lets specified punctuation sit fractionally outside the text block’s edge.

The first value handles opening punctuation, and last handles closing punctuation at the end of a block, while allow-end lets punctuation hang past the right edge rather than force-wrapping. The result is a text block whose edges read as genuinely flush.

In a recent development, underlines have a related problem. Browsers apply flat, one-size-fits-all thickness and position regardless of the font’s actual weight.

text-decoration-thickness: from-font reads the thickness the font’s designer intended. text-underline-offset gives descenders room to breathe, and text-decoration-skip-ink: auto interrupts the underline wherever a descender crosses it rather than drawing straight through the letter.

Variable fonts often include an optical size axis, or opsz. It lets a typeface use thinner strokes at large display sizes and thicker, more legible strokes when set small.

font-optical-sizing: auto lets the font make that adjustment based on its actual rendered size. The @supports block covers the older font-variation-settings syntax some browsers still need, while font-variant-ligatures and font-kerning enable the font’s own ligatures and kerning pairs.

Recent findings suggest that light text on a dark background genuinely reads heavier than the same weight on a light background. Where a font ships a GRAD, or grade, axis, the dark mode block dials that perceived weight down without changing glyph shape or width the way an actual weight change would. Fonts without a GRAD axis safely ignore the setting.

Recent findings suggest that mixing a monospace font into running prose often exposes a mismatched x-height at the same declared font-size. The size-adjust keyword, set once at the @font-face level, scales that font’s rendered output specifically, leaving the actual font-size value untouched.

Numbers in a table need identical widths so they stack into a clean column on the screen. Conversely, numbers in flowing text don’t need the same treatment and should sit naturally alongside the surrounding words.

According to recent reports, the tabular-nums and lining-nums keywords give table digits a fixed width and full cap height. oldstyle-nums and proportional-nums let digits sit alongside lowercase letters without sticking up and disrupting the sentence’s texture.

font-variant-emoji makes the choice between full-colour and monochrome emoji explicit. Without it, the browser or platform gets to choose a fallback, and the result can vary more than you expect. Apply .emoji-color or .emoji-mono to containers where you want to enforce that choice, rather than setting it globally on the body.

Quote style and character order differ by language and region. English nests single quotes inside double quotes, British English reverses that convention, and French uses guillemets with a thin space.

In a recent development, the quotes property declares the order for each language through :lang(). The native q element then inserts the right pair through open-quote and close-quote. The same markup can render correctly in each locale without hardcoding characters into the content.

Wrapping the rules in :where() keeps them at zero specificity, so a project can override the quote style with one plain class.

It has been revealed that default sub and sup styling is synthesized. The browser just shrinks the text and shifts the baseline, rather than using glyphs actually designed for that position.

In a recent development, font-variant-position switches to the font’s own purpose-built sub and superscript glyphs where they exist, resetting vertical-align, font-size, and line-height so they don’t fight against the real glyph’s intended size and position. Most typefaces only include proper numerals rather than letters, so check the specific font before applying this broadly.

:where() always resolves to zero specificity, which is useful for a reset. Every rule here is an opinionated default, and wrapping it in :where() lets a project override a property with a plain class.

According to recent reports, :is() solves a different problem: repetition. The heading selector list appears several times in a typographic stylesheet, and grouping it avoids the risk of forgetting a level.

Unlike :where(), :is() carries the specificity of its most specific argument.

In a recent development, here’s the complete reset, combining the stable layers. Unsupported declarations are ignored by the browser, so the stylesheet can be adopted gradually.

Industry observers note that much of this CSS removes work that used to leak into other parts of a build. text-wrap can take over orphan handling from JavaScript, container query units keep a component’s type scale tied to its own width, and text-box-trim avoids the negative margins once used to compensate for leading. quotes, font-variant-position, and font-optical-sizing hand several smaller details back to the language and the font instead of a collection of one-off fixes.

Sources indicate that browser support will continue to change, especially for text-wrap and text-box-trim. Unsupported declarations are ignored, but that only helps when the unenhanced typography is acceptable in its own right.

It has been revealed that some of these rules are still too latest for a baseline reset. A news article, a marketing page, and an editable product interface do not ask the same things of their text; the set that belongs in yours depends on the font, the content, and the browsers you still need to support.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michigan's regulator has approved the Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe's move of its Soaring Eagle online casino and sportsbook from GAN to White Hat Gaming. The rare platform swap gives White Hat a full platform role in a top-three US market while GAN's owner restructures the business.

Soaring Eagle Gaming has a new technology partner in Michigan. The Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe’s online casino and online sports betting operations now run on White Hat Gaming Inc.’s platform. White Hat replaces GAN, which had powered the tribe’s Michigan offer since launch. That launch came under the Eagle Casino and Sports brand.

Platform swaps like this are rare in Michigan. Players keep the same Soaring Eagle brand.

Industry observers note that the board reviewed the White Hat platform and the tribe’s branding submission before signing off. The tribe also filed a signed agreement with White Hat. Every supplier and vendor needed for launch had already been approved. Executive Director Henry Williams noted the board checked the latest platform carefully against its standards on integrity, security and consumer protection, which apply to any platform Michigan players use.

The approval carries conditions. Both companies are limited to games, sports events and bet types the board has approved, and must route business through approved suppliers, vendors and payment locations. Both companies must also fully adopt all internal control amendments the board has approved.

The board’s list of authorized platform providers now names White Hat as the tribe’s provider for online casino and online sports betting. The tribe already had a content tie to White Hat Studios, the games supplier. In June 2022, White Hat Studios revealed it would supply branded games, including Ted, Deal or No Deal and Peaky Blinders, to the tribe’s PlayEagle.com site.

Industry observers note that the stakes in Michigan remain sizable. Operators reported $355.7 million in combined online casino and online sports betting gross receipts for September 2026, up 5.4% from August. Online casino accounted for $300.2 million and sports betting for $55.5 million. Adjusted gross receipts came to $313.04 million. Online casino adjusted receipts, however, fell 0.9% from August. The figures are consistent with a market still growing year on year but flatter month to month.

The switch comes as GAN works through changes under latest ownership. In results for the six months to September 30, 2026, Sega Sammy said GAN is running a turnaround program that cuts fixed costs. The program will also move GAN ahead with migrating to a new platform. Adding GAN and Stakelogic raised group sales. It also widened the operating loss compared with the same period a year earlier.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that user interactions with agents today are where computers were in the terminal era: capable, and answering almost everything in text.
  • Today, we're releasing A2UI 1.0, the first stable version of our open protocol for generative UI.
  • It has been revealed that with A2UI, the agent describes what to show, and every app draws the UI with its own native components.

Recent findings suggest that user interactions with agents today are where computers were in the terminal era: capable, and answering almost everything in text. Users can ask an agent for anything by typing or talking, and what comes back is usually a wall of text, a poor way to compare three products or edit and approve a detailed blueprint.

Today, we're releasing A2UI 1.0, the first stable version of our open protocol for generative UI. It lets AI agents answer with interactive screens, such as a form to confirm or a chart. Developers can use it now with open-source renderer SDKs for the web, Android, and iOS and agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. Companies such as Atlassian, Alation, Bloomberg, and ByteDance are already building with it.

It has been revealed that with A2UI, the agent describes what to show, and every app draws the UI with its own native components. The application receives A2UI messages and each app renders the content securely and at native speed. People get the same low latency, high trust, and complete native fidelity whether they reach a manufacturer's agent in its own app or in a third-party AI assistant that hosts MCP apps, such as Gemini or Claude.

Sources indicate that you wake up sick. Getting through the morning takes six apps: book a video visit, move your meetings, tell your team, turn on an out-of-office reply, ask your partner to do school pickup and order soup. Ask a text-only agent instead, and you get a numbered wall of text, then round after round of “which ones?”. A2UI won't handle your sick day, but it gives developers the framework to build an agent that can. That agent could answer with one view of all six apps. Changing your blueprint is a couple of taps instead of another round of messages, and nothing is sent until you confirm.

#11237. Your AI Pipeline Works. But Can You Trust It?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2972 w)

Your AI Pipeline Works. But Can You Trust It?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2972 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • It has been revealed that AI is becoming a part of almost everything we do in technology today.
  • Industry observers note that and naturally, when we talk about building AI systems, most of the conversation revolves around model accuracy, performance, and deployment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

It has been revealed that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

It has been revealed that AI is becoming a part of almost everything we do in technology today. Whether it's detecting fraudulent transactions, assessing credit risk, forecasting demand, or personalizing customer experiences, organizations are increasingly relying on AI to make faster and smarter decisions.

Industry observers note that and naturally, when we talk about building AI systems, most of the conversation revolves around model accuracy, performance, and deployment. We spend considerable time making sure our models are trained well, our pipelines run efficiently, and our systems can handle production workloads.

But here's something we don't always pay enough attention to: Can we actually trust the data feeding these models?

Sources indicate that after all, even the most sophisticated AI model can produce misleading results if the underlying data is incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrectly interpreted. What's interesting is that these problems don't always show up as technical failures. Sometimes, everything appears to be working perfectly fine.

Imagine a financial institution that has recently deployed an AI-powered loan risk assessment system. The team has spent months preparing the data, training the model, testing its performance, and finally moving it into production.

Recent findings suggest that the deployment goes smoothly. Data pipelines are running on schedule, predictions are being generated, and all the monitoring dashboards are green.

Sources indicate that A few weeks later, however, the business team notices something unusual. The model has started classifying more customers as high risk than expected.

The data science team checks the model configuration. Nothing has changed. The engineering team reviews the pipelines. All jobs have completed successfully. Even the infrastructure looks healthy.

Recent findings suggest that it turns out that an upstream source system changed the definition of a customer income field from annual gross income to annual net income. The field name remained the same, the data type was still numeric, and none of the existing technical validations detected the change.

The pipeline continued running as expected, but the model was now receiving information with a different business meaning.

This brings us to an important point: Just because an AI pipeline runs successfully doesn't necessarily mean we can trust its output.

Sources indicate that building reliable AI systems requires us to look beyond the model itself. We need to understand where the data originates, how it changes as it moves through different systems, whether it meets quality expectations, and who is responsible when something goes wrong.

In this article, we'll explore three important elements of trustworthy AI pipelines (data quality, data lineage, and accountability) and look at how engineering teams can incorporate them into their existing workflows without making the process unnecessarily complicated.

In a recent development, most modern data pipelines come with some form of operational monitoring. Engineering teams track job completion, execution time, system availability, and processing failures.

These metrics are crucial because they help us understand whether our systems are functioning as expected.

Operational monitoring primarily tells us whether a pipeline executed successfully. It doesn't necessarily tell us whether the data being processed is accurate, consistent, or suitable for the model consuming it.

Suppose we're building a loan risk model that uses a customer's debt-to-income ratio as one of its input features.

The calculation is straightforward:.

Debt-to-income ratio = Monthly debt payments / Monthly income.

Now imagine that an upstream system starts supplying annual income instead of monthly income.

In a recent development, the calculation still executes successfully. The values are numeric, the transformation doesn't throw an error, and the model continues generating predictions.

However, the resulting debt-to-income ratio is incorrect because the numerator and denominator represent different time periods.

This is where traditional monitoring falls short.

To build trustworthy AI pipelines, we need to look at different dimensions of system health.

These approaches complement each other.

A pipeline can be operationally healthy while processing unreliable data. Similarly, a model can continue producing predictions even when the meaning of an important input field has changed.

For engineering teams, the objective should be to identify these problems as early as possible, ideally before they reach downstream models.

We've all heard the phrase "garbage in, garbage out.".

And despite all the progress we've made in artificial intelligence, this principle hasn't changed.

AI models may be capable of processing enormous volumes of data and identifying complex patterns, but they cannot automatically guarantee that the information they're receiving is correct.

This is where data quality becomes important.

Data quality refers to how well information meets the requirements of its intended use. In AI pipelines, it helps us determine whether incoming data is sufficiently reliable for model training, evaluation, or inference.

Let's look at four dimensions that are particularly relevant.

Imagine we're developing a loan risk model that relies on customer income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

What happens if 20% of the incoming records are missing income information?

Industry observers note that should we reject those records? Should we replace missing values using an approved statistical method? Or should we flag them for additional review?

There isn't one answer that works for every system.

The right approach depends on the model, the business requirements, and the potential consequences of the decision.

What matters is that missing information is handled deliberately.

For example, replacing missing income with zero may allow the pipeline to continue running, but it could significantly distort the model's predictions.

Validity checks whether values meet expected formats, ranges, and business rules.

Consider a customer record containing the following information:.

The credit utilization value immediately stands out.

Although credit utilization can exceed 100% in certain circumstances, a value of 450% may warrant investigation.

This highlights an vital distinction: Not every unusual value is incorrect, and not every technically valid value is meaningful.

A database may accept any numeric value, but the business may need additional rules to determine whether that value is appropriate for the model.

Engineering teams should distinguish between invalid records, unexpected observations, and legitimate exceptions.

This is one of the most common challenges in enterprise data environments.

Imagine two systems providing customer income information.

System A reports annual gross income.

System B reports monthly net income.

Both datasets contain a column called income.

If we combine these datasets without understanding their definitions, we risk introducing inconsistencies into downstream calculations.

According to recent reports, the data may look perfectly fine from a technical perspective. The problem is that the same field represents different business concepts.

This is why data definitions, units, and transformation rules are just as notable as schema validation.

Suppose a model predicts a customer's current financial risk using income information that was last updated 18 months ago.

The data might be accurate, complete, and consistent.

But is it current enough to support the decision?

Different AI applications have different freshness requirements.

A real-time fraud detection model may require near-real-time transaction information, while a long-term forecasting model may work with less frequently updated datasets.

The crucial thing is to define these expectations based on how the data will be used.

The good news is that improving data quality doesn't always require sophisticated enterprise tools.

A practical starting point is to define validation rules for the most important input fields.

For example, consider the following conceptual configuration:.

This is an illustrative data quality contract rather than executable configuration for a particular framework.

It defines basic expectations and specifies what should happen when the data fails validation.

Tools such as Great Expectations can help automate these checks. For smaller systems, custom SQL or Python validations may be sufficient.

However, technical validation alone isn't enough.

Remember our original example where the income field changed from gross to net income?

Both values could easily pass a rule requiring income to be greater than zero.

Detecting that kind of matter requires clear business definitions, communication with upstream systems, and appropriate change management.

In a recent development, in other words, data quality isn't just about checking values. It's also about understanding what those values represent.

Now let's assume our loan risk model generates an unexpectedly high risk score for a customer.

The model output is available, but we want to understand what contributed to the prediction.

We start investigating the input data.

The income information came from a customer application system. Outstanding debt came from another database. Both datasets went through several transformations before reaching the feature engineering pipeline.

The final features were then passed to the model.

At this point, a seemingly simple question becomes surprisingly difficult:.

Where exactly did the information used for this prediction come from?

This is where data lineage becomes valuable.

Data lineage describes how data originates, moves, and changes across different systems.

For AI pipelines, it helps us understand the journey from raw source data to the features used by a model.

A simplified flow might look like this:.

Source Systems → Data Transformation → Feature Engineering → Model Inference → Predictions.

Each stage introduces dependencies that can affect downstream results.

Data lineage can be captured at different levels of detail.

Dataset-level lineage shows relationships between datasets.

Loan Applications → Cleaned Applications → Model Features.

This helps us understand how datasets move through the overall architecture.

However, suppose the model's debt-to-income ratio suddenly changes.

Dataset-level lineage might tell us which datasets were involved, but it may not provide enough detail to identify the affected field.

That's where column-level lineage becomes useful.

debt_to_income_ratio = monthly_debt_payment / monthly_income.

Column-level lineage can show that the resulting feature depends on two upstream attributes.

If one of those attributes changes, engineers can trace the dependency and investigate the impact.

This is especially valuable in environments where multiple reports, applications, and AI models depend on shared data sources.

Large organizations may use dedicated metadata management and lineage platforms.

However, smaller teams can start by capturing essential metadata during pipeline execution.

OpenLineage provides an open standard for collecting and exchanging lineage metadata across supported systems.

For more detailed prediction-level investigations, teams may also need to retain feature snapshots or inference logs, subject to privacy and retention requirements.

It's key to understand that lineage doesn't automatically guarantee data accuracy.

A pipeline can be perfectly documented and still contain incorrect transformation logic.

But when something goes wrong, lineage gives engineering teams a clearer starting point for investigation.

Instead of searching across multiple systems and trying to reconstruct dependencies manually, they can identify where data originated and how it changed along the way.

Let's consider another situation.

An AI model starts producing unexpected results.

The data science team checks the model and finds no issues.

The data engineering team confirms that the pipelines are running successfully.

The source-system team verifies that data was delivered according to its interface.

Yet the problem remains unresolved.

Everyone has completed their individual checks, but nobody has identified who should coordinate the investigation.

This is where accountability becomes important.

According to recent reports, AI pipelines often involve multiple teams responsible for different stages of the data lifecycle. Without clearly defined ownership, even relatively simple issues can take longer to resolve.

A practical accountability framework should distinguish between three responsibilities.

Data owners are responsible for defining the business meaning and expected quality of critical information.

For example, someone needs to determine whether an income field represents gross income, net income, or another financial measure.

These definitions should be documented and communicated to downstream consumers.

Data engineering and platform teams typically manage data ingestion, transformations, validation mechanisms, and pipeline operations.

Their responsibilities may include implementing quality checks, monitoring failures, and assessing the technical impact of changes.

However, technical teams shouldn't be expected to make business-definition decisions without appropriate input.

Data science and ML engineering teams are responsible for evaluating model behavior, managing model versions, and assessing how changes in input data may affect predictions.

If a critical feature changes, the model team may need to determine whether additional testing, recalibration, or retraining is required.

Defining ownership is useful, but connecting it to an operational process is even more important.

Consider a critical data quality failure during feature generation.

A response process might look like this:.

The exact workflow will vary depending on the organization and the risk associated with the application.

The objective is to ensure that technical alerts lead to clear actions.

After all, an alert that nobody owns is just another notification waiting to be ignored.

So far, we've discussed why data quality, lineage, and accountability matter.

But how can we bring these concepts into everyday engineering practices?

Here are five controls that teams can introduce without redesigning their entire architecture.

Data contracts define expectations between data producers and consumers.

They can document schemas, field definitions, units, freshness requirements, and compatibility expectations.

For example, rather than specifying only that annual_income is numeric, a contract should clarify whether it represents gross or net income, the currency, and the applicable time period.

This reduces the risk of downstream systems misinterpreting technically valid information.

Quality gates validate critical data before it progresses through the pipeline.

These checks can be implemented during ingestion, transformation, feature generation, or inference.

For example, a feature engineering process calculating debt-to-income ratios should verify that debt and income values use compatible time periods.

Failure handling should reflect the severity of the problem. Some records may be quarantined, while more serious failures may require stopping the pipeline.

Pipeline execution should produce sufficient metadata to identify source datasets, transformations, and downstream outputs.

Where appropriate, teams should also capture model and feature versions associated with predictions.

This information supports impact analysis, debugging, and investigation when unexpected results occur.

AI systems evolve continuously.

Datasets change, transformation logic is updated, features are modified, and models are retrained.

Versioning helps engineering teams understand which components were active at a particular point in time.

Relevant evidence may include pipeline configurations, dataset snapshots, model versions, validation outcomes, and deployment records.

Retention should be designed around operational requirements, privacy considerations, and applicable policies rather than storing everything indefinitely.

Every critical data element or pipeline component should have an identified owner or responsible team.

More importantly, ownership should connect directly to incident management and change approval processes.

If a source definition changes, teams should know who evaluates the impact.

If a quality gate fails, the responsible team should receive the alert.

If model performance deteriorates, the investigation should have a clear escalation path.

These controls are most effective when they become part of normal development and deployment practices rather than separate administrative activities.

Implementing comprehensive governance across an entire data environment can be challenging, particularly for organizations with legacy systems and complex dependencies.

A more effective approach is to begin with one critical AI pipeline.

For example, a team operating a loan risk model could start by identifying the inputs that have the greatest influence on its predictions.

These might include income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

For each critical input, the team can document five things:.

Once these foundations are established, the team can implement automated checks and gradually extend the approach to additional datasets.

This incremental strategy also makes it easier to demonstrate the value of governance controls.

For instance, teams can track how promptly data-related incidents are detected, how long investigations take, and whether recurring complications are reduced.

The goal isn't to introduce governance for its own sake.

It's to improve the reliability, maintainability, and transparency of the systems developers are responsible for operating.

Explainable AI has become an key topic in machine learning.

Techniques such as feature importance analysis and SHAP can help teams understand which inputs influence model predictions.

However, explainability and data trustworthiness address different problems.

Suppose a model explanation identifies debt-to-income ratio as a major contributor to a customer's high-risk classification.

That explanation may accurately describe the model's behavior.

But if the debt-to-income ratio was calculated using an incorrectly defined income field, the explanation alone may not reveal the underlying data matter.

This highlights the importance of evaluating AI systems across multiple dimensions.

Model explainability helps us understand how predictions are generated.

Data quality helps establish whether inputs satisfy defined expectations.

Data lineage provides visibility into where information originated and how it was transformed.

Accountability ensures that identified problems can be investigated and addressed.

These capabilities are complementary rather than interchangeable.

None independently guarantees that an AI system is accurate, fair, secure, or compliant. Together, however, they provide a stronger foundation for evaluating and improving system reliability.

As AI systems become more integrated into business processes, engineering teams face increasing expectations around reliability, transparency, and accountability.

Model accuracy and operational performance remain essential, but they represent only part of the overall picture.

In a recent development, A pipeline can execute successfully while processing inconsistent information. A model can generate predictions using features whose definitions have changed. And an explanation can describe a model's behavior without identifying problems in the underlying data.

Building trustworthy AI therefore requires attention to the entire data lifecycle.

Data quality controls help detect unreliable inputs. Lineage provides visibility into how information moves through systems. Clear ownership ensures that issues can be investigated and resolved.

Importantly, these practices don't need to begin with large-scale governance programs or expensive technology investments.

Engineering teams can start with a single critical pipeline, identify its most important data elements, establish quality expectations, and introduce basic traceability and accountability mechanisms.

Over time, these practices can become part of standard development and deployment workflows.

The real measure of a trustworthy AI pipeline isn't simply whether it produces a prediction. It's whether the organization can understand, validate, and take responsibility for the information behind that prediction.

After all, a green dashboard is reassuring. But it shouldn't be the only evidence that an AI system is working as intended.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The DC Council’s Committee on Human Services will mark up and vote on B26-0656 at 3 p.m. on Nov. 18, the bill’s first movement since its only hearing on May 4. The bill would legalize online casinos and ban dual-currency sweepstakes casinos, and few legislative days remain this year.

The District’s online casino bill is moving again, with little time to spare.

The calendar is tight. Council Period 26 closes at 11:59 a.m. on Jan. 2, 2027. Any permanent bill that has not received final reading by the Dec. 15 legislative meeting lapses at the end of the period and must start over in Council Period 27.

The committee’s makeup may help. Its members include the bill’s sponsor, Wendell Felder, along with Christina Henderson and Zachary Parker. The committee also oversees the Office of Lottery and Gaming, which would regulate the new market.

Recent findings suggest that felder remarked in his introduction letter that the bill is meant to authorize, regulate and tax internet gaming in the District. If it passes, DC would join the small group of jurisdictions with legal online casinos.

The bill would also ban dual-currency sweepstakes casinos, and it comes with enforcement tools. The Office of Lottery and Gaming could send cease-and-desist letters. The DC Attorney General could go to court and seize profits.

Recent findings suggest that launch would not be immediate. The introduced bill says internet gaming cannot start until the District’s chief financial officer certifies that the regulatory system is ready.

The licensing terms favor operators already in the District. Suppliers would pay $50,000 to apply and $25,000 to renew. There is no cap on operator licenses, and each operator could run up to two skins.

In a recent development, holders of a DC sports wagering operator license or another gaming license would get expedited review. The Office of Lottery and Gaming could rely on earlier background checks. BetMGM, Caesars, DraftKings, Fanatics and FanDuel all offer online sports betting in DC.

Industry support was visible at the May hearing. Caesars, DraftKings and BetMGM all backed the bill. Thomas R. Burnside, executive director of the Office of Lottery and Gaming, testified and attached proposed changes to the bill.

October was a big month for DC Lottery players! Over $9 million in total prizes were won across DC Lottery games this October. From scratch-off tickets to DC 5 and iLottery games, players had plenty of exciting wins to celebrate.

In a recent development, the regulator also flagged a trade-off for its own business. Its director acknowledged that online casinos could eat into iLottery sales. He mentioned online casino revenue would offset any losses.

In a recent development, any amendments adopted at markup will show whether Burnside’s proposed changes made it into the committee version. Once the committee has voted on Nov. 18, the full Council’s remaining legislative meetings fall on Dec. 1 and Dec. 15.

#11233. CSS-Tricks, Version 20
