#11208. Tech Report: Coding Agent Horror Stories: The CVE That Did Not Exist

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2981 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Docker ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Coding Agent Horror Stories: The CVE That Did Not Exist

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2981 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is Part 6 of our AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series, where we look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents and at how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line.
  • Every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched.
  • In a recent development, this story is the opposite.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Part 6 of our AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series, where we look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents and at how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line.

Every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched. We have seen agents wander into home directories, drop production databases, leak credentials, and run shell commands that did something very different from what the developer expected. In each case, the damage came from the agent having more reach than it needed.

In a recent development, this story is the opposite. The agent in this one reached nothing at all, because it was deliberately built so that it could not. And yet, on the night in question, it was still the most dangerous thing in the pipeline.

This story was shared by Pratik Kumar Singh as part of our Agent Hall of Shame contest on social media.

It has been revealed that A platform engineer built a code review bot for his team. The idea was simple and useful. Every time someone pushes code, the bot reads what changed and writes a review into the pipeline, the same kind of first pass a human teammate would give before a person looks at the change.

He named the bot BuaJi. In India, your bua is your father’s sister, and in many families she is the relative who inspects everything you do and always manages to find something wrong with it. For a code reviewer, it is a fitting name.

Sources indicate that what made BuaJi interesting was how carefully it was set up. The bot runs on local models through Ollama, which means the model weights sit on the engineer’s own hardware and no request ever goes out to an AI vendor. It also runs as a job in his CI pipeline, triggered whenever someone pushes code. Taken together, this makes the whole setup self-hosted. The code it reads is tech giant source code, and with this design none of it ever leaves the building. That was a deliberate choice, because his company takes that seriously.

He also gave BuaJi one firm rule: it can read, and it can comment, and that is all. It cannot run terraform apply, which is the command that creates or changes real cloud infrastructure. It cannot run kubectl apply, which changes what is actually running in the Kubernetes cluster. And it cannot push a commit, so it has no way to change the code itself. Those are the commands that change the real world, and BuaJi was given none of them. On paper, this is exactly how you would want an AI reviewer to be built.

Industry observers note that the version of BuaJi in the companion repo is a deliberately minimal reviewer. It checks Go files against a handful of style rules. The report below is the kind of free-form finding any reviewer produces once you let it comment in prose rather than pass/fail, which is exactly the direction these bots get pushed in practice.

His product ships with a bundled copy of PostgreSQL. Older PostgreSQL releases have published vulnerabilities with CVE numbers attached, and upgrading to a newer patch release is how you make those known concerns go away. So he bumped the version.

This is about as boring and as responsible as a code change gets. It touches a few lines, it changes a version number, and its only purpose is to close security holes that are already public. Any reviewer, human or machine, should look at it and approve it in a few seconds. There is nothing in that diff to be suspicious about, and that is precisely why what happened next matters.

It has been revealed that buaJi responded with roughly fifteen hundred words rejecting the change. For context, a normal review comment is a sentence or two.

Recent findings suggest that the report described the version bump as an “architectural takeover,” a structural change smuggled into the codebase under the cover of routine maintenance. It claimed that the new PostgreSQL build was a vehicle for sending internal data to a third-party manufacturer, and it named that company outright. The company does not exist.

It has been revealed that it went further. It referred to specific Kubernetes resources by name, as though it had inspected the cluster and found them. Those resources had never existed, and BuaJi had no access to the cluster that would have let it look. It then wrote Go scripts to “isolate the infected PostgreSQL nodes,” even though nothing was infected. Finally, it told the engineer to revoke all IAM access immediately, an action that would lock out every person in the organization, including the people who would be needed to fix any real problem.

Holding the whole argument together was a CVE number that has never been issued by anyone. Of everything in the report, this is the detail worth pausing on. A CVE identifier is one of the easiest things in security to verify, since you can look it up in a public registry in a few seconds. The bot invented a fact in the one place where invented facts are easiest to catch.

In a recent development, and yet the report looked completely convincing. The Markdown was clean and well structured. The YAML it proposed would have parsed without errors. The tone was urgent and confident, the way a senior security engineer writes when they have found something serious and need you to act before it gets worse. The engineer spent about two minutes reading the CI logs, realized that none of it was real, and went back to what he was doing.

Caption: Comic illustrating how a confident, well-formatted security report from an AI reviewer can be entirely fabricated, and what happens when somebody acts on it.

It has been revealed that it is vital to say clearly that the read-only rule did its job. BuaJi could not carry out any of its own recommendations, and it never had any access to the cluster. Because of that, the entire episode cost the engineer two minutes of his evening and nothing more.

According to recent reports, the trouble is that the rule only controlled what BuaJi could do. Nobody had thought about what BuaJi could say. A read-only agent is still allowed to tell people what to do, and the person reading its output usually has exactly the access that the agent was denied. BuaJi could not run the scripts it wrote, but it could write them down and hand them to someone who could.

It has been revealed that this engineer caught the problem because he knows his own cluster well. He knew those Kubernetes resources were not real and that nothing had been compromised. Now imagine a newer engineer on call at two in the morning, half awake, looking at a long and alarming security report in the pipeline. Revoking all IAM access in production in the middle of the night is an outage all by itself. Running an unreviewed Go script against your database nodes could be considerably worse. In both scenarios, BuaJi would not have done anything. A person would have done all of it, in good faith, because the report told them to.

What makes this so hard to defend against is that no permission model would have flagged it, because no permission was ever violated. The agent stayed within its boundary. The engineer had every right to run those commands on his own systems. The only thing in the entire chain that was false was the content of the report.

Here’s the honest part: a sandbox is not a fact-checker. No microVM boundary will ever make a review comment accurate. What a boundary changes is what that fabricated output can do once it exists.

Remember where BuaJi’s read-only rule actually lived, in a convention. One engineer configured it in his own pipeline and has to keep remembering to leave it in place. Rules like that hold until someone is in a hurry, or a latest teammate copies the config and drops a section they did not understand, or a small exception made for a good reason quietly becomes permanent. None of this needs bad intent; it is just how real teams work.

Docker Sandboxes run agents inside isolated microVMs each with its own kernel, its own filesystem, and a network that denies everything by default. An agent inside one can invent anything it likes, but the invention has nowhere to go: no credentials to use, no cluster to reach, no commit to push, unless someone allowed that access ahead of time. The read-only rule stops being something a person remembers and becomes a property of the environment. And when a report claims it inspected your cluster, the policy log is your proof it never could have.

It has been revealed that that protects you from the agent. It does nothing for the human who reads the output, and no sandbox ever will. For that half, treat agent review output the way you already treat agent input, untrusted until something checks it: label it so it doesn’t carry a colleague’s weight, verify any CVE numbers, and never run agent-written remediation until a person has read and understood it.

This is the same pattern as the sandbox escapes Pillar published in July. The boundary itself was never broken; a file was written inside the sandbox, and a tool outside later trusted it. An agent’s output is always an input to whatever reads it next and somewhere downstream, something trusts what it receives. Very often, that something is a person.

Let’s move BuaJi into a Docker Sandbox, one step at a time. By the end, the read-only rule is enforced by the environment, not by memory.

Industry observers note that buaJi is a small Python script, buaji.py. Its GitLab job installs Ollama on a GPU runner, starts ollama serve, loads the model named in LLM, and runs the script.

The script reads review rules from rules.md and finds the changed files with git diff HEAD^ HEAD --name-only. It sends each file and rule to Ollama at http://localhost:11434 and prints the answers to the CI log.

The catch is that everything shares one container: the model, the script, the checkout and every CI variable, including CI_JOB_TOKEN. BuaJi is read-only only because the script happens not to write anything.

Recent findings suggest that we split the job in two. The model stays on the runner next to the GPU. BuaJi moves into a microVM that can read the code, talk to the model, and nothing else.

One open path to the model, everything else blocked, and a CVE check on the way out.

Inside a sandbox, localhost is the sandbox itself. So we read the Ollama address from an environment variable and keep the old value as the default:.

In a recent development, outside a sandbox, nothing changes. Inside one, we point OLLAMA_URL at the runner.

Today the job runs apt-get and pip3 install on every run, which needs internet access each time.

Instead, build a small image once with everything BuaJi needs, so the sandbox never downloads anything:.

Push it to your registry and store its name in a CI variable called BUAJI_TEMPLATE.

According to recent reports, ollama stays on the runner with the GPU. Install it once on the runner instead of running curl | sh in every pipeline.

In a recent development, the model never enters the sandbox. BuaJi reaches it through one port, opened in Step 5.

This step decides what BuaJi can see and change.

It has been revealed that notice what is missing: no GitLab token, no kubeconfig, no cloud credentials. Even if BuaJi tried kubectl or terraform, it would have nothing to connect with.

In a recent development, sandboxes block all outgoing traffic by default. We open one path, for this sandbox only. (This assumes the runner’s default policy is deny-all; on a balanced or open default, set the default to deny-all first.).

The allow target (localhost:11434) and the address BuaJi dials (host.docker.internal:11434) are two names for the same runner port,  the first from the runner’s point of view, the second from inside the microVM. Kubernetes, your cloud APIs, and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

Industry observers note that kubernetes, your cloud APIs and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

BuaJi runs as before, just in a fresh place with only two variables:.

The review is now just text. BuaJi cannot post it, act on it, or change what happens to it next.

According to recent reports, this check would have caught the fake report in seconds. It runs on the runner, so BuaJi cannot skip it.

It looks up every CVE ID in the NVD database and fails the job if any of them do not exist:.

In a recent development, because the job is allow_failure: true, GitLab marks it “passed with warnings.” The pipeline keeps moving, but nobody mistakes the report for a trusted one. This degrades the signal, it does not block the human. The warning is a nudge, not a guardrail ~ a tired on-call engineer can still scroll past it..

It won’t catch every made-up detail, like a fake Kubernetes resource name. But it catches the one that holds most fake reports together.

Finally, review the policy log and remove the sandbox:.

The log reveals every host BuaJi tried to reach. On a deny-all runner, a healthy run shows only the model on port 11434. Anything else is a signal worth looking at.

Removing the sandbox means every pipeline starts clean.

Put together, the buaji job in .gitlab-ci.yml looks like this:.

The runner needs a GPU and KVM, which usually means self-hosted. GIT_DEPTH: "2" gives buaji.py the two commits it compares. The cleanup sits in after_script, so it runs even when the job fails.

Recent findings suggest that before, the read-only rule lived in the script. Now it lives in the environment: a read-only checkout, one network path, no credentials, and only checked text coming out.

Sources indicate that what hasn’t changed is the human reading the output. The sandbox stops BuaJi from running its scripts. Only the CVE check and a careful reader stop someone else from running them.

Recent findings suggest that treat an agent’s security finding as a hypothesis, not a conclusion. A report from an AI reviewer is a claim with good formatting. When a human reviewer flags a security issue, there is an implied step where they checked their reasoning. With an agent, that step has not happened, so you have to do it yourself.

Recent findings suggest that verify every CVE number before acting on it. This is the cheapest check in the whole process and it catches the single most convincing part of a fabricated report. Automate it, as in Step 7, so it runs on every review without anyone having to remember.

Never run agent-written remediation without reviewing it first. Scripts and commands supplied by an agent are the point where a false finding turns into a real incident. Read them with the same care you would give an unknown script from the internet.

Make read-only a property of the environment, not a habit. A restriction you enforce by hand in a pipeline config is always one rushed change away from disappearing. Mount the code read-only, pass in no credentials, and open only the network paths the agent needs, as in Steps 4 to 6.

Sources indicate that clearly label agent review output as agent output. When a bot’s review looks identical to one from a senior engineer, it borrows authority it has not earned. A clear label helps readers apply the right level of skepticism.

Industry observers note that keep an eye on your signal-to-noise ratio. The curl story is the warning here. A review channel that fills up with noise eventually stops being read, and a review channel nobody reads is worse than having none, because people still assume it is protecting them.

The engineer who built BuaJi was right that the read-only rule protected him, and it genuinely did. BuaJi could not touch the cluster, could not revoke anyone’s access, and could not run a single line of the code it had so carefully written. What the rule could not do was stop BuaJi from asking somebody else to run it.

In a recent development, every other story in this series has been about an agent reaching too far. This one never reached at all. It stayed inside its boundary, did exactly what it was permitted to do, and still produced a document that would have caused a real outage if the person reading it had been a little more tired, or a little less familiar with their own cluster.

As we give agents more responsibility in our pipelines, containing what they can do is only half the job. A sandbox handles that half. The other half is deciding how much we trust what they tell us, and that part is still up to us.

Ajeet Singh Raina, Developer Advocate at Docker, writes and speaks on containers, Docker Compose & AI, helping devs build confidently.

Where should your code live in a Docker Sandbox?

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on.
  • You might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results.
  • In a recent development, sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on. You can share a checkout from your host, give it a separate working directory for a task, or keep the repository entirely inside the sandbox. Each arrangement changes how you, the human, participate in the work.

You might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results. sbx supports both. The way you organize the checkout can change as you ask the agent to take on more of the work.

In a recent development, sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use. Run sbx run from your project directory, and it mounts that directory at the same absolute path inside the sandbox:.

Open a file in your local editor while the agent works on it, and you’ll see changes as they happen. Git works from either side, so you choose whether you want to let the agent make commits or you do it yourself. Development servers on your host can pick up the edits through hot reload, using the runtime and dependencies installed on your host.

According to recent reports, this fits close collaboration on one task. The coordination cost comes from sharing that working tree: switching branches changes the files the agent sees, and your edits become part of its ongoing work. If you want to switch to something unrelated while the agent continues, you’ll need another checkout.

NOTE: Dependencies written into the shared checkout are shared too. Packages with native binaries, such as esbuild, may work in the Linux sandbox and fail on a macOS or Windows host. Reinstalling on the host can reverse the problem. Keep separate dependency installations, or run the app consistently in one environment.

It has been revealed that git worktrees give each task a directory and branch. You can mount each worktree in its own sandbox, while your original checkout remains available for other work. The agent’s edits appear in the worktree. You can inspect either with your local editor and development tools. Each task also gets its own running environment, with tools to prepare and a sandbox and worktree to clean up afterward.

In a recent development, there is a Git limitation with mounting only a linked worktree. Its .git file points to metadata outside the mount, which the agent can’t reach. It can edit files, but checking status, branching, and committing have to happen on the host. The future of software development still needs you to run git status.

It has been revealed that sbx supports a clone mode that gives the agent a separate checkout with Git available inside the sandbox. You keep your local project, but sbx mounts the host source as read-only and creates an independent clone for the agent. Its branch changes and dependency installations stay in its checkout.

Bringing the result back becomes a handoff. While the sandbox is running, you can fetch committed branches through the Git remote sbx adds on your host. Or the agent can push to the repository’s remote and you can retrieve the branch through your usual Git workflow. Your local editor and development server see the changes after you bring them into your checkout.

Industry observers note that A mountless sandbox has no host workspace directory attached. Clone the repository inside it, and the sandbox holds the checkout and its development environment. Your host copy of the project shares no connection with the sandbox checkout.

In a recent development, this workflow resembles working on a remote development machine. Agents connect to the project environment, and you can open a shell with sbx exec or connect an editor to the sandbox over SSH. Changes and dependency installations stay separate from your host. To bring work back, you push a branch to the Git remote.

Industry observers note that one sandbox per project can be a useful mental model here. The project and its tools persist across agent sessions and sandbox restarts. An agent can create worktrees per feature it’s working on, push branches, and create pull requests for review. Starting another task doesn’t require you to prepare another host worktree and sandbox, and the agent has Git access in each working directory. Clone mode supports this internal-worktree approach too.

In a recent development, those tasks share tools and services, so running servers or changing the environment still needs coordination. Separate sandboxes are useful when tasks need independent environments as well as separate files. Branches alone don’t isolate simultaneous edits in one working directory.

That independence adds some distance when you want to try the result. Your usual local editor isn’t looking at these files, and a development server running inside the sandbox needs a published port to reach it from your browser.

For a web app preview, ask the agent:.

Start the development server on port 8080, bound to 0.0.0.0.

Then publish the port from another terminal on the host:.

Open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. It’s possible to work interactively this way, but there’s more ceremony than opening a project already on your filesystem.

An environment file can make setup repeatable, selecting tools and cloning the repository at creation with something like the community github-clone kit. Recreating the sandbox then gives you a fresh environment. Push or copy out work you want to retain first: removing a sandbox deletes files held only there.

Industry observers note that an API change might need a corresponding frontend change, or another repository might provide useful reference material. You can mount several directories into one sandbox, with read-only access for reference repositories. Local editing and previews remain available, but each writable checkout needs branch and change coordination. Task-specific checkouts also leave directories to clean up afterward.

Sources indicate that A workspace manager such as jganoff/wsp can assemble selected repositories for a task. Mounting that workspace gives the agent the projects it needs together. These are standard clones with their own Git metadata, so the agent retains Git access, unlike a mounted linked worktree.

In a recent development, the same scope fits inside a mountless sandbox: clone the repositories needed there and keep the whole workspace in the sandbox. The number of repositories and where their files live are separate choices.

The checkout’s location, the sandbox’s lifetime, and the repositories it contains are choices you can combine. You can keep a project sandbox around for many tasks, or mount a workspace assembled for one job. What suits you may change when you want to work more closely with the agent, or give it more room to manage the work itself.

The Git workflows documentation covers the mechanics of direct mounts, clone mode, and host worktrees.

Docker publishes fixed images for both Java4Shell and the NGINX HTTP/2 in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog.

Run AI workloads on any cloud, store on Hugging Face: zero-egress storage with SkyPilot

📅 07 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud.
  • It has been revealed that together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs.
  • SkyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud. The GPUs you can get, whether for development, training, or serving, increasingly sit on a different cloud than your data. The moment those two come apart, you pay a cross-cloud transfer tax just to read your own data onto your own GPUs.

It has been revealed that together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs. Mount a Hugging Face Bucket or any Hub repo into a SkyPilot job with one hf:// URL and the HF_TOKEN you already have, then launch it wherever capacity is. Hugging Face charges no egress, so reading your data onto those GPUs costs nothing, on any cloud.

SkyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path. Hugging Face Storage now joins that list as store: hf, reached through the hf:// scheme:.

It has been revealed that that one hf:// scheme covers the whole lifecycle: read the model and dataset from their repos, write checkpoints to a Bucket while you train, publish the finished model back to a repo, and pull it onto inference servers when you serve. Most teams already keep their models and datasets on the Hub, so there is no migration step and no fresh storage account to create.

Industry observers note that MOUNT uses Hugging Face's hf-mount FUSE backend, so a bucket or repo highlights up as a local path next to SkyPilot's other FUSE mounts (gcsfuse, blobfuse2, rclone, goofys). The fetching happens at the filesystem layer: when your code concerns a read(), the driver pulls just those bytes from the Xet backend, so only the data you actually touch crosses the network, and hf-mount keeps an on-disk cache so repeat reads stay local. That on-disk cache is the behavior SkyPilot gives its other backends under MOUNT_CACHED, where a plain MOUNT instead streams every read from the bucket with nothing kept locally. For the hf store, MOUNT and MOUNT_CACHED behave the same, so either mode keeps the cache.

Because reads are lazy, a process can start working through a large file before the whole file has downloaded, instead of blocking on a full copy first. That keeps the GPU busy almost immediately, training on data as it streams in rather than sitting idle (and billing) while a dataset or checkpoint copies down. It pays off most on the first epoch, when nothing is cached yet. COPY takes the other route and downloads through huggingface_hub up front, with no special requirements.

Authentication is the token you already have. Set HF_TOKEN in your environment and hand it to a run with --secret HF_TOKEN; SkyPilot uses it for the mount on whatever cloud the job lands. One token works whether the job lands on AWS, GCP, Azure, Nebius, Lambda, or your own Kubernetes cluster, so there are no per-cloud bucket keys to juggle.

Sources indicate that GPU capacity rarely comes from one place anymore. To get enough H100s and H200s, teams hold reserved and committed capacity across several vendors at once (a block on a hyperscaler, a cluster on a neocloud, maybe an on-prem rack) and run wherever they have allocation. SkyPilot is built for this: one job spec, scheduled across 20+ clouds, Kubernetes, and on-prem, landing on whichever reserved cluster is free.

Sources indicate that object storage has been the catch. Object stores are regional and per-cloud, so feeding a GPU or an inference server that sits in a different vendor's data center means either keeping a copy of your data in every vendor's bucket or paying to pull it across. Most clouds charge egress (around $0.09/GB out of AWS) the moment data leaves their network, and often between regions inside one cloud. Pulling a base model onto every inference node, or iterating a dataset for several epochs from a cluster on another cloud, adds a hefty bill on top of GPUs you have already reserved. Teams end up pinning each run to whichever vendor holds the data and leaving the rest of their capacity idle.

Recent findings suggest that hugging Face Storage takes that cost off the table where it bites: the read side. With no egress or CDN fees and storage at $12-18/TB/month (versus AWS S3 at roughly $23/TB plus egress), the same bucket is reachable from every one of those clusters, and reading from it is free no matter where the GPUs run. Writing back still costs your compute cloud's usual egress, the same as it would to any off-cloud store, but for most AI work the reads dominate: a dataset streamed over many epochs, or model weights pulled onto every fresh training or inference node. So you stop pinning each run to whichever vendor holds a copy of the data.

Sources indicate that to collect some benchmark numbers, we ran a small fine-tune: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B on the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset with TRL's SFTTrainer, mounting the model read-only from its Hub repo and writing every checkpoint to a Hugging Face Bucket. The same SkyPilot YAML ran on AWS, GCP, and Lambda, changing only --infra. SkyPilot placed each job wherever GPUs were free, and all three read and wrote the same bucket.

Per cloud, checkpoints wrote to the bucket at:.

According to recent reports, hugging Face Buckets are built on Xet, which uses content-defined chunking to split files into ~64 KB chunks and store each unique chunk once. Because the boundaries follow the content, an edit changes only the chunks it touches and the rest are recognized as already stored. This pays off in a few places:.

How much you save depends on how much your artifacts overlap, but the deduplication is automatic: you write a checkpoint as usual, and only the latest chunks leave the machine.

In a recent development, add an hf:// mount to any SkyPilot task and launch. MOUNT needs a base image with glibc 2.34+ and /dev/fuse.

In a recent development, the initial store: hf support started as a contribution from Nikhil Jha. The Hugging Face team carried it forward and upstreamed the hf-mount FUSE fixes that let it mount in unprivileged containers, the default on many Kubernetes clusters. The SkyPilot team wired it into the storage backend. The whole path is open source: SkyPilot, Hugging Face's hf-mount, and the huggingface_hub client.

Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I help lead Google's agent skills program, at the moment with 175 agent skills that supplement community collections like go-skills.
  • Sources indicate that in Go, every slice or index operation that can panic at runtime compiles down to an explicit bounds-check trap in machine code, after the compiler's optimizer strips out the checks it can already rule out.
  • In this post, I'll walk through how the Gemini and Z3 pipeline works, why go test -fuzz missed two of those crashes (and the one-line change that fixes it), and where this approach fits in a day-to-day Go workflow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I help lead Google's agent skills program, at the moment with 175 agent skills that supplement community collections like go-skills. To keep that many skill files consistent, I wrote skill-lint, a standalone Go CLI that checks SKILL.md files and applies LLM-generated line edits before they ship. Even with skill-lint's own unit and fuzz test suite, a small slice or line-number mistake inside its Markdown parsers or edit applier can sit dormant until an unusual file or edit range triggers a runtime panic in the linter.

Sources indicate that in Go, every slice or index operation that can panic at runtime compiles down to an explicit bounds-check trap in machine code, after the compiler's optimizer strips out the checks it can already rule out. To hunt for crashes, I compiled key functions from my code to see which panic traps survived optimization, and Gemini 4 Argon translated the path to each trap into rules for the Z3 constraint solver. An LLM-written solver model isn't a sound proof system, but it gives the agent an independent way to reason about control flow and synthesize concrete Go reproducers, and every crash it finds is real because go test runs the offending bytes directly. That workflow caught all three bugs I planted in test parsers and turned up three latent bugs in skill-lint.

In this post, I'll walk through how the Gemini and Z3 pipeline works, why go test -fuzz missed two of those crashes (and the one-line change that fixes it), and where this approach fits in a day-to-day Go workflow.

According to recent reports, A recent post from Anthropic revealed how formal verification catches latent bugs in C and C++ by having frontier AI models write machine-checked Rocq proofs across OSS-Fuzz libraries. Instead of sampling random inputs like a fuzzer, a formal tool works backward from each failure condition to solve for the exact input that triggers it. Full theorem proving is still too heavy for most day-to-day Go projects, so I wanted to see how much of that bug-hunting power an agent can get from an LLM and a constraint solver in about a minute per function.

Industry observers note that in C and C++, reading or writing past the end of a buffer corrupts memory. Go catches out-of-bounds access at runtime instead, compiling every slice or index operation it can't prove safe into an explicit branch to runtime.panicBounds that panics, crashing the process unless recovered.

Sources indicate that before generating machine code, Go's SSA prove pass already eliminates most of those checks by tracking slice lengths and loop variables. That optimization pass leaves behind only the runtime.panicBounds traps the compiler couldn't rule out on its own, giving the solver a short list of candidate crash sites to target.

I compiled each target with GOOS=linux GOARCH=riscv64 go build -gcflags="-S -d=ssa/check_bce/debug=1" (-S prints the assembly listing and ssa/check_bce/debug=1 logs every surviving bounds check) and passed both the Go source and the disassembly to the model. Looking at Go source alone, you can't see which bounds checks the compiler already removed or where a register gets truncated to 8 bits; in the disassembly, both show up. I targeted RISC-V because it's the instruction set Anthropic's post targets for its Rocq proofs, and Go cross-compiles to it out of the box.

According to recent reports, from there, Argon read the Go source and disassembly and returned a Z3 script modeling the path to each surviving trap, along with a patched function whenever it flagged a bug. Z3 then checked whether those constraints could be satisfied, and whenever it found a crashing input, go test replayed those bytes against the real function. Using an LLM saved me from translating assembly into solver constraints by hand. Argon's translation dominated the runtime, at about a minute per function, while Z3 itself finished in milliseconds.

#11201. The Ecosystem is the Answer: Docker, the Blueprint Alliance, and the Importance of Collaboration in the Agentic Era

📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1291 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Docker ↗ Open Full Page

The Ecosystem is the Answer: Docker, the Blueprint Alliance, and the Importance of Collaboration in the Agentic Era

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, the average global Fortune 500 enterprise had fewer than 15 AI agents in use.
  • Today, most security leaders face an agentic Sophie’s choice: allow AI adoption without the right controls and hope for the best, or block it and become the obstacle to a priority the business has already set (while adoption continues in the shadows, anyway).
  • But there is a third option, one in which organizations fully tap into the transformative power of agentic agents without having to live in fear of a catastrophic security failure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, the average global Fortune 500 enterprise had fewer than 15 AI agents in use. Gartner expects that number to explode to more than 150,000 by 2028. Only 13 percent of organizations think they have the right governance for today, and AI is evolving and moving faster than any other technology paradigm in our history.

Today, most security leaders face an agentic Sophie’s choice: allow AI adoption without the right controls and hope for the best, or block it and become the obstacle to a priority the business has already set (while adoption continues in the shadows, anyway).

But there is a third option, one in which organizations fully tap into the transformative power of agentic agents without having to live in fear of a catastrophic security failure. The good news is history has already shown how to get there.

According to recent reports, historically, technology adoption has followed a reliable pattern. A capability spreads, each vendor and team builds its own approach, the inconsistency becomes expensive and ineffective, leading the industry to agree to a shared baseline. Adoption then accelerates.

It has been revealed that take the credit card industry, for example. The substantial credit brands each ran their own security programs, and merchants had to satisfy every one. This was, of course, cumbersome for the vendors, but also for the customers, too. Every time a customer wanted to adopt a new technology, they had to manually build out security and adoption plans, adding significant adoption and procurement delays.

Rather than continue on their own, the credit card companies came together to create PCI DSS 1.0 in December 2004 and formed the PCI Security Standards Council in 2006. Buyers now had one thing to ask for, and auditors had one thing to check. Collaboration overcame complexity, and everyone benefited.

Security-minded technologists can find another example closer to home in the Center for Internet Security (CIS). In the early days of the internet, cybersecurity was a veritable wild west. Enter the CIS, which was founded in 2000 because the industry lacked prescriptive, recognized hardening standards. To this day, each CIS Benchmark is built by consensus among volunteer experts, vendors, and academics.

Docker itself is no stranger to the development and furthering of shared standards. As just one example, in 2015, Docker contributed its image format and runC runtime to the Open Container Initiative. A shared baseline at the runtime layer let registries, runtimes, and clouds interoperate.

Each of these examples played a different role: PCI mandated, CIS guided, and OCI standardized.

Agents will need elements of all three.

Agents are in the everyone-builds-their-own phase. Each product solves a real piece of the problem, but which piece, and how the pieces fit, is rarely clear. “Agent governance” or even “AI governance” can mean almost anything.

According to recent reports, adoption is incremental. A developer allows common commands, widens filesystem access, then connects GitHub, a cloud tool and an MCP server, each through a prompt that makes sense on its own. The logs mostly record that the developer acted. Security is often the last to know.

According to recent reports, much of the risk is familiar. Shadow adoption looks a lot like early SaaS and cloud. Credential sprawl and supply chain exposure are old problems. Inventory, least privilege, audit, and joiner-mover-leaver discipline still apply.

Several things are latest, however:.

Existing controls still matter, but they were not built for this mix of programmability, access, and autonomy.

As with the credit industry and PCI, cybersecurity and the CIS, and containerization and OCI, collaboration offers the answer to this fresh era of complexity. That’s why Docker is not just focused on building tools like Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance, but in taking an ecosystem-centric approach to problem solving for our customers. Docker is already a founding participant in multiple initiatives aimed at developing valuable reference architectures for AI security workflows, including the Blueprint Alliance and Agent Baseline.

Both start from the same premise: no single vendor or enforcement point can solve this.

The Blueprint Alliance sets out how the pieces fit together. Okta, AWS, CrowdStrike, Databricks, Docker, Google Cloud, Lovable, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Wiz and Zscaler are founding members, with GE Appliances and World Central Kitchen as strategic advisors. The open, multi-vendor reference architecture answers four questions: Where are my agents? What can they do? What are they doing? How do I respond? Members have committed to interoperability testing over MCP, OCSF, SSF and CAEP, and to publishing reference integrations.

It has been revealed that agent Baseline sets out what each piece must do and how to verify it. It fills the gap between threat lists, which say what can go wrong, and the capabilities an enterprise needs in place. It defines six outcomes (Discover, Constrain, Authorize, Observe, Validate and Respond) and 35 open, versioned controls, each with a permanent identifier you can cite in an audit finding or RFP response. Docker, Snyk and Keycard drafted it, and the current release is v1.0-draft. Controls stay where they already live, in the identity provider, the sandbox and the SIEM.

Industry observers note that blueprint states how the pieces connect. Agent Baseline says what must be true and can be checked. Both advise starting with discovery before policy, and testing the kill switch before you need it.

For partners, the roles are defined. The Alliance whitepaper assigns integrators the operating model: assessing a customer’s current stack against the architecture, assigning ownership across the pillars, tiering risk, and running lifecycle and compliance over time. Technology partners get a published target to integrate against, and the reference integrations cross vendor lines by design. The partners who can design, integrate and operate across those lines are the ones customers keep.

It has been revealed that most Alliance members govern agents from the outside: who the agent is, what it can reach, and what it is observed doing. Docker governs the inside: the environment where the agent executes. As agents move from suggesting actions to taking them, trust has to extend beyond the model to the places where they run. Docker has helped define a shared baseline for the runtime before, and now we’re working with the Alliance and our partners to make that baseline concrete, open, and testable in the age of agents.

The execution environment is where policy gets enforced and evidence gets produced.

Sources indicate that that boundary is where policy gets enforced and evidence gets produced. The Alliance whitepaper notes that without runtime support to pause an agent without collateral impact, API-driven containment “provides a false sense of security.” Agent Baseline’s CON-03 calls for isolated, confined execution, which is the job of Docker Sandboxes, while Docker MCP Gateway and Docker Hardened Images cover tool access and the supply chain.The Secure Software Factory reference architecture, drafted in part by Docker authors, applies Agent Baseline to agents that ship code.

Baselines let adoption move faster, not slower. Security and platform leaders can assess against the baseline today. Agent Baseline controls are citable, and Okta offers an AI Blueprint Assessment Tool. Partners can start with the Docker Navigator Partner Program, which rewards AI governance work, and with the reference integrations the Alliance publishes. Docker’s VP of Partners Leon Jones explains the program here. Download the blueprint at blueprintalliance.ai and read the controls at agentbaseline.org.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that at Microsoft Build 2026, we announced Foundry Managed Compute and Hugging Face models on Foundry — a curated catalog of open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem, refreshed weekly, deployable in one click onto Foundry Managed Compute. Weights are pre-staged in Azure, runtimes are built and scanned by Microsoft, and every model in the Collection ships with the same enterprise security, governance, observability, and billing that applies to every other model on Foundry.

Microsoft Foundry is a platform for building and operating agentic AI applications. Foundry starts with the widest model selection on any cloud — models from Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Hugging Face, and others, spanning frontier, open-source, and custom weights — all accessible through a single endpoint and a single set of SDKs in Python, C#, JavaScript, and Java.

Recent findings suggest that on top of those models sits the Foundry Agent Service: multi-agent orchestration with built-in memory, knowledge grounding through Foundry IQ, and a catalog of connectable tools via agentic protocols, so agents can work with enterprise data. Once agents are running, Foundry provides end-to-end tracing, real-time monitoring, continuous evaluations, and a prompt optimizer that improves agent behavior based on eval results — observability and quality loops that are part of the platform.

Alongside that, developers get access to:.

Alongside pay-per-token (lowest-friction path to get started) and provisioned throughput (predictable, high-performance production workloads on frontier models), Foundry Managed Compute is the third deployment option in Foundry: a managed GPU platform-as-a-service for open-source and custom models.

You deploy a model instance described by the things that matter to your workload — parameter count, context length, and whether you want to optimize for latency or throughput — and Foundry handles the GPU topology underneath, whether the instance lands on one accelerator or several, so you think and blueprint in model terms.

Microsoft takes care of the machine: container updates, runtime upgrades, and security patches happen automatically on the supported runtimes — vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, NIM, TEI, llama.cpp — without redeploying your model, while model configuration, deployment behavior, and routing stay with you.

That consistency carries through the developer surface — pay-per-token, provisioned throughput, and Managed Compute share:.

Open-source models integrate with Foundry Agents the same way frontier models do, so you can mix model types in a single agent without a separate integration path.

Same code, same workflow. Quota is aligned to accelerator families, so a blueprint built on the H100 family today carries forward as new hardware generations come online.

Hugging Face is the public square of open AI: 15 million builders, 400,000 organizations, and over 3 million open models published, with upcoming frontier capabilities — agentic coding, video segmentation, speech, embeddings — landing weekly. It's the GitHub of open models, where the community publishes weights, writes model cards, compares evaluations, and pulls models for experimentation.

Open models have closed the gap with proprietary models on benchmark after benchmark, and they unlock things proprietary endpoints can't:.

The catch has always been the operational layer: discovery, license review, security screening, runtime selection, GPU sizing, image building, CVE patching, and standing the model up behind an enterprise-grade endpoint. Hugging Face, by itself, is not an enterprise serving platform. Hugging Face models on Foundry is that operational layer, run by Microsoft.

The Hugging Face Collection brings a curated subset of models directly into the Foundry Model Catalog:.

From your side, an open-weight model in the Hugging Face Collection looks and behaves like any other model in the Foundry Model Catalog, and every model in the Collection has been put through a multi-stage publishing pipeline before it ever shows up there.

Hugging Face and Microsoft work together to bring the most popular open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem to Microsoft Foundry — production-ready for enterprise environments — through a systematic curation process:.

Because weights are pre-staged in Azure storage and runtime images live in a Microsoft-managed registry, your deployments won't need outbound network access to Hugging Face Hub — you can deploy to production inside a private network.

Hugging Face models on Foundry are powered by a versatile collection of community-built, open-source inference runtimes — each selected and tuned for Foundry Managed Compute, and matched to the model architectures it serves best. Across all runtimes, the systematic curation process means new versions and patches land on Foundry rapidly, and existing model deployments are upgraded automatically — without requiring you to redeploy.

vLLM — the default high-throughput serving engine for open large language models, tuned for production GPU workloads. Because Hugging Face is a direct contributor to vLLM, any model in the Transformers library can run on vLLM out of the box — so when a fresh model lands on Hugging Face, it can be served on Foundry the same day, with no waiting on a custom integration.

Industry observers note that SGLang — a serving engine for language and multi-modal models, with strong support for structured outputs (JSON, regex, grammar-constrained generation) that agentic and tool-using workloads depend on. Hugging Face and the SGLang team have built a Transformers backend integration for SGLang, so any model in the Transformers library runs on SGLang out of the box — and reaches Foundry the same day it lands on Hugging Face.

According to recent reports, text Embeddings Inference (TEI) — the runtime for embedding, reranker, and sequence-classification models. Accelerator-specific images ship with kernels compiled for each GPU and CPU family Foundry supports, keeping the embedding hot path lean for RAG and semantic-search workloads.

According to recent reports, llama.cpp — the CPU and small-GPU path for GGUF-quantized models. Useful for cost-optimized deployments, smaller models, and CPU-only regions, with the same OpenAI-compatible API as vLLM and SGLang.

TensorRT-LLM and NIM — used on NVIDIA hardware where NVIDIA's optimized kernels and Triton-based serving deliver meaningfully better latency or throughput for specific model families.

hf-serve — Hugging Face's own multi-model inference server, used for model architectures outside the LLM and embedding fast paths (vision, audio, segmentation, and other Transformers-native pipelines) so the Collection can cover every modality with a consistent serving layer.

The Hugging Face Collection in the Foundry Model Catalog is where you start, and deployment is five steps:.

A deployment template is the unit of choice in step 2: a named, versioned asset that pins the runtime, the accelerator family and count, the context length, and the runtime-specific tuning needed to serve the model well — so picking a template is the only knob you turn for "how do I want this model to run.".

qwen3-32b, for example, ships with four templates the deploy wizard exposes side by side:.

Sources indicate that each template arrives pre-tuned for the model — runtime settings, tool-call and reasoning parsers, scoring path, health probes, request concurrency, and any model-specific context-extension settings are all set by Microsoft, with any trade-offs called out inline in the template description. When you script the deploy, you reference the template and Foundry handles the rest.

The deployment is reachable through the unified Foundry endpoint with the OpenAI SDK — the `model` field takes the deployment name you just created:.

A chat-completions model from the Collection slots into Foundry Agents as an admin-connected model and is callable through the Foundry Responses API with the same OpenAI SDK — same auth, same endpoint, same observability.

Available now in preview: the Hugging Face Collection in the Microsoft Foundry Model Catalog — thousands of models across every modality, refreshed weekly, deployable onto Foundry Managed Compute with NVIDIA A100, NVIDIA H100, or AMD MI300X accelerators in Global and Data Zone scopes, behind a unified Foundry endpoint with Playground support, first-class Azure Monitor metrics, per-deployment billing tags, and curated runtime upgrades and CVE patching applied automatically to your deployments.

On the roadmap: broader coverage of the Hugging Face ecosystem, additional accelerator families, and Bring Your Own Weights for fine-tuned and proprietary variants deployed through the same templates and governance as Collection models.

Recent findings suggest that hugging Face is where open models are published and discovered. Microsoft Foundry is where enterprises operationalize them — on curated, license-screened, security-screened weights hosted in Azure; on community-built and CVE-scanned runtimes; behind a single endpoint with enterprise identity, networking, observability, and agent integration on top. The breadth of the open-source ecosystem, with the operational layer Microsoft runs underneath. For a deep dive on Foundry Managed Compute — pricing, accelerator SKUs, data residency, enterprise readiness, observability, and the full Responses API + memory pattern — see the Managed Compute launch blog.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pick up your work exactly where life made you stop — on the same machine or from elsewhere.

Industry observers note that mercurius gives you long‑lived graphical sessions that you can leave, return to, and resume whether you’re on the same laptop or somewhere else on the network. The session model works locally without any networking at all; the network simply lets your sessions inhabit more powerful machines when you want them to.

Sometimes life interrupts. Work calls, dinner is ready, or you need to switch tasks. Mercurius treats sessions as first-class objects so your applications belong to the session, not the physical device in front of you.

Recent findings suggest that suspend a coding session, switch to a gaming session, and resume either one later with every window exactly as you left it. Built for powerful workstations, modern GPUs, and fast local networks, Mercurius uses the network to extend your experience, not to justify its existence.

Recent findings suggest that it used to be normal to share the big, expensive computer in the corner. Today everyone has a laptop, but the economics of computing have changed again: RAM and GPUs are costly, and workstation‑class machines deliver far more capability than most people carry around. Mercurius lets you use that capability without giving up the convenience of your own environment.

According to recent reports, mercurius keeps your work on your own machines, so you’re never at the mercy of a cloud subscription just to read your own documents. With the rising cost of local RAM and high‑end GPUs, sharing the expensive computer again is a smart alternative. Mercurius lets an organisation concentrate its investment in a few powerful GPU‑rich workstations and make full use of them, instead of buying every developer a high‑end laptop that can’t run the heavy workloads anyway.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that score, a CNCF Sandbox project, recently joined the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program to strengthen the security of its container images and release pipeline.
  • According to recent reports, in September 2025, the CNCF announced a partnership with Docker to expand infrastructure support for project maintainers through the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program.
  • This aligned closely with the discussions held at the Maintainer Summit NA 2025 in Atlanta, which centered on increasing collaboration across CNCF projects and demonstrating security best practices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that score, a CNCF Sandbox project, recently joined the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program to strengthen the security of its container images and release pipeline. In this post, the Score maintainers share what we adopted (Docker Hub, Docker Scout, Docker Hardened Images, the Docker GitHub Builder, and OIDC connections), the results we measured, and how other open source projects, within the CNCF and beyond, can apply the same practices by default.

According to recent reports, in September 2025, the CNCF announced a partnership with Docker to expand infrastructure support for project maintainers through the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program. The partnership gives CNCF projects access to Docker’s security scanning tools, container registry, and best-practice resources at no cost.

This aligned closely with the discussions held at the Maintainer Summit NA 2025 in Atlanta, which centered on increasing collaboration across CNCF projects and demonstrating security best practices.

The Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program supports non-commercial open source projects with Docker tooling and infrastructure.

Before: Score publishes different container images: the CLIs of score-compose, score-k8s, score-helm and score-radius; and the sample-score-app used for demos and testing. We previously published them in the GitHub Container Registry here.

After: Through the DSOS Program, we now publish these images on Docker Hub, which increases their visibility and gives the community a verified, trusted source.

All the container images are now available on Docker Hub.

The program also provides usage analytics that show how the community uses these images. Here is an example:.

Sources indicate that before: As a CNCF project, Score follows the OpenSSF best practices. In addition, the OpenSSF Scorecard GitHub Action runs continuously. This was a solid foundation, but we had no dedicated security scanning tool in place.

Recent findings suggest that after: The DSOS Program gave us access to Docker Scout, which we now use in our pull requests and on our container registry (Docker Hub). This gives us clear visibility into the CVEs introduced or fixed by each pull request and release.

The following GitHub Actions step uses docker/scout-action on every pull request to compare the image built from the PR branch with the one built from the main branch:.

Here is an example of a comment posted by this docker/scout-action step in a recent Pull Request:.

The comment details the comparison between the two images (before versus after): size, packages updated, added or removed, CVEs introduced and resolved, and compliance with our policies in place (run as non-root, no critical CVEs, no packages with AGPL v3 licences).

The analysis goes beyond the images themselves: it also covers the Go libraries and binaries they contain.

The Docker Scout console also provides a single view of CVEs, packages, base images, and policies across all of our container images, which makes it easy to see what is used where, and in which version.

When Docker made Hardened Images freely available under Apache 2.0, we saw an opportunity to simplify our security posture while staying compatible with our existing Dockerfiles and workflows, even though we were already using multi-stage builds and distroless base images.

Docker Hardened Images are minimal, security-focused container base images designed to reduce inherited risk in downstream projects. They are built and maintained with security and transparency as defaults, and offer:.

The migration was straightforward.

Take the score-radius CLI, which used a golang:alpine and a distroless images and now uses dhi.io/golang and dhi.io/static images. The changes required in the Dockerfile were minimal:.

It has been revealed that in the associated PR here, image size dropped by 0.3 MB while the number of packages stayed the same and the CVE count remained at 0. We could have stayed with Debian, but chose to move to an Alpine base image (DHI provides the two options):.

The same applies to the NodeJS sample-score-app, which used nodejs on top of an alpine image and now uses a dhi.io/node image. The changes required in the Dockerfile were minimal:.

In the associated PR here, 22 packages were removed (including the package manager and the shell), along with 2 CVEs:.

Note: We were able to present a short walkthrough of our DHI integration during the CNCF webinar held on January 23, 2026, which accompanied the Docker Hardened Images announcement for CNCF projects.

Although not directly part of the DSOS Program, we took the opportunity to adopt the newly introduced docker/github-builder GitHub reusable workflow to release our container images.

This model provides a build pipeline maintained in the Docker organization, with a version-controlled BuildKit environment, multi-platform builds distributed across runners where beneficial, and signed SLSA provenance recording both the source commit and the builder identity.

The trade-off is intentional. You retain control over when the build runs and which inputs it uses, while the build implementation itself lives in the Docker-maintained workflow rather than in per-repository job steps.

Before, the GitHub Actions workflow to release our container images was using this sequence of actions:.

After, this same workflow is now only using the reusable workflow docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml:.

Industry observers note that docker GitHub Builder gives us a Docker-maintained build pipeline with signed SLSA provenance and SBOM attestations, helping consumers verify the builder identity and trace images back to their source commit. Signing uses GitHub OIDC, so we don’t need to manage long-lived signing keys. With caching enabled in our workflow, cache entries are also signed and verified before reuse, helping protect against cache poisoning. See the Docker GitHub Builder documentation for more information about its security model.

The following command verifies the signature on the attestation manifest for the selected image platform:.

Most recently, with an update released on July 21, 2026, Docker introduced OIDC connections. This feature allows pulls and pushes to Docker Hub to use a short-lived token instead of a long-lived Organization Access Token (OAT).

An OIDC connection establishes a trust relationship between Docker and a trusted third party, so you no longer need to maintain long-lived credentials. Docker exchanges short-lived tokens with the other vendor, which can grant fine-grained access to your Docker resources.

By replacing a static, long-lived token with a short-lived one and making it issued on a per-workflow basis, we removed a credential that could otherwise be stolen and misused.

In a recent development, participating in the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program has been rewarding, and it has helped Score adopt a security-by-default foundation. Using Docker Scout, Docker Hardened Images, OIDC connections, and the Docker GitHub Builder has strengthened the security posture of our container images and brought broader benefits to the Score projects and repositories.

In a recent development, if you maintain a CNCF project or any open source project, we encourage you to explore the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program. The security improvements were measurable, and the onboarding process was straightforward.

The full implementation across the Score repositories is tracked in GitHub concern #376.

Recent findings suggest that attending KubeCon NA 2026 in Salt Lake City? Feel free to connect with the Score maintainers during the Maintainer Summit on Sunday, Nov 8th and at the Kiosk #P-17B on Thursday, Nov 12th between 10:15am and 2pm, you will see Score in actions with the new Score Labspace! You can also meet the Docker team at booth #141 in Hall C!

Recent findings suggest that note: This work was completed after I joined Docker. It was, however, an initiative we wanted to pursue as CNCF project maintainers from the moment it was revealed in September 2025, both to improve our security posture and to share what we learned with the broader community.

We hope this post helps you strengthen the security of your own projects.

  • Previously, getting started on SageMaker Studio after discovering a model on Hugging Face required navigating multiple steps between opening Amazon SageMaker AI in the AWS Console, creating a domain, configuring IAM permissions, and sometimes requesting GPU quota.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we’re excited to announce a deep-link integration between Hugging Face and Amazon SageMaker AI. Developers can now go from model discovery to hands-on experimentation in SageMaker Studio with a single selection. Whether you fine-tune a foundation model (FM) from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart or deploy it to an Amazon SageMaker Inference endpoint, you can now land directly inside the relevant SageMaker Studio workflow. Your selected model is pre-loaded, and the environment is fully configured and ready to go.

Previously, getting started on SageMaker Studio after discovering a model on Hugging Face required navigating multiple steps between opening Amazon SageMaker AI in the AWS Console, creating a domain, configuring IAM permissions, and sometimes requesting GPU quota. For developers who want to iterate swiftly, this friction slows down the path from inspiration to experimentation. The integration creates a more direct path from discovery to enterprise deployment.

According to recent reports, “At Arcee, we build open models so developers and enterprises can actually own what they run: inspect the weights, post-train on their own data, and deploy on their own terms. This integration takes that promise the last mile. Going from an open model on Hugging Face straight into SageMaker Studio in a single click, then fine-tuning or deploying it inside your own AWS environment with nothing to wire up, is the kind of experience open models have been missing. Open weights you own, running in the cloud you control. That is exactly the combination our customers have been asking for.”.

— Mark McQuade, Founder and CEO, Arcee AI.

In a recent development, with the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience, choosing Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI on a supported Hugging Face model page takes you directly to the console. SageMaker AI then automatically provisions a upcoming domain with pre-configured permissions in seconds and carries the model context through.

This launch introduces three capabilities that shorten the path from a Hugging Face model to a working SageMaker Studio workflow.

When you browse models on Hugging Face, you’ll now see action buttons alongside supported models that map directly to SageMaker Studio workflows:.

Each entry point preserves the context, meaning you don’t need to search for the model again once inside Studio.

New Studio environments created through this flow come with permissions already configured for the full range of SageMaker AI capabilities, including model customization, training jobs, notebook experimentation, and endpoint deployment. A new managed policy, AmazonSageMakerModelCustomizationCoreAccess, is created and attached for you. It provides permissions for serverless model customization jobs using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), with supported deployment to SageMaker AI or Amazon Bedrock endpoints. This alleviates the need to manually create and configure AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and policies before you can start experimenting. For existing Studio environments, actionable messages with direct links to documentation guide you through adding these permissions.

In a recent development, when selecting instance types for deployment or training, the Studio UI now surfaces quota availability directly in the instance selection list. You can immediately see which GPU instance types (G5, G6) are available under your account’s current limits. You don’t need to navigate separately to Service Quotas. If you still need to request a limit increase, you’re redirected directly to the Service Quotas page for the respective instance type.

Let’s walk through the experience of customizing or deploying a model starting from Hugging Face.

In a recent development, on the Hugging Face model page, click on “Deploy” and select “Amazon SageMaker AI”. If the model is supported, you will see two buttons, “Deploy on SageMaker AI” and “Customize on SageMaker AI”. Then select “Customize on SageMaker AI” for a supported model.

Sources indicate that you’re prompted to sign in to AWS using your existing credentials. If you already have an active console session, this step is skipped automatically. For more information, see Sign in to the AWS Management Console.

According to recent reports, you arrive directly on the Model Customization page inside SageMaker Studio with your model pre-selected. Next, configure your fine-tuning parameters such as training data, hyperparameters, and instance type, then submit the customization job.

Recent findings suggest that alternatively, selecting Deploy on SageMaker AI opens the endpoint deployment page in Studio with the model pre-configured. Select your instance type (quota visibility included), review the settings, and deploy.

After you deploy your endpoint, test inference directly from Studio’s endpoint testing interface.

You can try this experience today:.

It has been revealed that the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience minimizes the friction between discovering a model and experimenting with it. By connecting Hugging Face directly to the SageMaker Studio workflows, developers can stay in their flow. There’s no context switching, no manual environment setup, and no permission troubleshooting.

To get started, visit the Amazon SageMaker Studio page or explore models on Hugging Face and choose Deploy or Customize on SageMaker AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, trusted content is the foundation security-conscious organizations expect all builds to start from. Docker has made that possible for everyone by providing the foundation free. Docker Hardened Images (DHI) are open source under Apache 2.0, with a catalog of 4,000+ minimal images (and growing) built from source and continuously maintained by Docker. The catalog also carries customizable Helm charts and over 65,000 hardened system packages. For most services, adopting DHI is as simple as changing the FROM line.

Teams building on a secure foundation now want the same assurance for the open source their applications install. That open source is a different layer of the supply chain, where thousands of upstream projects are pulled in at build time by pip, npm and Maven, and by coding agents as well.

Recent findings suggest that docker is committed to one standard for trusted content across everything teams build on. A upcoming partnership with ActiveState, the tech giant that has been securing open source since 1997, extends that standard to the packages themselves. Together, we give teams the same assurance on both layers, from the hardened images Docker maintains to the packages developers and their agents install on them. Once configured, the integration allows developers and AI coding assistants to continue using familiar package managers and development workflows, while approved dependencies are sourced through governed repositories rather than directly from public registries.

In a recent development, most applications still start from a large, generic base image, and the cost of that choice keeps growing. A large image increases the attack surface and accumulates stale dependencies, and the CVEs it generates land on developers long after the image was chosen. By removing unnecessary packages, rebuilding components from source and continuously maintaining the image, Docker Hardened Images reduce the vulnerabilities inherited from the container foundation. Images can achieve near-zero known CVEs, which means less remediation work and less scanner noise before application code is introduced. The hardening and patching are handled once in the foundation, for every service that builds on it.

Sources indicate that above the base image sit the dependencies an application brings with it. DHI secures the operating system packages and the language runtime that ship in the image. The application’s own libraries are pulled in at build time by its package managers from public registries, where trust is assumed and seldom verified. That layer needs what the image now has, a source that admits only the versions a team has approved and stands behind the fix when one of them needs it. Coding agents now pull those packages too. As Mark Lechner, CISO wrote in April, a compromised dependency pulled by an agent has the same blast radius as a compromised developer machine.

Sources indicate that this year’s supply chain incidents have followed one pattern. As Lechner documented, attackers steal developer credentials, use them to poison trusted packages, and the compromised packages steal more credentials. The axios compromise earlier this year put two backdoored versions of a library downloaded 83 million times a week into circulation for about three hours. Most of these attacks burn out within hours. A build that resolves fresh from a public registry, with no lockfile or cooldown in front of it, has nothing between it and a version published an hour ago. The slower failure is the vulnerability that surfaces in one of those libraries months later, when no one outside the team is accountable for the fix. Either way, without trusted content on both layers, the risk lands on your team.

Docker Hardened Images are the foundation, and Docker stands behind them. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, with full, unsuppressed CVE visibility. A security team can see what is in the image and how it was built. For teams that need remediation on a predictable clock, DHI adds a 7-day SLA on critical and high CVEs, FIPS and STIG variants, and secure customization on its paid tiers.

Sources indicate that while DHI secures the image, ActiveState hardens the open source built on it. ActiveState provides the Curated Catalog, a private, policy-governed repository of open source components that security teams curate and developers and AI coding assistants consume safely. The catalog holds only the packages a team has approved. ActiveState compiles every component from original source code in a SLSA Level 3 environment with full provenance and complete SBOMs, in place of pre-compiled binaries from a public registry. When a fix becomes available upstream, ActiveState rebuilds the component and publishes it to the catalog automatically under SLAs of 5 business days for critical CVEs and 10 for highs.

With DHI and the Curated Catalog together, both layers carry provenance, SBOMs and a remediation SLA from the hardened image to the packages built on it. That gives security teams a consistent evidence trail across the software supply chain. The artifact repository teams already run, Artifactory or Nexus, points at the Curated Catalog as its upstream the way it points at PyPI today. Developers keep the same pip and npm workflow, and coding agents are served the governed version. None of this replaces the pinned digests, cooldown periods and sandboxed agents Lechner recommends. It gives those controls a governed source to point at.

AI coding agents are changing how quickly organizations create software. They can generate applications, select dependencies and initiate builds at a pace that traditional security review processes were never designed to support. Still, faster development should not mean blindly accepting more supply chain risk. Docker Hardened Images reduce the security burden of maintaining container foundations. ActiveState’s Curated Catalog extends governance and managed vulnerability remediation to the open source libraries those applications depend on. The result is a more consistent approach to software supply chain security, with trusted foundations, governed dependencies, verifiable build evidence and clear remediation responsibilities.

Industry observers note that the goal is not to add another security checkpoint that causes friction in your build process. It is to make the secure path the easiest path for developers, platform teams and AI coding agents alike.

Security scales when the defaults are strong and the foundation is maintained by a team accountable for it. In an increasingly agent-driven development environment, the security of what gets built depends heavily on the trustworthiness of what those agents are allowed to consume. Docker now resells the ActiveState Curated Catalog alongside DHI, and ActiveState resells DHI to its customers. The hardened image and the packages built on it are both available through Docker.

Principal Product Marketing Manager, Docker.

Vishrut Iyengar is Principal PMM for Security at Docker, focused on Docker Hardened Images, supply chain security, and securing what AI agents build.
