The case of the flaky Dynamo export tests

📅 11 Mar 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1454 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pytorch

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for months, Dynamo export tests have been intermittently failing with “AssertionError: whole graph export entails exactly one call”.
  • Recent findings suggest that when trying to debug a tricky problem, it pays to reduce experiment iteration time.
  • According to recent reports, next, I wanted to better understand what exactly was going on when things failed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for months, Dynamo export tests have been intermittently failing with “AssertionError: whole graph export entails exactly one call”. Flaky tests that you can’t reproduce are pretty difficult to debug, since you can’t easily make a change and see if it fixes the problem or not. So when I noticed that my local pytest runs were reliably failing in a similar way (so reliably, that initially I thought that they were failing deterministically), I figured I should stop what I was doing and get to the bottom of the problem, because it seemed pretty unlikely anyone else would be able to figure it out otherwise.

Recent findings suggest that when trying to debug a tricky problem, it pays to reduce experiment iteration time. In my case, it took a few minutes to run the full test suite: I wanted to trigger the flaky test to trigger within the first few runs. I initially wanted to do this by running all the tests in a fixed order, and then delta debugging removing running tests until the flakiness went away. But it turns out pytest doesn’t really have any built-in way to do this; stock unittest does, but in fact the tests stop failing when you don’t run with unittest (for those guessing at home, this is an notable clue!) However, pytest does support boolean operators in the -k argument flag, e.g., you can say -k foo and bar to select tests that only contain foo and bar in their name. So I used this to successively pare down tests to something that could be run in a few seconds: PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 pytest test/dynamo/test_dynamic_shapes.py -k 'Unspec and export and not dupes and not reorder' -v -x -s. Great.

According to recent reports, next, I wanted to better understand what exactly was going on when things failed. A good start is to turn on DEBUG logging and look through the logs. Unfortunately, turning on logging also makes the bug go away. So it’s back to good old fashioned print debugging. After a bit of triangulating, I finally determine that in the buggy case, we’re arriving at this block of code:.

We successfully setup the Dynamo frame callback, we call fn and… the frame callback just doesn’t get called.

OK, so this sounds like something has gone wrong with the callback setup. Can we log that? Yes we can! torch/csrc/dynamo/eval_frame.c has an undocumented TORCHDYNAMO_DEBUG preprocessor macro that, if defined, turns on a bunch of debug logging that looks like this:.

(There is in fact a very notable clue in this log, though I didn’t figure it out until later.) I also added some more debug logs for when we modify the eval frame callback, to see if we were unsetting the custom frame callback and then forgetting to reset it. And indeed, this is precisely what was happening:.

Compare this with the success case right below, which re-enables the custom callback:.

Modifying the internal exception callback to reset the Dynamo callback indeed “fixed” the test failures. But there were some unresolved mysteries. Why was the callback internal erroring? Why did this fail nondeterministically? Was it possible that we intentionally were keeping the callback disabled in case of error?

I decided I wanted to understand why the test was failing nondeterministically. What was different about this test versus another? Here was an example of a test that was succeeding:.

Sources indicate that each begin log line tells us whenever Dynamo’s custom frame handler is invoked. We see some context manager stuff, a call to enable_dynamic, and then a call to the actual function to be traced. Everything before the function is skipped, and the function itself creates a cache entry. This all makes sense, and we can line up each log entry with actual Python code that is executing after the eval frame is setup.

We see some familiar faces: this trace still calls enable_dynamic. But then, there are a bunch of random frames that don’t seem to correspond at all to the Python code executing. Where did it come from? There are some clues: there are a lot of clues to __del__, which is responsible for object finalization. And this , where the heck did that come from?

It’s the GC! I quickly check what happens if I disable GC with pytest-gc, and indeed, this also solves the problem. Non-determinism mystery solved: the failure happens nondeterministically because when GC triggers is nondeterministic; and you have to get unlucky enough to trigger a GC right after Dynamo’s frame handler is installed, but before we actually get to the actual frame in question. We can also confirm this by installing the frame handler after entering the context managers. This also explains why the error is easier to reproduce in pytest: pytest has some reference cycles in its implementations, and causes the GC to run a lot more frequently.

So, we have multiple ways we could fix the problem. It also seems like maybe it’s a good idea not to run Dynamo during GC? cpython - How to detect if frame evaluation is occurring during GC in Python - Stack Overflow Though, I did some CPython reading and it seems to not be possible. But does this mean we’re done debugging?

Why is it a problem for GC to run while the Dynamo frame handler is installed? Although it’s weird, it seems like the frame handler should still get called as normal. But instead, the callback is failing with an internal error. But how can it be failing with an internal error if we never actually call the callback?

We can force CPython to print out what a raised exception is, and then restore the exception so that it keeps propagating as normal, using the following trick:.

(It’s important to use Py_XINCREF, since ptype/pvalue/ptraceback could be NULL).

Sources indicate that the printed backtrace shows that we’re failing on the very first line of the callback handler. I can’t even print: before the print runs, I just immediately fail out. Could it be… that there is already a Python error active when I enter the eval frame? A quick check of PyErr_Occurred() before the callback confirms this!

In a recent development, why is there a Python error active? I’m not really sure, but I’m reminded of a little bit of CPython trivia: when a generator is exhausted, it finishes by raising a GeneratorExit exception. So maybe we’re in the process of unwinding a generator when this happens?

I submit my first patch, and go to bed.

Industry observers note that in the morning, all of the regular test suite is passing… but some tests running under the ‘dynamo’ configuration are failing. Sometimes, fixing bugs in Dynamo can cause previously passing tests to start failing because of latent bugs. I could have skipped those tests and moved on with my life.

In a recent development, I resolve that I should at least convince myself that the fresh failures are not my fault. Fortunately, the failures are deterministic. Oddly, the test in question is xfail’ed, but now we are somehow skipping xfail handling and still erroring with the exception. I use pdb to step through the stack unwinding and confirm that, yes, somehow we’re just not hitting the finally handler. Fortunately, it turns out just throwing an exception and having a non-trivial handler is sufficient to repro the problem.

I carefully inspect Dynamo’s rewritten bytecode and confirm that, yes, the bytecode is still properly setting up the context manager. It seems like there’s something wrong with my patch. I can think of a few possible alternate ways to write it that might work….

Alban, who at this point I’ve roped into the sordid saga, wants to understand why there is an error active at frame entry. Alban reads through the source code for _PyEval_EvalFrameDefault and notices two things:.

This is consistent with everything we’ve seen so far: the naughty frames are invariably frames, and I do a quick test and confirm that, indeed, throwflag is true when we get here. It also seems clear that returning NULL is different from unwinding, since unwinding causes a bunch of extra finalization code to run. This leads us to our final patch:.

This is the end of our debugging story. No stone has been left unturned: we have successfully explained every observed behavior in the original problem. By continually asking why, we have avoided landing an incorrect fix which would have suppressed the initial problem, but opened us up to an even more subtle and more rarely triggered bug. The moral of the story?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Prepares to unleash full wrath of Digital Services Act over Chinese e-tailer's alleged sales of illegal products.
  • Sources indicate that chinese e-tailer Temu has a reputation for selling low-quality knockoff products at low prices made possible through use of forced labor.
  • The Commission issued that finding yesterday, accusing Temu of breaching its Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to operate serious measures that mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prepares to unleash full wrath of Digital Services Act over Chinese e-tailer's alleged sales of illegal products.

Sources indicate that chinese e-tailer Temu has a reputation for selling low-quality knockoff products at low prices made possible through use of forced labor. Now, the European Commission has made a preliminary finding that the company also runs a low-quality compliance regime that means it’s not meeting its regulatory obligations.

The Commission issued that finding yesterday, accusing Temu of breaching its Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to operate serious measures that mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform.

Temu is a marketplace that allows third parties to sell on its platform, a model that doesn’t relieve it of responsibility for the goods available on its site and apps.

Eurocrats therefore have beef with Temu over several matters, including:.

Requiring sellers who use the platform to test the quality of “only a very small share of products,” and then often not bothering to check the reports;.

Not doing enough to prioritize checks of products in known high risk categories, like toys and cosmetics, then not following up on those checks;.

Running a moderation system that mostly considers whether products comply with Temu’s terms and conditions, rather than product safety;.

Not hiring enough human moderators to keep pace with growth in listings on Temu;.

When it finds stores selling non-compliant goods, Temu acts against that store – but not the trader who may sell the same products in multiple stores;.

Allowing stores to commit many serious infringements, including selling products that fail safety checks, before suspending their stores.

A Temu spokesperson told The Register the company respectfully disagrees with the EC's findings.

In a recent development, "Temu invests significantly in compliance infrastructure and human expertise and implements a suite of control measures that effectively mitigate illegal product risks with a consistently low incidence of problematic products," the spokesperson said. "We will review and respond to the preliminary findings carefully and will continue to engage constructively with the Commission. We are confident that we will reach an amicable resolution of the matter that fully addresses the Commission's remaining concerns.".

It has been revealed that the EC has already tangled with Temu. In 2024 Eurocrats investigated its risk assessment processes. In May 2026, Eurocrats found Temu’s processes inadequate and levied a €200 million fine.

Brussels also sent a €550 million fine to another Chinese e-tailer, Alibaba, for not doing enough to stop the sale of dangerous goods.

This announcement of upcoming action against Temu invoked Article 35 of the Digital Services Act, the sweeping regulation of online businesses under which the EU could fine Temu up to six percent of its global revenue and order corrective actions.

Europe is concerned that the low prices Chinese e-tailers charge are enabled by forced labor and ignoring dangerous products. EC officials believe those practices mean the likes of Temu don’t compete on a level playing field with continental retailers. The bloc has tried to make life harder for Chinese e-commerce outfits by charging a temporary €3 customs duty for every shipment sent from outside the EU and valued at under €150. Google recently revealed that newly introduced charge saw its advertising revenue from Asian customers fall.

Beijing sees its e-tail giants Temu, Shein, and Alibaba as key actors in its strategy to grow China’s exports and overall economy, which hasn’t performed strongly in recent years. Indeed, Chinese consumers have slowed their discretionary spending to the extent that Beijing last year subsidized purchases of consumer electronics – including Apple products –  to keep cash registers ticking over. ®.

Latest Update: Native-speed vLLM transformers modeling backend

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, TL;DR: The transformers vLLM backend is now as fast (or faster) than custom vLLM implementations for many LLM architectures.
  • It has been revealed that the transformers library has become the reference modeling library for Machine Learning.
  • We have fully embraced this role in the ecosystem and are investing a lot of effort to make it easier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, TL;DR: The transformers vLLM backend is now as fast (or faster) than custom vLLM implementations for many LLM architectures. Model authors can automatically leverage their transformers implementations to get ultra fast vLLM inference, for free.

It has been revealed that the transformers library has become the reference modeling library for Machine Learning. It supports 450+ architectures through consistent APIs, and is designed with the main goal that model implementations are self contained and easy to understand. Going through transformers code makes it easy for contributors to learn how an architecture works, and then port it to other frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, MLX, llama.cpp, and many others.

We have fully embraced this role in the ecosystem and are investing a lot of effort to make it easier. A significant step in this direction was the integration last year of transformers as a modeling backend in vLLM. This has been allowing model authors to run transformers models (LLMs and VLMs alike) inside vLLM, without having to port anything. Transformers provides the modeling code, and vLLM provides extremely optimized inference techniques such as continuous batching and custom attention kernels.

This integration gets better now 🚀!

We put the transformers modeling backend for vLLM head to head with vLLM's hand written native implementations across three very different Qwen3 models:.

Industry observers note that running any* Hugging Face model through the transformers modeling backend is a single flag — --model-impl transformers. It composes with the usual parallelism options, so nothing about your serving setup changes:.

In a recent development, *Models that use linear attention are not currently supported, but they will be soon! Custom models where the code lives in a Hub repo are unlikely to work as they will not have been written compliantly.

Each model is compared under three conditions that are identical in every way except the code path:.

The full, reproducible runner is available as a gist: benchmark.sh.

The transformers modeling backend for vLLM used to focus on attention as the bottleneck for inference. By plugging vLLM’s attention implementation at runtime, we could make a transformers model run efficiently inside the vLLM engine. But there are many dimensions to deployments that only a custom port can target to extract maximum inference performance. Parallelization across GPUs, compilation, fused kernels, and many more, all contribute to leveraging your hardware to achieve ultra-fast inference.

When model authors wanted the absolute best performance, they were still writing custom vLLM implementations.

The latest iteration of the transformers modeling backend for vLLM dynamically applies inference specific layer fusions at runtime to match the speed of custom code implementations, for compatible architectures.

Sources indicate that the transformers modeling backend for vLLM now uses torch.fx to perform static analysis on the model’s graph. This process searches for known patterns that can be optimised. After any patterns have been identified, it uses ast (abstract syntax tree) to manipulate the source code and rewrite some of the operations in place.

As shown above, this results in native vLLM inference speed for compatible models, without having to write a single line of code to optimize the model for inference.

We are in the process of writing a detailed blog post to dive deep inside these optimized inference methods and explain in detail how we manipulate the model to adapt to them.

One provenance implication here is that the model definition and the executed inference graph are no longer the same artifact boundary.

If the runtime rewrites model code and replaces modules with fused kernels, deployment evidence probably needs to preserve both the source model identity and the transformation/runtime path.

Docker Sandboxes vs. Containers: Choosing the Right Isolation for AI Agents

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve used Docker for a while, “Docker Sandboxes” might read as “a container with an AI agent inside.” Containers have been the unit of nearly everything Docker ships for over a decade, and a sandbox might sound like one more way to package a workload.
  • They’re actually different technologies.
  • In his WeAreDevelopers keynote, Docker President Mark Cavage stated containers are doing exactly the job they were designed to do, but we’re asking them to do a different job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve used Docker for a while, “Docker Sandboxes” might read as “a container with an AI agent inside.” Containers have been the unit of nearly everything Docker ships for over a decade, and a sandbox might sound like one more way to package a workload.

They’re actually different technologies. A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel with everything else on the machine. Docker Sandboxes are dedicated microVMs with their own Linux kernel, filesystem, network, and Docker Engine, built for autonomous coding agents that need a whole development machine to work in. A sandbox can run containers, which is part of why the two are easy to conflate.

In his WeAreDevelopers keynote, Docker President Mark Cavage stated containers are doing exactly the job they were designed to do, but we’re asking them to do a different job.

Containers were built to isolate applications, which they still do well. But a coding agent is an actor: it makes decisions and operates on your systems the way a developer uses a laptop. It clones repositories, installs packages, starts databases, builds images, and tries again for hours. It can also act on instructions from files, web pages, and tool output that nobody reviewed.

According to recent reports, that different job needs a different boundary, and where that boundary sits determines how far an agent’s mistake can travel. This post covers how Docker Sandboxes and containers isolate workloads, what changes beyond the kernel, what a sandbox costs you in setup, and how to pick.

Industry observers note that A container is a process, or a group of processes, running on the host with its own view of the filesystem, process tree, and network. Linux namespaces provide that view, and cgroups meter CPU, memory, and I/O. Every container on the machine also shares the host kernel, which is why containers start quickly, pack densely, and carry so little overhead.

This design has more than a decade of tooling behind it. Compose, Kubernetes, OCI registries, image scanners, and nearly every CI system treat the container as the common primitive. If the job is to run a service, execute a code snippet, process one request, or run an evaluation and disappear, a container is usually the obvious pick, and it will stay that way.

ⓘ Containers share one kernel, even inside a VM. On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs your Linux containers inside a virtual machine, which keeps them off your host operating system. Every container in that VM still shares its single kernel, so the isolation between one container and the next is unchanged.

Recent findings suggest that docker Sandboxes run an AI coding agent inside a microVM that has its own Linux kernel, its own filesystem and network stack, and a private Docker Engine. The agent gets sudo inside the isolated environment. It can install packages, run services, build images, and bring up an entire Compose application without reaching the host Docker daemon, the host filesystem outside its workspace, or other sandboxes on the same machine.

Getting one running takes a single command, using sbx, the Docker Sandboxes CLI:.

That creates the sandbox and starts the agent. You can stop it, resume it, and come back to everything the agent installed until you remove the sandbox.

Recent findings suggest that coding agents need a full machine because their sessions build up state over hours and they act on unvetted instructions. A container is built for a process with a known set of dependencies, and an agent’s work doesn’t fit that shape.

In a recent development, an agent needs the authority of a whole machine and a boundary designed for one. The capabilities that make an agent useful, such as running code, installing packages, and reaching the network, are the same ones that wear at the walls around it. An agent probes the edges of its environment because the job requires changing that environment.

According to recent reports, A coding agent’s session looks like a developer’s afternoon. It clones a repository, installs packages, starts PostgreSQL, runs migrations, builds images, releases the app with Compose, reads the logs, changes the code, and tries again. That loop can run for hours, and each step depends on what the previous one left behind.

A container is designed to be rebuilt from an image and a few explicit volumes. The packages, databases, and build output an agent creates outside those volumes are lost when the container is recreated. That’s less than ideal for a session where every step builds on the last.

Box by ASCII describes this distinction neatly: “It uses the sandbox the way a developer uses a laptop, so the sandbox has to behave like one.”.

The program deciding which command to run is probabilistic, and it can read instructions from many places at once, including source files, problem descriptions, web pages, package metadata, and MCP tool output. Some of that input is untrusted, and a malicious instruction planted in a README or a tool description can steer the agent on purpose. The code it generates may also be wrong or actively hostile.

Sources indicate that we’ve already seen an agent that deleted a production database after misreading its task. Once the agent is running unattended in YOLO mode, there’s no permission prompt left to catch it. A workload with that much authority and that little predictability needs a boundary designed for it.

Recent findings suggest that put these facts together and you get the reason why we built Docker Sandboxes. An autonomous coding agent needs machine-shaped capabilities without access to everything on the developer’s machine, which comes down to four things:.

The next sections show what each looks like, starting with containment.

It has been revealed that the short version is that a container’s boundary is the host kernel it shares, and Docker Sandboxes have a hypervisor boundary around a kernel the agent has to itself. That one difference decides how far a compromise can travel, and it also settles the awkward question of how an agent could get access to Docker.

In a recent development, this is where containers and containment part ways. A container can be part of containment, and often should be, but containment covers the whole environment around the agent. It starts with a boundary the model can’t rewrite, which is why Docker uses a microVM with its own kernel for autonomous agents.

A container’s boundary is enforced by the kernel it shares, so escaping it requires a kernel exploit or a side-channel attack. Those aren’t everyday finds. Past that bar, though, sits the entire host kernel, every other process on the machine, and any credentials mounted alongside them.

Recent findings suggest that ⓘ This scenario is specific to Linux environments. On Docker Desktop (macOS and Windows), the shared kernel is the Docker Desktop VM’s kernel, not the host kernel, so an escape would land in that VM rather than the operating system.

Docker Sandboxes give the agent its own kernel behind a hypervisor boundary. If an agent escapes its container, it lands in a disposable microVM, and the host stays out of reach. And you can delete the sandbox and start another. Each agent also gets its own microVM, so two agents running on the same machine can’t reach each other’s sandboxes either. However, the agent can still reach whatever you chose to share with it, including the workspace, allowed network destinations, MCP servers, and skills.

In a recent development, mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container is the long-standing way to give it Docker access, and it turns up in Compose setups, CI pipelines, and observability tools. It also hands the container control of the host Docker daemon, which Docker limits to trusted users because it can mount host paths and start privileged containers.

An agent doesn’t need an exploit to use that. Put one in a container started with the socket mounted, and it probes its surroundings, works out that it’s in a container, and finds the hole in the configuration. In Mark’s keynote demo, that was enough for an agent to reach a secrets file on the host with no zero-day involved.

According to recent reports, the socket is one hole among several, and agents find them because probing their environment is part of the work. Docker-in-Docker, mounted credentials, and broad host mounts are others. Containers were built to isolate an application that behaves as configured. But an agent keeps testing that configuration, so if there’s a gap, it’s likely to find it.

Docker Sandboxes put the missing boundary in the right place. The agent talks to a private Docker Engine inside the guest. It can build images, run Testcontainers, and start a whole Compose stack, and the host daemon and its socket stay outside the microVM the entire time. Containers keep doing what they do best, inside a boundary the agent can’t widen.

It has been revealed that let’s say you ask an agent running inside Docker Sandboxes to find a secrets file on the host. It’ll find a Docker socket, try to use it to mount host paths and start privileged containers, but won’t reach the host. A microVM can give it a much stronger trust boundary than a container. The architecture behind Docker Sandboxes goes deeper on why a microVM was the right shape for this.

In a recent development, containment draws the boundary. Control is what you can see and stop inside it: what the agent is allowed to reach, and the ability to block it when it heads somewhere it shouldn’t. In a sandbox, those controls are enforced by the host, outside the agent’s reach, so the agent can’t switch them off or reason its way around them. Outbound traffic, credentials, and organization-wide policy all work this way. Control also means knowing what the agent can still touch, because a microVM can’t hide what you choose to share with it.

Runs its own Linux kernel in a microVM.

Needs the host socket or a nested daemon.

Uses a private Docker Engine inside the microVM.

Uses a direct read-write mount or an in-VM private clone.

Uses the container network and whatever controls its operator supplies.

Sends outbound traffic through a host proxy with deny-by-default policy.

Commonly receives environment variables, files, or mounted sockets.

Uses host-side credential injection for supported HTTP services.

Usually rebuilt from an image and explicit volumes.

Keeps packages, images, containers, and agent history until sbx rm.

Fits Compose, Kubernetes, and most CI systems.

Uses the sbx lifecycle and experimental environment files.

It has been revealed that these controls hold because they run outside the agent process. A rule the agent can reach is a rule it can work around, so the rules that matter live on the host. Outbound traffic goes through a host-side proxy with a deny-by-default policy, which means a destination the agent wants stays blocked until someone adds it to the list. Credentials follow the same logic. For supported HTTP services, the proxy injects them into outbound requests, so the agent can use a credential without the raw value ever entering the VM.

When one developer’s setup needs to become a team standard, Docker AI Governance can move network, filesystem, and MCP policy into organization-wide controls.

A microVM can’t hide what you choose to share with it, so the shared parts deserve the most attention.

The workspace is the largest of them. It’s mounted read-write by default, so the agent can edit or delete files in your project. Clone mode gives the agent a private in-VM clone to work in, which protects the host working tree, though the original repository stays readable inside the sandbox.

According to recent reports, MCP servers and skills are shared too. A local stdio MCP server runs on the host and shared agent skills use a host-side store, so the agent’s reach extends to both.

So whichever mode you pick, be sure to read the diff before you run modified code.

According to recent reports, docker Sandboxes may cost some configuration and a supported hypervisor. But Kits and environment files account for the configuration, and they’re also where you get choice over agents and tools and the capacity to reproduce a setup across a team.

Kits make setup repeatable by packaging tools, files, commands, network rules, credentials, and agent instructions. They’re published for different agents, tools, and IDEs, so you can swap what runs inside the sandbox without rebuilding the environment around it. An sbxenv.yaml file records one project’s sandbox configuration, and committing it to the repo lets a teammate recreate the same sandbox with one command, so every developer works from the same setup. (Kits are in early access and environment files are experimental, so plan for changes to both.).

Sources indicate that the host-enforced controls take some setup too. Network policy requires someone to decide which destinations belong in the workflow, credential mediation adds service bindings and approved domains, and clone mode adds a fetch step before changes land in the host repository.

Recent findings suggest that running a sandbox takes more from your machine than running a container does. It needs a supported hypervisor, which today means Apple silicon on macOS 14 or later, Windows Hypervisor Platform, or KVM on supported Ubuntu systems, and running inside another VM requires nested virtualization. The separate kernel and Docker Engine also consume more memory and disk than one additional container would.

In a recent development, if your machine is the limiting factor, Docker Cloud Sandboxes run the same microVM isolation on Docker-managed compute, and one command moves a sandbox between your laptop and the cloud. Local and cloud sandboxes keep separate secrets and network policies.

Choose a container when you control the code and its dependencies, and choose Docker Sandboxes when the workload generates or fetches code at runtime and needs its own boundary.

Reach for Docker Sandboxes when.

You control the code and its dependencies.

The workload generates or fetches code at runtime.

Execution is short-lived and rebuilt from an image.

The session accumulates state for hours.

The workload doesn’t need Docker, or runs in CI that already provides it.

The workload needs its own Docker Engine with no path to the host socket.

You want maximum density and a fit with Compose or Kubernetes.

You need host-enforced network and credential policy the workload can’t switch off.

The kernel boundary is enough for the code you’re running.

You want a hypervisor between the workload and your kernel.

If any of the signals below apply to your project, you should start with Docker Sandboxes.

It has been revealed that start with sbx run claude. Add clone mode, kits, network policy, credential mediation, and organization governance as your workflow grows.

Recent findings suggest that containers aren’t going anywhere. For services, CI jobs, and anything you package to ship, they draw the right boundary, and the ecosystem around them is the reason they’ll keep doing that work. A coding agent needs more than a container to be trusted with real work. It needs containment, meaning a boundary the model can’t rewrite, controls it can’t reason its way around, and the freedom to choose its tools and scale its setup.

In a recent development, docker Sandboxes provide that containment in a microVM that can still run your containers. The boundary is also what lets the agent move faster. With it in place, you can stop approving every command and let the agent get to work. Containment involves the whole environment around an agent: the boundary it runs in, what it can reach, which tools it uses, and how you reproduce it. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A coding agent in Docker Sandboxes runs inside an isolated VM, the sandbox controls which hosts it can reach, and credentials stay on the host behind a proxy. The same controls keep the agent from opening a docs page, reading a changelog, or looking up an API that shipped after its training cutoff, so it writes code against the version it remembers. The usual fix is to widen the allowlist until the agent can fetch anything, which hands back most of what the sandbox took away.

The Firecrawl kit gives the agent web search, page scraping, and site crawling through one added host, api.firecrawl.dev, and every page comes back as clean markdown.

The Firecrawl kit is a mixin (kind: mixin): it extends whichever workload you already run rather than defining a new sandbox. Its descriptor, firecrawl/firecrawl.yaml, declares four typed capabilities:.

The kit adds to the sandbox’s allowlist and does not narrow it, so everything else is set by your global sbx policy. Docker’s balanced preset allows package registries, GitHub, and a curated list of vendor domains, and returns a 403 for general websites, including most documentation sites, so Firecrawl is the agent’s route to those. Under deny-all, it is the agent’s only web host.

Kits are experimental and in Early Access, so the kit format and sbx commands may change. The steps below are current for October 2026; the repository README carries the latest.

Kit: docker.io/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl:1.0.0 on Docker Hub, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. Source: github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl-docker-sandbox.

Industry observers note that 1. Store the key once on the host. The command prompts for the key. Service secrets are global by default, so every sandbox that requests the firecrawl service can use it once you approve. The kit never sees the value; the proxy injects it at request time.

In a recent development, 2. Start a sandbox with the kit. The kit is an ordinary OCI image with its descriptor in the manifest, so a version tag is all you need. Each --kit adds a mixin to the workload, and the trailing . mounts your project directory.

It has been revealed that on the first run, sbx asks you to approve sending the firecrawl credential to api.firecrawl.dev. Accept the defaults. The credential is required: with no secret stored, sbx refuses to create the sandbox instead of letting the agent hit a 401 mid-task. A detached or CI run cannot answer the approval prompt, so approve interactively once or write the binding to ~/.config/sbx/credentials.yaml first.

3. Give the agent a task that needs the live web. Documentation sites are blocked under balanced, so this one has to go through Firecrawl.

Recent findings suggest that the kit’s instructions tell the agent to scrape blocked hosts through Firecrawl, so it calls fc.scrape(...) unprompted. Its response, trimmed:.

In a recent development, 4. Verify each layer. In the same session, ! runs shell commands inside the sandbox.

Expected: FIRECRAWL_API_KEY=proxy-managed. A real fc-... value here means the key came from somewhere other than the kit.

Expected: the page as markdown, starting with # Changelog and the latest version heading. The same URL returns a 403 to curl from inside the sandbox, so output here proves the SDK, the credential, and the network rule at once.

The kit also describes itself inside the sandbox. This prints the published descriptor, and the agent instructions sit next to it as firecrawl-context.md:.

In a recent development, running from source. To review or modify the kit before you run it, clone the repository and point --kit at the firecrawl/ directory; sbx builds source kits on demand:.

In a recent development, with the kit installed, the agent can look things up on the web while it works. The sandbox only needs to talk to one new address, api.firecrawl.dev, and Firecrawl fetches the pages for it. This matters because the default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites. Without the kit, you’d have to allow each site one by one, and every new site you allow makes the sandbox a little less locked down.

Without the kit, you had a choice to make. The default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites, so you could either leave the agent working from what it remembered, or allow sites one by one and loosen the sandbox a little each time. The kit avoids that choice. Your Firecrawl API key stays on your machine, behind the proxy, and the agent still reads the web as it is today.

The result is fewer made-up APIs, fewer failed upgrades, and less time spent correcting an agent that was confidently out of date.

According to recent reports, the kit is published under the firecrawl organization on Docker Hub as firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl, with source, changelog, and CI on GitHub under Apache-2.0. The SDK pin is verified against PyPI’s package hashes at install time, and every release passes Docker’s kit-tck conformance suite in CI. Review the descriptor and allowlist before running it, as with any kit.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is notoriously sensitive to numerical instability: even tiny discrepancies between rollout generation and gradient updates can destabilize training or stall convergence.
  • In a recent development, in practice, production RL stacks run sampling and training through separate, specialized execution paths.
  • Sources indicate that our zero train–inference mismatch (Zero-TIM) implementation, developed in Tunix and verified at multi-host scale across 64 TPU v5p chips (DP8×TP8), closes this numerical gap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is notoriously sensitive to numerical instability: even tiny discrepancies between rollout generation and gradient updates can destabilize training or stall convergence. In LLM RL, the model serves as the policy, π(action | previous tokens), and true on-policy learning requires every action in an patch to be generated and evaluated by that exact same policy. While a synchronous loop ensures each rollout batch is scored using the same weights that generated it, a critical numerical requirement remains: the sampler and trainer must evaluate that policy identically.

In a recent development, in practice, production RL stacks run sampling and training through separate, specialized execution paths. The sampler chooses each action token during incremental decoding and records its behavior logprob. The trainer evaluates the same token in batched forward-backward passes to compute its current logprob and gradients. Under the same weights, these differing execution paths can still assign different logprobs to the same token and context. The training schedule is on-policy, but the numerical execution has introduced a hidden off-policy gap that compounds over multi-turn trajectories.

Sources indicate that our zero train–inference mismatch (Zero-TIM) implementation, developed in Tunix and verified at multi-host scale across 64 TPU v5p chips (DP8×TP8), closes this numerical gap. At the same weights, the sampler and trainer assign bitwise-identical logprobs to the same action and token history—bringing state-of-the-art, true on-policy stability to TPU RL training.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pre-digital tech can't be transformed and automated.

Recent findings suggest that shanghai is one of the world’s largest and busiest cities but is surprisingly quiet. Electric automobiles cruise silently, chased by hushed flocks of electric scooters.

It has been revealed that when I visited in early November to attend the local edition of the AI Engineer conference, I found China's attitude to AI is also quite relaxed. That's not to say interest in the topic is low, but I didn't perceive any anxious artificial-general-intelligence-is-coming-and-will-destroy-us vibe.

The only conference talk that referenced AGI came from Ying Yang, a neuroscience PhD and serious influencer who has over 3.4 million followers on Chinese micro-blogging service Weibo, who enthused about the marketing and product development opportunities opening up to those who prepare for what’s coming.

AGI isn't P(doom) for the Chinese AI practitioners I met; it's a great new marketing tool.

Some of this may be due to the fact that the major US model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are effectively inaccessible on the Chinese side of the Great Firewall.

Engineers in China use DeepSeek or Kimi or GLM or MiniMax or MiMo or Qwen, all of which are now more than good enough for almost any task, and all offered without reference to The Terminator.

Recent findings suggest that that's not to say that Chinese engineers and designers aren't facing the same crisis of self-worth we've seen elsewhere. A spectacular keynote from Ryo Lu asked, "When we can do anything, do we still know what we want?" Are our measures of self-worth pointless when we can no longer prove who we are by how many lines of code we've written, or frameworks we've designed?

Ryo landed on a line I'm hearing more frequently: "I want to build tools to help me be more and more involved, not prove that I'm needed less and less.".

What followed highlighted just how good that tooling has become and what an AI engineer can do with it.

Industry observers note that I saw an impressive demo from AutoArk of a 35 billion-parameter model running in just 2.5GB of smartphone RAM on an iPhone 16 Pro. DYNA's Zhong Shen demonstrated how it builds robot hardware that will work with AI models updating every month.

My favorite presentation came from a bottle cap manufacturer called named Zhu Shihui, who reminded everyone in the audience that “the last mile is half the journey.”.

Zhu flayed the class of consultants who never realize some manufacturing equipment is pre-digital but still insist every process can be easily automated. Never mind that workers in those factories lack deep digital skills (Zhu's average employee is in their late 40s) and that companies of this sort operate on margins so thin that resources simply aren't available to mount a complete transformation. Instead of swinging in on an AI wrecking ball, Zhu suggested the best approach is to exercise humility by seeking out an organization's tacit knowledge and using that as the basis for transformation.

It has been revealed that not long after Zhu left the podium, one of my Australian fellow travelers noted the significant proportion of women at the conference. I hadn't noticed, because having equal numbers of men and women at an engineering conference felt perfectly normal. Yet it's not something I've ever experienced at AI events in Australia or America. Whatever else the Chinese are doing with AI, they've put gender politics aside in AI engineering.

To put that in context: not long after leaving Shanghai, Alice Huang became major global news. A Shanghainese woman working in AI might look suspicious to an American who only ever sees men working in the field. Fei-Fei Li, Mira Murati and Daniela Amodei stand out as exceptions that prove the rule, but none of them, despite stellar work, have anywhere near the profiles of their male peers. In China, it's different.

It's become commonplace to be dismissive of Chinese progress in AI, ascribing it to copying, "distillation" and outright theft. Yet the Chinese make both the best small models and the best robots, and are moving ever-closer to making them work well together.

According to recent reports, chinese labs share their results with their peers and their competitors: nearly every model, closed or open, has benefited from the research done by DeepSeek and Alibaba. Practicality, balance and openness seem to be serving them well. Perhaps, after OpenAI follows Anthropic out to the public markets, and shareholders get a voice, stability, sanity and a bit of quiet will cross the Pacific. Those are some Chinese imports I'm looking forward to. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the third post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.

According to recent reports, the series "Profiling in PyTorch" is meant to make you comfortable reading profiler traces and tables. In Part 1 we profiled basic math operations like addition and multiplication. We saw how the profiler table uncovers hotspots, and how the profiler trace demonstrates the order in which an algorithm runs over time.

In Part 2 we wrapped that addition and multiplication into a torch linear layer. We then stacked several linear layers on top of each other (a multilayer perceptron) and profiled that. Along the way we also profiled fused and hand-tuned kernels.

According to recent reports, from the perspective of the Transformer architecture, the next logical step for us to profile is yet another fundamental algorithm, attention. While being infamous for its quadratic-time complexity, many clever tricks exist to mitigate that glitch and make it fast. Our goal here is not to cover every trick in detail. Instead, we want to see how each one looks different under the profiler.

Sources indicate that the scripts for this blog post live here: 04_a_naive_attention.py, 04_b_inplace_ops_attention.py, 04_c_sdpa_attention.py, and 04_d_kernels_attention.py. Like before, it helps to open them in a separate tab and walk through the code as you read. We use an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to set up a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.

Attention works with Queries (q), Keys (k), and Values (v). The interaction between them can be written as a short sequence of steps:.

Industry observers note that so attention is really a collection of primitive operations. Some of them we already know (the matmuls), and the rest are easy to spot. Let's write a naive attention module in PyTorch and profile it.

According to recent reports, before opening the trace, let's do our usual exercise and guess what we should see. Tracing the forward of this module, we expect:.

Sources indicate that figure 1 shows the CPU lane of the profile (the GPU lane is folded so it does not overwhelm us). Inside attn_fwd (our annotated forward call) we can see exactly the operations we guessed. The matmul is an old friend by now, and the new operations are easy to spot:.

Now let's unfold the GPU lane and see which kernels were actually launched.

Sources indicate that figure 2 shows the GPU lane next to the CPU lane. Let's zoom into a single attn_fwd block on the GPU lane to look at the kernels one by one.

Figure 3 lets us read off the individual kernels for one profiler step:.

Five of these are expected. The memory copy is the odd one out, so where does this come from? The clue is that PyTorch has in-place operations. When you operate on a tensor the ordinary (out-of-place) way, PyTorch often makes a copy, applies the requested operation to it, and returns the copy. Following the sequence of operations, the culprit here is our masked_fill.

What if we replaced this with an in-place operation?

All we change is masked_fill to masked_fill_ (note the trailing underscore, PyTorch's convention for in-place operations), and we run the same script.

Let's look at the trace and see if something changed.

It has been revealed that the in-place version (Figure 5) wraps far fewer CPU ops inside the masking step than the out-of-place version (Figure 4). This is an encouraging signal. Let's unfold the GPU lane to confirm what happened there.

On the GPU lane the Memcpy kernel is gone for good (Figures 6 and 7). With a one line change we shaved a whole kernel off each forward pass. This may not look like much on its own, but remember this is a single attention operation. In the context of a transformer based large model (LLMs, Diffusion models, etc.), it repeats once per layer, and there are many layers, so the saving adds up rapidly (and if it earns you a raise, sharing at least 10% with us feels only fair).

It has been revealed that out-of-place is PyTorch's default for a reason. To compute gradients, autograd has to remember the tensor values it saw on the forward pass, because many backward formulas reuse them. An in-place operation overwrites those values in memory, so the backward pass would read the wrong numbers. Due to the fact that we run forward under torch.no_grad, in-place is safe for us, with no backward pass and nothing to corrupt. It is also noteworthy that in-place operations do not only save time (like we see in our case) but also memory (due to no extra copy) which is great for large tensors like logits!

We just built attention from primitives, and even shaved off a Memcpy. The good news is that the PyTorch team has done all of this for us, and packaged the whole pipeline into a single function:.

In a recent development, this one line replaces our hand written module, and is_causal=True even saves us from building the mask by hand. It is worth pausing to appreciate how much this one call hides. And it hides more than just code lines. Scaled Dot Product Attention (SDPA) does not have a single implementation. Under the hood it dispatches to one of the several backends and picks the fastest one that supports our inputs (dtype, head dimension, mask, hardware, etc.).

The official SDPA tutorial walks us through this selection, and the backends themselves are listed in the torch.nn.attention.SDPBackend enum:.

It has been revealed that normally SDPA chooses for us, but we can pin a specific backend with the torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel context manager. This is what we do in our scripts. This lets us profile each backend on its own and read how differently they show up in the trace. Let's go one at a time.

Recent findings suggest that before we open anything, let's guess. We have replaced hand written attention (matmul, mul, mask, softmax, matmul) with a single one liner, so we should expect the trace to get simpler and faster. Fewer kernels, less CPU dispatch, maybe even a fused kernel. Let's check the profiler table first.

This is our first surprise, the one liner is 3.7x slower.

Opening the trace (Figure 9) shows why the alarm bells ring, the math backend launches 20 GPU kernels per forward instead of the 5 launched with our naive attention implementation (Figure 8). This is the opposite of what we guessed. Let's figure out why this happens.

In Part 2 we learned to read a kernel name like a fingerprint. Let's use that habit here:.

The A100s we used to capture these traces ship with Tensor Cores, specialised hardware for accelerated matmuls that is known to be far faster than the ordinary CUDA cores. To see why that matters here, it helps to know what lives inside a GPU. A Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) is the compute unit of a GPU, and each SM has two kinds of arithmetic units, the CUDA cores and the Tensor Cores. CUDA cores are general purpose and process a handful of elements at a time, while Tensor Cores multiply and accumulate a whole small matrix tile in a single instruction. So the question is simple, "Is each backend actually using the fast path?".

The kernel names answer it. The s16816 in the naive kernel (Figure 10) is the signature of a bfloat16 Tensor Core matmul (the 16x8x16 Tensor Core instruction), so the naive version is on the fast path. sgemm (Figure 11) is the classic single precision (FP32) matmul that runs on the ordinary CUDA cores. In other words, the math backend never touches the Tensor Cores at all: to trade speed for numerical accuracy it upcasts tensors to FP32 (doubling the data moved, even when the inputs are in bf16) and falls back to the slower CUDA cores.

In a recent development, in the naive version we built the causal mask once and reused it. Here we passed is_causal=True and the math backend materialized one for us, on every single call. You can watch it happen on the CPU lane:.

Here is what we see in Figure 12.

Industry observers note that on the GPU this demonstrates up as a triu_tril_kernel, several where kernels, and an add_. The convenience flag that let us stop thinking about the mask did not remove the work, it just moved it one layer down, where the mask is rebuilt from scratch every forward.

Our hand written version called plain aten::softmax. The math backend calls aten::_safe_softmax, and the difference is again visible as extra kernels (Figure 13):.

Recent findings suggest that A row that is fully masked (every entry -inf) would make an ordinary softmax compute exp(-inf)/sum(exp(-inf)) = 0/0 = NaN. _safe_softmax guards against exactly that. Our naive kernel never bothered, and would have quietly produced NaNs in that corner case.

It has been revealed that put together, the math backend is the reference implementation. It is a straightforward, dtype-safe, NaN-safe decomposition of attention into primitive ATen ops. It is essentially the naive attention we wrote by hand, but more careful. That carefulness is exactly what makes it extremely slow.

Its job is not to be fast, but to always work. This makes it the perfect baseline. Every backend we profile next (flash, efficient, cudnn) is trying to collapse the 20 GPU kernels into essentially one fused kernel that stays in bf16 and never materializes the intermediate matrices at all.

Where the math backend launched 20 kernels across one profiler step, the efficient backend launches only one fmha_cutlassF_bf16_aligned_64x64_rf_sm80 (as seen in Figure 14).

Let's decode the name of the kernel:.

According to recent reports, this is the memory efficient attention kernel that grew out of Meta's xformers library and was upstreamed into PyTorch. When people say "the xformers backend," this fmha_cutlassF kernel is what they mean.

The void pytorch_flash kernel (Figure 15) is FlashAttention-2 (Tri Dao's implementation), vendored into PyTorch.

Before we read the trace any further, it is worth answering the question you should be asking by now: why is there a whole backend named "flash", and why does it matter so much?

Let's go back to the math backend for a moment. Its real problem was not the count of 20 kernels, it was what those kernels handed to each other.

Recent findings suggest that step 1 builds the full score matrix attn = q . k.T, which is [seq, seq] per head. For a sequence length of 4096 that is 4096 x 4096 ≈ 16 million numbers for a single head. That matrix is written out to the HBM (the GPU's main memory), if there is even enough space to do so. Then, it is read back to be scaled, written again for the mask, read again for the softmax, and so on. Attention's cost is dominated by this back and forth traffic to HBM, not by the matmuls themselves.

Recent findings suggest that flashAttention attacks exactly this. Instead of computing the whole s matrix and only then reducing it, it walks over k and v in tiles, keeps a running softmax as it goes (the "online softmax" trick), and accumulates the output one tile at a time. The full [seq, seq] score matrix is never written to HBM, it only ever lives on-chip. This is the single idea that lets the entire attention pipeline collapse into one fused kernel that stays in bf16 on the Tensor cores.

Here is where flash surprises people who read profiler footprints. It is the fastest backend, yet the profiler reports it with very low occupancy (shown in Figure 16). To see why that is fine, we need three quick definitions.

A GPU kernel is essentially a series of instructions executed by many small execution units. These individual execution units (threads) take care of loading variables, adding them together, storing them back, etc. For each kernel, we launch many, many threads, and to keep track of them, we group them by blocks.

Blocks are scheduled onto Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), the main compute units of a GPU. A block lives entirely on one SM, and an SM can host multiple blocks at once if it has enough resources. Those resources include registers, shared memory, maximum resident threads, and maximum resident warps. So when we say a kernel has low occupancy, we mean each SM has fewer resident warps than it could theoretically support.

According to recent reports, if you want to know more about threads, blocks, grids, etc. here is a great resource.

If you click the flash kernel in the trace, its footprint tells the story (Figure 17).

Recent findings suggest that flash uses a lot of per-thread registers and a large amount of shared memory per block. For example, if a block has 128 threads and each thread uses 255 registers, that block needs 128 × 255 = 32,640 registers. On an Ampere SM with 65,536 registers, only two such blocks fit at once. Each 128-thread block has 128 / 32 = 4 warps, so two blocks give only 8 resident warps. Against a maximum of 64 resident warps, that is roughly 13% occupancy. Flash has low occupancy not because it is poorly optimized, but because each block is deliberately very "heavy" in on-chip resource usage.

According to recent reports, and that is the whole point. High occupancy helps hide latency by keeping many warps ready to run, but it does not make the work itself efficient. Flash spends those registers and that shared memory on purpose, to keep attention tiles on-chip, reuse data aggressively, and avoid ever materializing the full attention matrix in global memory.

In a recent development, by now the pattern is familiar. Like flash and efficient, cuDNN gives us one fused, flash-style kernel per forward (Figure 18). So the natural question is: if flash already fuses attention, why does PyTorch ship yet another flash backend? The answer is who writes the kernel and how it is built, and that difference is what makes the trace look different.

Flash and efficient are fixed, pre-compiled kernels vendored into PyTorch. You get the same binary every time. cuDNN is NVIDIA's own deep learning library, and its attention kernel is generated and tuned for the specific problem at hand. It is closer in spirit to torch.compile's codegen than to a fixed cuBLAS binary. You can read that straight off the (very long) kernel name:.

That one fact, generated per problem, explains everything else that looks unusual in the trace.

In a recent development, no transposes: The CPU lane goes from _cudnn_attention_forward straight to a couple of aten::empty allocations and then the kernel, with zero aten::transpose (Figures 19, 20 and 21). Flash and efficient each insert four (metadata) transposes to reshape the tensors while cuDNN consumes the native [B, H, S, D] layout directly because its generator emits a kernel for that layout.

It introduces through cuLaunchKernelEx, not cudaLaunchKernel: Every other kernel in this whole series went through the runtime API cudaLaunchKernel. cuDNN uses the driver-level extended launch, which carries launch attributes (Figure 22).

The profiler reports 0% achieved occupancy: Do not take that at face value, it is a measurement gap, not a stalled GPU. CUPTI (the profiling backend) cannot attribute occupancy to a driver-API (cuLaunchKernelEx) launch the way it does for cudaLaunchKernel, so the field reads 0. The footprint fills in the truth (Figure 23): 240 registers × 256 threads = 61,440 registers per block against the SM's 65,536, so only one block fits per SM (8 warps ≈ 12.5%), right in line with flash.

The "no transposes" story tempts us to expect cuDNN to be the leanest backend on the CPU. It is the opposite.

Even with zero transpose ops, cuDNN spends about 214 µs per forward on the CPU, more than flash (138) or efficient (117). Almost all of it sits in aten::scaled_dot_product_attention self time (26% of the whole run) and _cudnn_attention_forward. That is cuDNN's runtime engine selecting and preparing the strategy (the "knob" search) on every call.

According to recent reports, fewer visible ATen ops did not mean less CPU work, it moved the work into the library, where the profiler can only show it as one fat, opaque bar. When a trace suddenly gets cleaner, the work has not always disappeared, sometimes it has just moved somewhere the profiler cannot break down.

Recent findings suggest that on the GPU, cuDNN (186.3 µs) lands between efficient and flash. On this very flash-friendly shape, hand-written FlashAttention-2 edges it out. cuDNN often wins on other shapes (larger head dimensions, different sequence lengths) precisely because its generator retunes per problem, but that retuning is also what you just paid for on the CPU.

Before we wrap up, here is a single table to review every attention variant we profiled and the one lesson each trace taught us.

If you take away only one thing from the whole series, let it be the habit we repeated before every single trace which is to guess first, then look.

Sources indicate that state out loud what you expect the trace to contain, open it, and treat any mismatch as the most interesting thing on the screen. Every real insight in these three posts, the hidden Memcpy, the addmm epilogue, the 20 kernel math backend, flash's "wrong-looking" occupancy, cuDNN's fat CPU bar, came from a guess that did not match the trace.

It has been revealed that profiling is not a separate, intimidating skill reserved for GPU experts. It is just the discipline of looking closely and asking "wait, why is that happening?" until the answer clicks. You now have the vocabulary and the reflexes to do that on your own models. Open a trace, form a guess, and go find the mismatch.

Sources indicate that thanks for reading the Profiling in PyTorch series. Now go profile something. 🤗.

Some of us in the team are non-english speakers and think LLMs (which are mostly trained in the English Language) can rectify silly grammar mistakes or rephrase sentences that sound less intimidating and cleaner. Hope this helps with the idea of "why should I read, if this was LLM generated". 🤗.

Thanks for the series, really delightful!

The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt.
  • A model decision is not automatically an authorized action.
  • Industry observers note that the answer can’t rely only on the model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt. It can execute code, access files, connect to services, and call external tools. That creates a upcoming security question for enterprises: how do you give an agent enough freedom to be useful without giving it more access than it actually needs?

A model decision is not automatically an authorized action. That distinction becomes important the moment an agent can turn a model output into an action in a real system.

Industry observers note that the answer can’t rely only on the model. Agent behavior can vary, while security controls need to be clear and enforceable. That means putting controls around the environment where the agent runs, what it can access, which tools it can use, and what happens when a policy allows or blocks an action. For a CISO, this creates a trust gap. Approving the use of AI agents means being able to answer more than whether the model is capable: what access does the agent have, where are those boundaries enforced, and what evidence is available afterward? The goal is to let teams adopt agents without making model behavior itself the security boundary.

Docker AI Governance approaches this through three areas: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility.

Together, they address three practical questions security teams need answered: Where can the agent operate? What can it do? And can we see what happened?

In this article, I use “trust layer” as shorthand for the infrastructure between what an agent wants to do and what the organization actually allows it to do.

There is a related trust question too: what software artifacts are these agentic workflows building and using? Docker Hardened Images address that software supply-chain side of the problem, alongside the runtime controls discussed below.

Figure 1: The three layers of Docker AI Governance: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility.

Industry observers note that an agent needs enough access to get real work done. A coding agent may need to install packages, build containers, edit project files, or connect to external services. The security challenge is deciding where those actions are allowed before the agent starts taking them.

According to recent reports, docker Sandboxes give each agent an isolated microVM environment a lightweight virtual machine with its own Docker Engine, filesystem, and network. Docker AI Governance adds policy around that environment so security teams can control network and filesystem access centrally.

Network policies can allow or block specific domains, IP ranges, and ports. Filesystem policies control which host paths can be mounted into a sandbox and whether that access is read-only or read-write. These controls are enforced at the network proxy and filesystem mount layers rather than depending on the agent to follow an instruction.

For an organization, that means the same boundaries can follow developers across their sandboxes instead of being configured differently on every machine. Teams still get the access they need for their work, but an individual agent cannot simply expand those boundaries on its own.

A developer can check the effective boundary before starting the agent:.

The key part is that the result comes from the active policy, not from an instruction the agent is expected to follow.

This answers the first governance question: Where can the agent operate?

Once an agent has a controlled place to run, the next question is what it should be allowed to do through external tools.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) gives agents a common way to connect to external tools, services, and capabilities, but that also expands what an agent can act on. For enterprise use, making a tool available should not automatically mean every agent can use it.

Docker AI Governance puts policy around MCP activity handled through Docker’s MCP Gateway. Administrators can control which MCP servers may be registered and what agents can do through them, including tool calls, resources, prompts, and approval requirements. These organization policies are written in Cedar, a policy language used to express authorization rules. When MCP policy enforcement is active, governed requests are denied unless a matching policy permits them. For example, a policy can permit read-only tool calls for a specific registered MCP server:.

It has been revealed that here, readOnly comes from the MCP tool’s annotations. Those annotations are supplied by the server and are advisory, so this example relies on metadata provided by that server.

This makes tool access an explicit policy decision rather than something left to each agent or developer to configure independently. A team can be given access to the tools it needs, while other servers or actions remain unavailable. Policies can also require confirmation for specific tool calls when an action needs an additional checkpoint.

Industry observers note that one boundary is worth making clear: MCP policies apply to activity handled by Docker’s MCP Gateway. If an agent connects directly to a remote MCP server from inside a sandbox, that connection falls under the sandbox’s network policy instead.

With the environment constrained and tool access governed, we can answer the second question: What can the agent do?

It has been revealed that setting a policy is only part of the job. Security teams also need to know when that policy was applied, what action triggered it, and whether the action was allowed or denied.

Industry observers note that docker AI Governance records sandbox policy decisions and sandbox session events as structured audit records. Each record captures details such as the principal, action, target, decision, and time. The records contain governance metadata rather than the contents of prompts or agent responses.

According to recent reports, audit records can be kept locally or delivered to the cloud. With cloud delivery enabled, teams can search the organization-wide record, export it for further analysis, or forward events into existing SIEM (security information and event management) workflows.

Denied actions are especially useful. A team can see not only that an action failed, but that a governance rule blocked it and why. Allowed decisions matter too: they provide a record of how policy was applied while the agent was working.

Industry observers note that current audit coverage includes Docker Sandboxes policy decisions and sandbox session events. The same schema can support additional Docker AI sources as they become available.

That closes the third part of the governance loop: Can we see what happened?

Industry observers note that AI Governance controls access around the agent at runtime. There is a separate question that matters to the workflows those agents participate in: what container images and software artifacts are they building, testing, or deploying?

Docker Hardened Images provide minimal, secure, and production-ready container images, Helm charts, and system packages maintained by Docker.

Sources indicate that in practical terms, this gives teams evidence about what is inside an image and how that image was produced. Docker Hardened Images include signed SBOMs, VEX information, cryptographic signatures, and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance. Instead of simply trusting where an image came from, teams can inspect what is inside it and verify information about how it was built.

For organizations with additional compliance requirements, Docker also provides FIPS-enabled and STIG-ready variants through relevant DHI offerings. These capabilities sit alongside the broader DHI security and supply-chain controls rather than making any single standard the foundation by itself.

AI Governance and Docker Hardened Images solve different parts of the trust problem. Governance controls the authority an agent has while it works; DHI helps establish trust in the container artifacts that the workflow depends on.

Figure 2: Docker Hardened Images combine minimal container images with signed supply-chain metadata and verifiable build provenance.

Consider a developer using a coding agent to investigate an matter, revision a service, and use an approved internal tool along the way.

Sources indicate that the agent begins inside a Docker Sandbox. It can work with the project and run the commands needed for the task, but its access is still bounded by policy. If it tries to reach a network destination or mount a host path that the organization has not allowed, the applicable sandbox policy can block that access.

Now suppose the agent needs an MCP tool to look up information from another service. The request goes through Docker’s MCP Gateway, where organization policy determines whether that server and tool are permitted. A routine lookup might be allowed, while a more sensitive tool call could require confirmation or remain unavailable altogether.

According to recent reports, for governance activity at the moment covered by AI Governance Audit Logs, Docker records the policy decision and relevant session metadata. Security teams can see who initiated the activity, what policy-controlled action was evaluated, and whether it was allowed or denied. Those records can then feed the organization’s existing monitoring and SIEM workflow.

Sources indicate that if that same agent builds or tests a containerized application, the software entering the workflow matters too. Docker Hardened Images provide a more verifiable software foundation for that workflow, while AI Governance controls what the agent is authorized to do at runtime.

Sources indicate that the model is still making decisions about how to complete the task. What changes is the authority around those decisions. The agent can work autonomously inside the boundaries the organization has defined, while access outside those boundaries remains a policy decision.

That is the practical value of the three layers working together:.

Sandbox Policies define where the agent can operate.

MCP Tool Governance defines what tools it can use.

Audit + Visibility indicates how governed activity was handled.

Industry observers note that taken together, the pattern is straightforward: define the boundary, check it before the agent starts working, enforce it while the agent is running, and use the resulting audit trail to understand what happened. If a boundary needs to change, the policy changes, not the expectation that the model will simply behave differently.

The challenge with agentic AI is not simply that agents can make decisions. It is that those decisions can now lead directly to actions.

According to recent reports, that makes the boundary around the agent just as notable as the model itself. Docker AI Governance addresses that boundary through Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility: controlling where agents can operate, what tools they can use, and how governed activity is recorded.

Docker Hardened Images address a related supply-chain concern by helping teams work with smaller, verifiable container artifacts.

The goal is not to remove autonomy from agents. It is to make sure autonomy does not automatically come with unlimited authority.

As agents take on more real work, that distinction will matter more and more.

Meet the Newly introduced Docker: Built to Run on Trust

💡 Key Takeaways
