  • Let’s start with the massive picture.
  • Sources indicate that but it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Docker is officially launching its fresh brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change.

Let’s start with the massive picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.

Sources indicate that but it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents?

That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a fresh Docker.

A upcoming Docker, but a familiar story.

Ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a new way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one big constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment.

Enter a manufacturer you might have heard of: Docker.

Together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure. Docker turned the frustration of “Well, it works on my machine!” into the assurance that “Yes, it works everywhere.”.

Today, of course, the challenge confronting us is new and evolving, and we all need to evolve with it. We cannot simply continue to do what we’ve always done and expect to succeed in this new era. That applies to business leaders, developers, tech companies, everyone. It certainly applies to Docker. That’s what this rebrand is about: evolving to meet the moment for our customers.

According to recent reports, let me be unequivocal: this is not about leaving Docker’s legacy or heritage behind. We’ve spent more than a decade earning your trust. This is about building on that foundation, not replacing it.

Sources indicate that the qualities you value us for aren’t changing. We’re still committed to openness and industry collaboration. We’re still, and always will be, developer-first. We’re still fanatical about simplicity, and about showing up everywhere you need us.

Recent findings suggest that on the product front, the containers you know and love aren’t going anywhere. Containers still play a huge role in the software development lifecycle. As long as that’s the case, Docker will continue leading the way.

Agents have introduced a fresh problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors.

Agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control.

Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe.

In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the latest Docker is all about trust.

Trust Docker because our track record speaks for itself. Trust Docker because we’re proven, neutral, and secure. Trust Docker because it’s pretty darn clear you can’t trust the agents to manage themselves.

Recent findings suggest that trust us because we have a software supply chain that is already the standard for building securely. Trust us because nobody isolates agents where they run better than we do. Trust us because we’re taking a comprehensive approach to improving governance and minimizing risk across the entire enterprise.

Trust Docker because we’re not egotistical enough to think we can solve a challenge this big alone. Trust us because everything about our history, our heritage, and our actions over the past year tells you we’ll partner with the smartest and build alongside the best, and not create vendor lock-in.

Most of all, trust Docker because we’re not just talking the talk. We’ve got the goods to back it up: trusted supply chain for your agents to build from, trusted runtime to isolate your agents, and a trusted ecosystem to ensure all the layers of trust are covered, whether made by Docker or not.

As our product team innovated to meet the moment and our messaging in the market began to shift, one thing became clear: the speed and scale of evolution happening inside Docker called for an equally momentous evolution on the outside. Something that makes it unmistakably clear that it’s a newly introduced day for Docker. Something that says and highlights, loud and clear, for all the world to see, that Docker is not just about containers anymore.

Something, dare I say, whale sized.

I’m talking, of course, about our beloved Moby.

Sources indicate that if you know Docker, then you know Moby, and if Docker is evolving, Moby should too. The only question was to how and to what extent? We looked at a lot of whales, folks. (I may or may not have been seeing whales in my sleep.) Ultimately, with the help of our friends at the strategic brand transformation tech giant, Motto, we landed on a new Moby for the new Docker.

Watch Moby’s transformation here:.

According to recent reports, in many ways, Moby is a microcosm for Docker and the changes we’re making: the Moby you love and trust, evolved for a fresh era. Just as the new Docker is no longer singularly defined by containers, neither is the new Moby.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our upcoming website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think.

Sources indicate that wherever this upcoming era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that I briefly helped with Microsoft Australia’s PR efforts in the early 2000s, when IE 6 and Windows were so bug-prone they essentially represented a welcome mat for hackers and required a deluge of patches admins couldn’t handle.
  • A quarter of a century later, Microsoft’s business practices still make its customers reluctantly share the cost of its failings – most recently last week’s massive M365 outage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft is asking customers to apply for reimbursement. They should protest.

Industry observers note that I briefly helped with Microsoft Australia’s PR efforts in the early 2000s, when IE 6 and Windows were so bug-prone they essentially represented a welcome mat for hackers and required a deluge of patches admins couldn’t handle. Microsoft responded to that mess with a message about security being a shared responsibility involving people, process, and technology.

A quarter of a century later, Microsoft’s business practices still make its customers reluctantly share the cost of its failings – most recently last week’s massive M365 outage.

To protest that mess, Microsoft customers should create a new cloudy meltdown – on the pages the software giant uses to process applications for compensation after it fails to meet service level agreements.

Yes, you read that right: “applications.” When Microsoft experiences an outage, customers must apply to get the service credits they’re entitled by finding the “Outage ID” related to each incident. The application page is buried deep in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center and the Outage ID is recorded elsewhere. Microsoft appears not to offer a facility for bulk uploads, so the channel partners who manage so many M365 implementations have extra work to do.

According to recent reports, that’s outrageous because the implicit promise of the cloud is that it delivers more value for less effort. Yet Microsoft requires users to do extra work to seek redress for its mistakes.

Cloud also delivers fat profits for investors. Which is probably why Microsoft, which can clearly bill its customers regularly and reliably and therefore knows which services they use, hasn’t done the work to link its uptime meters and billing systems so it can automate crediting customers after outages.

According to recent reports, I understand Microsoft thinks AI is quite good at that sort of integration. Maybe its enormously reduced workforce will need it to get the job done.

But rather than vibe-coding its way out of this, decency demands Microsoft quickly decide that all users impacted by last week’s automatically receive service credits, rather than asking them apply for their entitlements.

If Microsoft doesn’t get proactive, the magnitude of this outage represents a moment in which its customers can show the software giant it must do better – perhaps by filing so many applications for credit that managers who oversee Redmond’s systems and finances can’t help but notice a spike of activity.

According to recent reports, thinks of this as a distributed denial of satisfaction attack signaling that Microsoft can't solve this particular outage with a glib apology and a blog post. ®.

Introducing Real World VoiceEQ: Measuring the human quality of voice AI

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Existing benchmarks suggest voice AI is nearing human-level performance but real-world conversations tell a different story.
  • It has been revealed that voice is rapidly becoming AI's primary interface.
  • According to recent reports, over the last few years, voice models have improved dramatically.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Existing benchmarks suggest voice AI is nearing human-level performance but real-world conversations tell a different story.

It has been revealed that voice is rapidly becoming AI's primary interface. From customer support and healthcare to education, entertainment, and personal assistants, speech is increasingly replacing text as the way people interact with AI.

According to recent reports, over the last few years, voice models have improved dramatically. Word error rates continue to fall, latency has reached conversational speeds, and many established benchmarks are approaching saturation. Yet anyone who regularly uses voice AI knows something still feels off.

Voice models can sound like different people over the course of a conversation, miss hesitation or uncertainty, and struggle with accents, noise, or emotional speech. Those shortcomings are easy to miss in benchmarks focused on latency and word error rate. People care whether a voice system can truly listen, respond appropriately, and remain natural and reliable in real conversations.

According to recent reports, to measure those qualities, we built Real World VoiceEQ—a benchmark designed to evaluate the human quality of voice interaction. It assesses whether voice systems can recognize, produce, and respond to the acoustic information transcripts leave out, from tone and emotion to speaker identity and background context.

Real World VoiceEQ evaluates more than 40 leading proprietary and open-source voice models across 15+ key evaluation dimensions and more than 60 metrics spanning Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Text-to-Speech (TTS), Speech-to-Speech (S2S), and Speech Understanding.

Real World VoiceEQ was developed from more than 1 million individual human ratings collected across different demographics, speaking styles, and acoustic environments. The current benchmark includes 785,000 TTS ratings and 48,000 STS ratings, making it one of the largest human evaluations of voice AI conducted to date.

Every evaluation was conducted using Kairos, our flexible, voice-native evaluation platform. The same infrastructure enables frontier AI labs and enterprises to run custom evaluations tailored to specific use cases, identify granular failure modes in production voice systems, generate human preference data, and continuously improve models through reinforcement learning and human feedback.

The race for a single "best" voice model is giving way to a collection of specialized capabilities.

Today's leading systems optimize for different strengths—including technical accuracy, emotional understanding, conversational intelligence, expressiveness, and robustness. One model that excels at repeating booking reference numbers, bank account details, or complex pharmaceutical names may struggle to produce emotionally expressive speech. Another may sound remarkably natural but be less reliable on precision-oriented tasks.

As voice AI matures, measuring progress increasingly requires evaluating these capabilities independently rather than collapsing them into a single overall score. In our TTS evaluations, no system configuration ranked among the top five across all eight capability groups—underscoring why there is no single "best" voice model.

According to recent reports, speech-to-Speech models highlighted the widest variation of any category we evaluated. Some systems recognized emotion exceptionally well but struggled to respond naturally. We found that access to audio did not guarantee that agents used the paralinguistic information it contained. Some systems remained largely transcript-driven, relying on the words being spoken while overlooking cues such as tone, pacing, hesitation, emphasis, and volume.

Humans naturally use these cues to infer confidence, uncertainty, frustration, sarcasm, and empathy. Today's models often miss them.

In a recent development, imagine a banking agent asking whether you recognize a potentially fraudulent transaction. A confident "Yes" and a hesitant "…yes…" may have completely different meanings, even though the transcript is identical. Humans recognize that difference immediately. Many of today's voice models do not.

According to recent reports, many established benchmarks are nearing their limits and don't reflect real-world conditions. Models still struggle with accented speech, overlapping speakers, emotion, background noise, and longer conversations. In our evaluation, performance varies far more across leading open-source and proprietary models than traditional benchmarks suggest. In one example, transcription word error rates on noise-backed speech were roughly four times higher than on music-backed speech, showing how a single background-audio score can hide the real failure mode.

According to recent reports, in preliminary research, we found signs that some models may be optimized for established public benchmarks. Several reproduced known errors in reference transcripts, followed arbitrary spelling conventions, and even reconstructed masked words that were not present in the audio.

Industry observers note that LLMs are now widely used to evaluate text-based models, but our findings suggest that speech-language models (SLMs) should be used more carefully for voice evaluation. When we compared leading SLMs with trained human raters on text-to-speech assessments, agreement was highest on tasks with clear, verifiable answers, such as pronunciation accuracy.

Agreement declined on more subjective evaluations. SLMs sometimes appeared to infer emotion from text-based contextual cues, and agreement was weakest for open-ended judgments such as whether a voice fit an acting role or maintained a consistent identity. Automated evaluators can be valuable for well-defined tasks, but they are not yet a substitute for human listeners when judgments depend on acoustic-context, perception, and social interpretation.

As voice becomes one of AI's defining interfaces, speed and technical accuracy alone will no longer determine which systems succeed. The models people ultimately choose will be those that can understand, express, and respond like humans—not just under ideal benchmark conditions, but across the complexity of real-world conversation.

Industry observers note that for decades, speech AI has advanced by optimizing against quantitative metrics on standardized benchmarks; from WER for transcription accuracy to objective perceptual metrics like PESQ and DNSMOS for speech quality. We hope Real World VoiceEQ can extend this paradigm by providing a human-grounded metric for evaluating the components of synthetic voice interactions.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article explains how Elixir implements type inference and type narrowing using reverse arrows: a small set of composable ideas, rather than special cases hardcoded into the type checker.
  • Thanks to this work, the upcoming Elixir v1.21 passes all tests in the If-T: Type Narrowing Benchmark by Guo et al..
  • The type system was made possible thanks to a partnership between CNRS and Remote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article explains how Elixir implements type inference and type narrowing using reverse arrows: a small set of composable ideas, rather than special cases hardcoded into the type checker.

Thanks to this work, the upcoming Elixir v1.21 passes all tests in the If-T: Type Narrowing Benchmark by Guo et al.. This means v1.21 can find even more sure bugs in existing Elixir programs and, once type signatures are introduced, narrowing will give us more precise types and fewer false positives.

The type system was made possible thanks to a partnership between CNRS and Remote. The development work is currently sponsored by Fresha, Supermethod and Dashbit.

Elixir performs type inference by refining the dynamic type. This is quite different from how inference and gradual typing are implemented in most type systems, so let’s break it down.

In a recent development, in many gradual languages, the dynamic type, often known as any, is a “black box” and can be used in any context. For example, imagine this Elixir function, where x starts with type dynamic(), as there is no type signature:.

Recent findings suggest that the program above uses x both as a number (more precisely, as integer() or float() in x * 2) and as a bitstring in byte_size(x). In some gradual type systems, the type checker will accept the program above, even though it will crash at runtime, because the dynamic type can be used in any context.

However, in Elixir, the dynamic() type can be refined, and the above will report the following typing violation:.

According to recent reports, as you can see in the error message, Elixir infers that the type of x after x * 2 is a dynamic(float() or integer()). This means that x can be given to any function that accepts at least one of float() or integer(). However, because byte_size(x) expects a bitstring, we have a typing violation.

In a recent development, this is possible because dynamic() in Elixir actually means dynamic(term()), where term() is the top type. Then, as a variable is used throughout the code, its dynamic type is refined by intersecting its type with the arguments of the functions the code invokes. In other words, we go through the following steps:.

Industry observers note that x is given to x * 2. The left operand of * expects integer() or float(), which we then intersect with term(), and therefore x gains the type dynamic(integer() or float()).

x is given to byte_size(x), which expects a bitstring. The intersection of integer() or float() with bitstring() is empty, which will lead to a typing violation.

Now, let’s take a look at this program:.

This time, we pass x to the remainder function, rem, which expects all of its inputs to be integers. This means that, at the end of this function, Elixir will correctly infer that x can only be an integer, because x was refined from dynamic(term()) to dynamic(integer() or float()) and then only to dynamic(integer()). The inferred type for using_x_as_integer is a function, commonly written using the arrow notation: dynamic(integer()) -> :ok.

In a recent development, the best part is that all dynamic types in Elixir are refined and therefore the type system is always doing its best to find bugs, even in the presence of dynamism. And the refinement itself is often quite precise, thanks to reverse arrows, which we will explore next.

In a recent development, an arrow is the type of a function: integer() -> boolean() is an arrow that indicates “given an integer, this function returns a boolean”. The type on the left of the arrow is its domain (what it accepts) and the type on the right is its codomain (what it returns). Every function has arrows, whether they come from a type signature you wrote or are inferred by Elixir from the function’s clauses.

Industry observers note that functions in Elixir can be typed with multiple arrows. As an exercise, let’s take a function that negates numbers, such as negate(1) returning -1:.

You could give it this type signature with a single arrow:.

In a recent development, however, this type says that, if you give it an integer, it may return a float, which is never the case! This signature is too broad. Instead, we could give it this signature with two arrows:.

This precisely captures that, if you give it an integer, it returns an integer. If you give it a float, it returns a float. Multiple arrows are an excellent way to type functions with multiple clauses, which are common in both Erlang and Elixir.

With this in mind, and remembering that rem only works on integers (its type is integer(), integer() -> integer()), what do you believe is the inferred type of x in the function below?

You may think x is dynamic(integer() or float()), because that’s the domain of negate. However, x will once again be inferred to be dynamic(integer()), because Elixir propagates types through the arrows in reverse: it starts from what the outermost call expects and walks inwards, from results to arguments, until it reaches the variables. Let’s break it down.

We start type checking the function and we find rem(negate(x), 2). rem has a single arrow, integer(), integer() -> integer(), so we know that negate(x) must return an integer() for this to type check.

Now we type check negate(x). negate has two arrows: integer() -> integer() and float() -> float(). Since its result must be an integer, we can discard the float() -> float() arrow, as it never returns an integer. The only remaining arrow is integer() -> integer(), so the argument of negate must be integer().

Now we type check x itself. x starts with the type dynamic(term()). We then intersect it with integer(), resulting in dynamic(integer()).

In other words, inference goes in two directions. Going forward, from arguments to results, arrows tell us what each call returns. Going in reverse, from results to arguments, arrows tell us what each argument must have been for the call to produce the expected result. As we give precise type signatures to our programs using multiple arrows, the type system will use these same arrows to infer precise types. As we will learn next, Elixir uses this technique to infer types from guards and to perform type narrowing (also known as occurrence typing).

It has been revealed that now we have the foundation to understand how Elixir performs type inference of guards. Take this function clause:.

Both x and y start with type dynamic(term()). We also know that a guard only succeeds if it returns true and we have the following type signatures (roughly):.

Therefore, to infer the types of when is_integer(x) and is_bitstring(y), we start with true, which is the only result for which a guard succeeds, and propagate it through the arrows in reverse:.

The only arrow of and that can return true is true, true -> true, therefore we know that both operands must be true.

The only arrow of is_integer that can return true is integer() -> true, therefore we know x must be an integer.

The only arrow of is_bitstring that can return true is bitstring() -> true, therefore we know y must be a bitstring.

If multiple arrows could return true, we would then simply union their domains.

Sources indicate that it is worth emphasizing that this behaviour is not hardcoded to a handful of functions the type checker knows about. It works with any function, in any context. Let’s see more examples.

Occurrence typing refines the type of variables and expressions based on the branch taken in a conditional or pattern match, so the same variable may have different types in different branches. For example:.

Industry observers note that the mechanism we use to perform occurrence typing is quite similar to the one from the previous sections. Within the do-branch, we consider the scenarios where is_bitstring(x) will return true. Within the else-branch, we consider the ones where it returns false.

It has been revealed that and since our foundation is built on reverse arrows, the narrowing also applies to patterns and case-expressions! For example:.

Here, parse has no type signature, but Elixir infers its arrows from its clauses: integer() -> {:ok, integer()} and bitstring() -> :error. Within the first branch, we know parse(x) returned a tuple, and the only arrow that returns a tuple has integer() as its domain, so x must be an integer.

The If-T benchmark is a collection of test scenarios designed to evaluate both the precision and soundness of type narrowing. Elixir v1.20 already handled 12 out of the 13 tests, but it could not infer the proper types for this example:.

Industry observers note that to narrow x, we need to reverse the arrows of is_integer(x). In Elixir v1.20, we only did so for the expression given directly to if or case. Here, the expression given to if is the variable y. All v1.20 knew about y is that it was a boolean(). Inside the do-branch, y is true, but by then the connection between y and is_integer(x) had been lost at the assignment, so there were no arrows to reverse.

This would be quite harmful once we add type signatures, because it means trivial refactoring techniques, such as extracting an expression into a variable, could lead to false positives.

According to recent reports, elixir v1.21 solves this by keeping track of the expression each variable was assigned to. Now, when y is narrowed to true, we know y came from is_integer(x), so we continue propagating true in reverse through the arrows of is_integer, narrowing x to integer(). This works across any number of assignments:.

Our implementation also performs the narrowing lazily, by cross-referencing the variables in the if and case expressions with the variables used in each clause, trying to find any assignment they share with each other. If the clauses above do not access z, y, or x, then no narrowing is performed.

Finally, because Elixir defines reverse arrows for almost all operations, it can refine expressions which are not presently refined in TypeScript, such as data constructors:.

In the program above, even though foo is set as the value of a map, refining the map still refines the original variable.

Sources indicate that elixir’s approach to type inference and narrowing is built on a few ideas that compose well. Dynamic types are refined as variables are used, multiple arrows give precise types to functions, and propagating types through those arrows in reverse lets us infer and narrow types across conditionals, patterns, and assignments, all without hardcoding knowledge about specific functions.

According to recent reports, in Elixir v1.21, we use these techniques to find sure bugs in existing Elixir programs, without requiring any changes to your code. The same mechanisms will apply once type signatures are introduced: the more precise the signatures, the more precise the narrowing and the fewer false positives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that openJDK and Oracle disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) on November 17, and NGINX released fixes for two HTTP/2 flaws the next day. Docker began publishing fixed images for both in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog starting that same day.

Recent findings suggest that what we know about Java4Shell is that it’s a memory-corruption bug in the Java runtime that can let an attacker with no credentials run code inside a Java application. Many container images contain a Java runtime, including application images that bundle their own, so it affects teams well beyond the ones that write Java.

Docker Hardened Images are the trusted foundation your applications should run on, because a flaw in the runtime inside an image is fixed only when that image is rebuilt, and Docker rebuilds its hardened images as soon as upstream fixes become available. Fixed images for the Amazon Corretto, SapMachine and Azul Zulu runtimes and for NGINX are in the catalog today, with Eclipse Temurin following as soon as Adoptium completes its fixed builds.

It has been revealed that to decode Base64 quickly, the HotSpot JVM uses a hand-written routine built on AVX-512 instructions. That routine miscalculates a length when the input ends in unexpected padding and writes up to 62 bytes past the end of a buffer on the Java heap. Calif, the researchers who found it, turned that into heap disclosure and remote code execution.

According to recent reports, they demonstrated code execution before authentication against default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and after authentication against Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. They note there is no universal exploit: each application needs its own, and they have not published those. As of November 18 there are no public reports of exploitation in the wild.

Sources indicate that oracle rates the issue 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1. The researchers rate it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. CISA has issued an alert urging immediate patching.

To check a host’s CPU, run this on the host or Kubernetes node. Hardened runtime images have no shell, so it will not run inside the container.

grep -m1 ‘^flags’ /proc/cpuinfo | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep -E ‘^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$’.

The host is affected if all four flags are printed.

Two other ways to check, for when a shell on the node is hard to get.

Ask the JVM. This works in hardened images:.

docker run –rm –entrypoint java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX.

UseAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check says otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on.

According to recent reports, ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type demonstrates the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true.

Check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network.

Sources indicate that not read by javac, keytool or other JDK tools. DHI FIPS images set it. Java 8 ignores it.

Nothing downstream inherits it.

JAVA_OPTS, JENKINS_JAVA_OPTS, MAVEN_OPTS, ES_JAVA_OPTS and similar.

A start script, which copies the value onto one java command line.

Each script has its own rules. If nothing in the image reads the variable, it does nothing.

According to recent reports, five rules follow from that table. We tested each on DHI images.

JAVA_OPTS only works where a script reads it. With JAVA_OPTS=”-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” set and a plain java command, the intrinsic stays on. No warning is printed.

Industry observers note that A flag on the command line stops at that process. We started a JVM with the flag on its command line and had it start a second JVM. The child ran with the intrinsic on. With JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS in the environment, the child ran with it off. A child started with a cleared environment gets nothing, whichever variable you use.

Check what the image already sets before you set anything. In Docker and Kubernetes, your value replaces the image’s value. It is not appended.

docker inspect –format ‘{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}’ \  | grep -E ‘^(JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS|JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS)=’.

In a recent development, our FIPS images use these variables to configure the FIPS provider. dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-fips sets both. When we replaced its JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS with only the flag, the JVM started normally, but the org.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only property was gone. Nothing warned us. If the command prints a value, copy it and add the flag at the end:.

env:  – name: JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS    value: “ -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics”.

Not every FIPS image uses the same variables, so run the check for each image.

Keep JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS away from Java 8. Java 8 is not affected and does not know the flag:.

Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:-UseBASE64IntrinsicsUnrecognized VM option ‘UseBASE64Intrinsics’Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.

In a recent development, adding -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions to the variable does not help on Java 8. Where Java 8 shares an environment with a newer Java, either scope the variable to the containers that need it or use JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, which Java 8 ignores. Java 11 accepts the flag, so it is harmless there.

It has been revealed that verify the process, not the environment. Running java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version inside a container starts a new JVM. It tells you what the environment gives a new JVM, not what the JVM already serving traffic was started with. For the running process, use the startup log line. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS prints one too, starting with NOTE: Picked up. In an image that includes the JDK you can also ask the process directly:.

jcmd VM.flags | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics.

The answer must be -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. If the flag reached the JVM through an environment variable, it will not show in the process’s command line, so ps is not a reliable check.

Some applications discard these variables on purpose. Elasticsearch’s start script, for example, ignores JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and expects ES_JAVA_OPTS. Check your application’s documentation.

It has been revealed that pull the new image and redeploy. Four things catch people out:.

Industry observers note that then confirm with java -version that what is running reports a fixed build. After that, remove the flag from every place you set it.

It has been revealed that the day after Java4Shell, NGINX released fixes for two memory errors in the way it handles HTTP/2 connections, tracked as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. A crafted request can crash a worker process, and where an attacker gets past the operating system’s memory protections it can run code inside that worker. Both flaws need HTTP/2 to be enabled on the server, and the same releases fix other NGINX problems that do not depend on HTTP/2, so enhancement either way.

It has been revealed that the Docker Hardened Images for NGINX were rebuilt on NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 and published on November 18, the same day as the upstream release. To patch, pull the image again and redeploy, and move any tag pinned to an older exact version to a fixed one. nginx -v prints the version, and the fixed ones are 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. The notes on pull policy, mirrors and your own images in the section above apply to NGINX images in the same way.

Industry observers note that the vulnerable code is in the Java runtime inside the image, and if you are using DHI, shipping the fix becomes our job. Whether that code can be reached in your deployment depends on things an image cannot see: the CPU it is scheduled onto, the options you start it with, the processes it starts, and the traffic you send it.

With Docker Hardened Images, Docker will.

Track every Java vendor and ship fixed runtimes in DHI as soon as they are released.

Track every Java vendor yourself and rebuild your base images on each fixed runtime.

Tell you which images are fixed and which are still waiting.

Find out from each vendor which of its builds are fixed.

Tell you what we know, and revision this post.

Follow the OpenJDK, Oracle and vendor advisories as they change.

Three jobs stay with you whichever image you run.

It was only four weeks ago that the news was PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Calif, the security research team that found Java4Shell and helped find PHP2Shell, says it used AI to find this flaw in about an hour and that the whole effort cost less than $200 in tokens. When a flaw like this can be found and weaponized at that price, it is reasonable to expect more of them.

If you lead a team or answer for how your organization builds and ships software, the questions after a week like this one are whether you were exposed and how promptly you can prove you were not. It is imperative to have a trusted foundation in place before the next flaw appears, and Docker Hardened Images is that foundation to adopt. This week Docker began publishing fixed Java and NGINX images to the catalog within a day of each disclosure, with the images still waiting listed in the status table above. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, so you have a record of what it contains and how it was built.

The Docker Hardened Images catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, and moving one of your services onto a hardened image typically means changing one line in its Dockerfile. If you are not building on Docker Hardened Images yet, start today.

Java4Shell is a reason to use Java

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mccue

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we're less than a day into dealing with "Java4Shell", an concern stemming from how the Java Virtual Machine intrinsifies Base64 encoding code.
  • Industry observers note that this is just one in a string of high profile outages and vulnerabilities.
  • Vulnerabilities tend to be bigger problems when they stem from native code, and they tend to be widespread problems when they come from dependencies many people share.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we're less than a day into dealing with "Java4Shell", an concern stemming from how the Java Virtual Machine intrinsifies Base64 encoding code. If you have a Java deployment you haven't updated yet, add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to the VM flags. Then upgrade your VM to a version where the issue is patched when you can.

Industry observers note that this is just one in a string of high profile outages and vulnerabilities. AI is a good fuzzer, people are finding latent problems with much lower effort than the past. People are pretty worried about this because we're all pretty sure there are more latent problems to find.

Vulnerabilities tend to be bigger problems when they stem from native code, and they tend to be widespread problems when they come from dependencies many people share.

Recent findings suggest that java4Shell is both of these things. A lot of people use Java and the problem stems from a handwritten assembly intrinsic. Fun times.

According to recent reports, but, for a moment, lets say we trust the VM. It is a massive dependency, but it is only one dependency. We can all agree to audit it more closely, reduce the amount of native code in it, proactively run AIs against it, etc. Of course.

Recent findings suggest that normal Java programs are memory safe. If you use a library which wants to call native code you will get a warning, later a hard error, unless you the person using the library adds --enable-native-access=the.specific.library to their command-line options. This means even with a sprawling dependency tree, which is a problem for all programming language ecosystems, you can know your exact exposure to native code and what dependencies you need to audit more closely.

Recent findings suggest that compare that to C#, which lets any dependency write assembly inline. Python, JavaScript, Go - everything speaks C and lets any one of your dependencies bring along native code. As we are all learning the hard way, this carries risk.

Not only are Java programs memory safe. They are also fast. The exact mechanism which caused Java4Shell (the ability for the VM to swap out normal Java code for native code) combined with JIT compilation can make the actual performance of a Java program competitive with C. Sometimes a Java program can even be faster. A JIT compiler knows what code paths are actually taken and can optimize around them. They can even refocus what is optimized if the workload changes. It is pretty cool!

Somewhat recently I went through the raytracing in a weekend book with Java.

Recent findings suggest that benchmarks can be problematic, I know. What I want you to take away is that the JVM makes your code fast enough that most people don't need native code. Unlike, to take a potshot, CPython. There everything is slow as molasses unless you make it a native extension.

Sources indicate that so if you are worried AI is going to find security problems with your code, use Java. The problems are likely to be less severe.

Or use Kotlin, Clojure, JRuby, etc. Whatever. Most of what I talked about applies to all of them. Its only what I didn't talk about (the module system) that is Java specific.

TPU Model Design Considerations and Optimization Guide

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (456 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google designed TPUs from the ground up to be exceptionally efficient for machine learning workloads, delivering top-tier performance per total cost of ownership (TCO).
  • Recent findings suggest that performance tuning starts with model definition.
  • According to recent reports, how to use this guide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google designed TPUs from the ground up to be exceptionally efficient for machine learning workloads, delivering top-tier performance per total cost of ownership (TCO). Because TPUs trade general-purpose hardware scheduling for wide systolic arrays, dedicated SparseCore engines, and custom interconnect fabrics, adhering to specific architectural best practices is essential to achieve maximum performance. To help developers get the most out of TPUs, we are launching the open-source AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide. This post highlights its key principles—spanning shape alignment, architectural choices like LatentMoE, and parallelism strategies—to accelerate LLMs, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, and other hardware-intensive workloads on TPUs.

Recent findings suggest that performance tuning starts with model definition. Architectural choices made before the first training step set permanent ceilings on MFU (Model FLOP Utilization), cost, and serving latency. This guide gives concrete, hardware-grounded design rules for teams building or adapting models for TPUs, organized into three groups:.

According to recent reports, how to use this guide. The shape rules apply to anyone designing a fresh model. If you are adapting an existing model rather than designing one, the Expressing Parallelism section applies without touching the checkpoint. The general rules hold for any large-matmul architecture (dense LLMs, multimodal, and world models), and the companion AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign repository grows model- and workload-specific sections over time.

Industry observers note that eighth-generation TPUs. These principles carry forward to TPU 8t and TPU 8i and to the newly declared TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max. The reasoning stays the same and the thresholds move with the hardware. TPU 8t and TPU 8i both add native FP4. For training, TPU 8t also brings more balanced Vector Processing Unit (VPU) scaling. For serving, TPU 8i adds the Boardfly topology, a Collectives Acceleration Engine (CAE), and 3x more on-chip SRAM. We note the effects inline in Principles 5–8, and follow-up posts will cover eighth-generation designs in depth.

Measured evidence. Alongside the published sources, notes marked Measured carry results from our own Ironwood profiling program: open 20–30B MoEs (a Qwen3-30B-derived LatentMoE variant; GPT-OSS-20B) plus dense controls, single slice (except for the 512-chip TPU v7x and 1,024-chip TPU v4 ablations in Principle 4), BF16, training shapes up to 32K sequence, all against tuned-systems baselines. Treat the trends and rankings as transferable, the exact percentages as config-specific.

In a recent development, TPUs are purpose-built custom ML ASICs designed from the ground up to deliver state-of-the-art performance per total cost of ownership (TCO). While their architectural choices—such as wide 256×256 systolic arrays, software-managed VMEM, dedicated SparseCore engines, and direct multi-dimensional ICI fabrics—enable exceptional efficiency, they inherently create specific structural constraints and programming patterns that must be carefully followed to unlock maximal performance. Reaching peak efficiency requires aligning model shapes, routing, and parallelism directly with these underlying hardware characteristics:.

Welcome Inkling by Thinking Machines

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that patch: Inkling 2 Small is here!
  • Inkling is Thinking Machines' family of open multimodal models, and it now spans two generations on the Hub:.
  • It has been revealed that in this post, we start with the first-generation architecture, then walk through what changed in Inkling 2 Small and how to run it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that patch: Inkling 2 Small is here! 🤗 Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Small, the next generation of the Inkling family. We have updated this post with a fresh section on Inkling 2 Small, covering what changed in the architecture and how to run it with transformers.

Inkling is Thinking Machines' family of open multimodal models, and it now spans two generations on the Hub:.

It has been revealed that in this post, we start with the first-generation architecture, then walk through what changed in Inkling 2 Small and how to run it. The rest of the post covers inference, use cases, post-training, and deployment, with examples built on the first-generation checkpoints.

Inkling is the first large open model with ~1T parameters and 1M context window to natively receive image, text, and audio inputs, trained on 45 trillion tokens of text, images, audio and video. It’s focused on reasoning across modalities such as audio, images, and text. It is intended for domain adaptation via fine-tuning. We’ve tinkered (pun intended) with this model to build some demos and explore the architecture, and we think it’s great for building a newly introduced wave of multimodal reasoning apps.

Inkling is a decoder-only multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) model with 975B total and 41B active parameters. There are a lot of things going on, so let’s break each part down:.

Here’s a quick glance of the architecture.

Relative attention: Instead of RoPE, which is the usual method to inject positional information in transformers models, Inkling uses relative attention to encode position information. Each attention layer learns position directly in the attention logits. Aside from key-query-values, there's a fourth projection producing a per-token, per-head relative feature R. This projection tensor is then tweaked with distance information (distance between the key and the query vector) and propagated into the attention module.

Recent findings suggest that hybrid attention: The decoder layers alternate between global attention (attending to the full context length at once) and sliding window attention (attending to a fixed context window in a sliding fashion). The architecture has a pattern of 5:1 sliding window to global attention layers. This hybrid attention scheme provides efficiency in computation. The final layer uses global attention to help build feature-rich representations.

Short convolution: The model uses a distinctive short 1D convolution, or SConv over the hidden states. SConv reads the current token and the previous W-1 hidden states, with W being the sliding window size. The intuition here is that SConv helps with local attention while freeing the attention and MoE modules from local representations.

Industry observers note that moE with shared experts sink: In Inkling, the router scores both routed experts and shared experts. Top-k selection is performed over 6 experts, plus 2 shared experts always active.

Vision understanding: The model includes a simple hierarchical MLP patchifier consisting of several linear layers. Each layer merges pixels progressively, until the final layer produces one embedding per patch.

Audio understanding: The architecture employs a discretized mel spectrogram, where each of the audio chunks (of 100 ms) are converted to the mel scale and then classified into the exact mel spectrogram bin.

Sources indicate that the multimodal towers are relatively simple modules, unlike other models that employ separate encoders for each modality. Each image patch passes through the image embedding tower and the audio chunk is passed through the audio embedding tower to get both media embeddings. Image inputs also include an additional temporal dimension for video processing. We expect this capability to be useful for downstream fine-tuning, but we haven’t evaluated out-of-the-box video performance. The tower folds the patch grid, a small local block of neighboring tokens is stacked into the channel dimension and goes through hMLP. The audio waveform is converted to mel scale, which is then classified into a discrete mel bin. These mel bin values are embedded in the audio embedding tower and the embeddings are then summed to construct the final audio input.

Inkling 2 is the next generation of the family. It takes text and image inputs (but no audio), and generates text. It keeps the core ideas of Inkling's decoder:.

Industry observers note that almost everything around that core was redesigned, though. The layers read from the residual stream differently, attention is bounded and gated, the MoE is simpler and wider, and the vision tower is now a real vision transformer.

Here's how the two generations compare:.

Let's go over the most notable changes together:.

Block attention residuals: In a standard transformer, every layer adds its output to the residual stream, and the next layer reads it. Inkling 2 has no single residual stream. Instead, it groups its 48 layers into 8 blocks of 6 and keeps one sum per block:.

According to recent reports, A sublayer (attention or MLP) doesn't read one of these sums directly. It attends over depth, which means at each token position, it treats the finished block summaries plus the current partial block as a short sequence, and takes a softmax-weighted mix of them.

It has been revealed that the query is a single learned vector per sublayer. The keys and values are the RMS-normalized block summaries at that position. So the weights differ from token to token, depending on what each block wrote there.

It has been revealed that in other words, each sublayer learns how much to draw from each earlier stage of the network, rather than always reading the sum of everything. By the last layer, there are up to 9 sources to choose from (the embeddings, 7 finished blocks and the current partial block), and the final norm reads its input the same way. Global attention layers learn three queries, so their query, key and value projections can each draw on a different mix of blocks.

Dynamic short convolutions: The short convolutions on keys and values in the global attention layers are now dynamic. The 4 taps of each convolution are a fixed learned weight plus a per-token weight predicted from the input, shared within each key/value head. So the model can change, token by token, how much local context goes into each key and value. All short convolutions also rescale their residual sum to keep its variance stable through depth.

A leaner, wider MoE: Each layer has 384 routed experts with 8 active per token, and the shared experts are gone.

According to recent reports, A newly introduced vision encoder: Inkling encoded images with a lightweight hierarchical MLP. Inkling 2 uses a 23-layer vision transformer based on the Perception Encoder. It has the following properties:.

Several images are packed into one sequence, and each image only attends to itself.

Inkling 2 uses the same Auto classes as Inkling. Make sure to have updated transformers to run the model.

Inkling comes with day-0 transformers support and is supported in major inference engines like SGLang and vLLM.

This model is huge. The bf16 checkpoint requires 2 TB of VRAM, while the nvfp4 version requires 600 GB of VRAM. You can try the model through serverless inference routers like Inference Providers, or use ggml quants for local deployment with llama.cpp.

Sources indicate that the easiest way to infer with transformers directly is to use the any-to-any pipeline. You can use either the 16 bit "thinkingmachines/Inkling" on Hopper or later GPUs, or the quantized NVFP4 checkpoint "thinkingmachines/Inkling-NVFP4" on Blackwell Nvidia GPUs. Make sure to have the latest version of transformers (5.14.0 was released today) (pip install -U transformers).

After initializing the pipeline, you can pass in the prompt as follows.

Industry observers note that going one level lower, you can use Auto classes. For inference, you can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class for models and AutoProcessor class for processors. For different reasoning tasks, the tokenizer takes in a reasoning_effort argument. Existing options for reasoning effort are "none", "minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", and "max".

In a recent development, for multimodal inference, you can use the same classes. We provide example snippets for each different modality in the model card.

According to recent reports, inkling also takes in audio input. Below is an example inference snippet, which still uses the same AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

For more realistic parallel deployment in a cluster of several nodes, please refer to the Slurm section below.

SGLang is one of the fastest deployment frameworks for Inkling at the time of release, as it includes a custom model implementation. The launch command below shards the model across 8 GPUs and serves an OpenAI-compatible API on port 30000.

Match --tp-size to your GPU count. Add --mem-fraction-static (e.g. 0.85) if you need to leave more headroom for the KV cache.

It has been revealed that vLLM is strong for production serving. A single vllm serve command downloads the weights from the Hub, shards the model across your GPUs with tensor parallelism, and starts an OpenAI-compatible server on port 8000. You can view the vLLM Recipe for the model here to customize to your hardware.

Industry observers note that in practice, you might need multiple nodes and a distribution tool like SLURM (see below). Key parameters are --tensor-parallel-size to the number of GPUs on your node, and use --max-model-len to cap the context window if you hit KV-cache memory limits.

You can infer with this model using several inference providers through Hugging Face. You can see all the code snippets to consume here. Below you can see how to use with the OpenAI client.

Using the “:auto” suffix routes to your preferred provider in your settings; you can also use “cheapest” or “:fastest” as well. For this release, we cover the inference costs for 2 hours within the release for everyone.

Note: audio support in Inference Providers is work in progress and will be added shortly.

In a recent development, you can use llama.cpp to run quantized versions of the model on limited hardware. Unsloth have quantized the model down to 1-bit precision, reducing VRAM consumption by 95% over the original model.

This starts an OpenAI-compatible server running at http://localhost:8080/v1 that you connect to in your preferred tool or clients. Heading there, you can start chatting with the model, and set it up with your favorite MCPs, pass in images or files conveniently and more!

According to recent reports, llama cpp also ships with a built-in UI that supports tools, mcp, and agentic workloads. Checkout Inkling running at 1-bit precision in the llama app:.

Inkling GGUFs are also runnable in Unsloth Studio with dynamic 1-bit GGUFs which retain ~74.2% of top-1% accuracy whilst being 86% smaller.

Industry observers note that pi is a minimal coding agent harness you can use with different language models. You can use Pi with either an inference engine server endpoint, such as llama.cpp, or with Inference Providers on Hugging Face by adding this to your ~/.pi/agent/models.json after installation.

Sources indicate that then you can start Pi in your project directory by calling pi and you’re good to go! In this demo, we give the model a hard math reasoning problem and it uses tools in pi to solve it.

Inkling is focused on broad multimodality reasoning and low token consumption, so try it out with document processing or audio tasks.

Industry observers note that MTP adds extra layers to the model that predict several tokens at once, not just the next one. During inference, the extra layers act as “drafters” for speculative decoding, speeding up generation without compromising performance. With MTP, you get the exact same generated outputs, multipliers in generation speed-up at small memory cost in VRAM (due to serving the drafter). Thinking Machines also provides an MTP drafter with this release.

Sources indicate that we have prepared a small suite of reasoning questions from expert-level sources and university entrance exams. We have taken photos of the screen with watermarks in the screenshot to challenge the model. The model has solved all of them on high one, failed one in highest and medium reasoning efforts, so we provide a link to the model answers for you to check out how the model sounds and provide the number of tokens the model has taken to solve each of them. Note that we provide no system prompts in these vibe evals, and these reasoning questions should often be run with a good system prompt. The vibe eval images and results live here.

Industry observers note that we have vibe-evaluated the model on some audio reasoning examples from BigBenchAudio and a few multilingual audio examples of GlobeAudio (Russian and Chinese multi-choice questions asking the last word in transcription). The BigBenchAudio examples we tested consist of logical statements and questions that either ask for formal fallacies (whether an argument can be logically deduced from the context given in audio) or object counting (stating multiple distinctive objects in the audio, asking for the total count of a certain one). Although this benchmark is initially made for speech-to-speech reasoning, we just want to see audio reasoning capabilities of this model. For GlobeAudio, the questions are relatively straightforward, so we ran with reasoning efforts of 0.1. We ran the first example of each language within GlobeAudio. All tests pass on all questions and efforts, except for second formal fallacy example on lowest effort, so we only provide the number of tokens spent in each question against reasoning effort. Vibe eval results and audio files live here.

In a recent development, if you would like to use Inkling for post-training, Thinking Machines have built tinker, a managed tool for post-training open weight models. Their cookbook includes examples for fine-tuning, distillation, and reinforcement learning.

According to recent reports, we post trained Inkling with tinker and OpenEnv, an agentic RL environment tool. We used the ECHO algorithm that trains a model to predict the environment without a verifier, applying next-token cross-entropy loss to tokens produced by the environment, alongside the usual policy learning on agent actions. This teaches the policy an implicit world model without requiring a separate model, teacher, or additional rollouts. Check out the example.

If you’re working with Transformers Reinforcement Learning we suggest using Inkling as a teacher model in a knowledge distillation setup. For example, take advantage of Inkling’s document understanding abilities to improve the performance of a smaller (on-device) model. In this example, we use the transformer reinforcement learning library and the GOLD algorithm to distill knowledge. GOLD is handy here because it matches token logits between different tokenizers, so you can distill to any model on the hub.

Below you can find each Inkling checkpoint as well as their VRAM requirements.

To deploy Inkling on a cluster, we provide SLURM scripts serving with transformers API, as well as how to query the endpoint with different modalities. You can adapt these scripts to vLLM or SGlang by updating the commands. These scripts live here.

You can deploy an Inkling-Small NVFP4 checkpoint using Inference Endpoints. We provide a pre-tested configuration to deploy it on 8 RTX PRO 6000s with an aggregated VRAM of·768 GB, giving large space for KV cache, costs $ 22 per hourly uptime (scales to zero when unused). To deploy, run hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4 using the Hugging Face CLI or alternatively, head to https://endpoints.huggingface.co/fresh/thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4. With this setup, you can get 140 TPS (single user inference, prepared for multi-user support with continuous batching).

Once the endpoint is up, you can query as follows.

Releasing a natively multimodal model (text, vision, and audio) open-weights is a huge step forward for the open-source AI ecosystem! Having variable and controllable thinking effort built into a MoE architecture makes Inkling a really attractive foundation for fine-tuning. Excited to test out the smaller 12B active parameter variant for local agent workflows at https://geometrydashsubzero.io.

UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Parliamentary committee notes tech giants can't be left to mark their own homework when it comes to AI safety.
  • UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far.
  • In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Parliamentary committee notes tech giants can't be left to mark their own homework when it comes to AI safety.

UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far.

In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed.

Recent findings suggest that it could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation.

The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta.

Sources indicate that all four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything.

"We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP.

Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation.

"Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested.".

The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers.

The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns.

In a recent development, MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny.

Recent findings suggest that former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses.

It has been revealed that there's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. Using OECD productivity estimates, the committee calculates that AI could leave Britain's economy up to £400 billion larger over the next decade. It also sees an opportunity for the UK to make money from independently testing AI models, building on the expertise already established at AISI. MPs argue that stronger safeguards could encourage businesses, particularly smaller firms, to adopt the technology.

In a recent development, "AI firms must be required to substantiate their safety claims, independent experts must be able to scrutinize them, and a regulator must have the power to intervene when risks cannot be controlled," Byrne remarked. "Ministers, accountable to Parliament, must decide what risks the public should be asked to bear.".

MPs want the new laws on the books in the next parliamentary session, and say Britain should use its turn at the G20 helm in 2027 to get other countries on board with tougher rules for AI testing, incident reporting, and risky model releases.

Whether ministers are prepared to hand a watchdog the power to stop AI development is another matter. The committee's recommendations aren't binding, and the government has yet to commit to the proposed legislation. ®.
