📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Yelp Migrates Cassandra to EKS by Moving EBS Volumes.

Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.

Yelp has moved its Cassandra fleet from legacy self-managed Kubernetes clusters to Amazon EKS by re-pointing existing EBS volumes at upcoming pods, rather than streaming data between nodes. A blog post by the site reliability team details a migration. It covered about 90 production clusters. There was zero downtime for customers and no data loss. The largest cluster, a 54-pod user-data store, took about 12 hours end to end.

Yelp had already moved its stateless workloads to EKS through its PaaSTA deployment layer, but Cassandra stayed behind. Kubernetes has no built-in way to migrate StatefulSets and their persistent volumes across clusters. The usual approach is to add nodes to the new cluster and shut down the old ones. This would temporarily double compute capacity but also lead to data transfer costs. For the largest clusters, streaming alone could have taken weeks. Yelp also considered a regional failover and rebuild, and a new Cassandra datacenter in EKS, but rated both as less transparent to customers.

Recent findings suggest that yelp's "Rolling PV Transplant" relies on the fact that an EBS volume is bound to an Availability Zone, not to a Kubernetes cluster, and that a PersistentVolume is effectively a pointer to a volume ID. The team pre-creates PVs and PVCs in EKS that reference the existing volume IDs, then creates an identical StatefulSet there, whose pods wait in ContainerCreating. The automation then deletes one pod at a time on the legacy cluster, waits for the volume to detach, and lets the EKS pod claim it. The pod rejoins the ring with the same data and token range, and the process repeats for the next pod. Cassandra's replication tolerates the few minutes each node is offline.

In a recent development, yelp set a skipReconciliation: true flag on the custom resources in both clusters. This was done because two operators managed the same logical ring during the migration. The flag helped prevent them from conflicting over pod state. The flag was cleared on the EKS side at the end.

Recent findings suggest that across roughly 1,000 pods, about 1,000 TiB moved by pointer rather than over the wire. No node was ever decommissioned from the ring, so rollback was the same operation in reverse. Yelp used it a handful of times, for a missing subnet definition and a certificate mismatch, and restored pods within minutes. After a week of manual dev runs and a week of automation, one engineer ran the production rollout in about three weeks, migrating three to six clusters on a typical day.

The team had Claude generate the orchestration script, roughly 800 lines of bash, from its validated manual runbook, rather than asking it to design the procedure. The script needed minor adjustments after two days of testing.

The approach relies on a previous Container Storage Interface migration by Yelp's Compute Infrastructure team. This work gave the Data Infrastructure team confidence in the volume detach and attach process. Yelp also used the technique for Kafka clusters, and claims it applies to any AZ-pinned stateful workload on Kubernetes. The legacy clusters are now retired.

Industry observers note that the one failure specific to this technique was a stale VolumeAttachment object left behind by the AWS CSI controller after pod deletion. The EKS pod sat in Pending with no error, and deleting the object on the legacy cluster fixed it. Yelp advises building explicit timeouts for stalled detach and attach operations into any automation. Two other findings were unrelated to the mechanism. Backups failed with IAM AccessDenied errors for 48 hours because a latest -eks role was not yet being assumed by scheduled jobs, and the alert only filed a ticket instead of paging. Pausing repairs for the migration also exposed one cluster whose repairs had been silently disabled for three months, leaving accumulated data inconsistencies. Teams planning a similar move should audit repair state, backup IAM roles and alert severity before starting.

Industry observers note that yelp's approach is not the only way to move Cassandra between EKS clusters. Monday.com's engineering team describes a different one in a post on zero-downtime Cassandra migration between EKS clusters. K8ssandra-managed clusters had to move without any downtime or data loss. So, the team created a workflow to add new Cassandra data centers, safely transfer data, and remove the old ones. That is the streaming model Yelp considered and rejected. The new cluster is brought up alongside the old one and receives data over the network, and the original is retired only afterwards. The team believes success relied more on control, automation, and handling failures than on speed. They automated long tasks like rebuilds and planned the migration in stages based on operator behavior.

In a recent development, the two migrations differ in what they trade away. Yelp's disk transplant skips data transfer and extra compute. It allows for a rollback by swapping the pointer. However, it relies on EBS volumes being linked to an Availability Zone, not a cluster. Monday.com's approach does not rely on that property, and it keeps the old environment intact until the end. The cost is a longer migration and the capacity to run both sides at once, which Yelp calculated would have taken weeks for its largest clusters.

Recent findings suggest that despite the different mechanics, the post-migration lessons are similar. Monday.com devotes part of its write-up to verifying that backups work after the migration, along with monitoring, dashboards and alerts. Yelp's own backups failed on an IAM role mismatch within 48 hours of its first production clusters landing in EKS. Teams planning either approach should treat those checks as part of the migration proposal, not as cleanup afterwards.

European Commission scrambles to contain AI-assisted cyberattack

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Staff HR and medical reimbursement systems taken offline as officials investigate whether personal data was compromised.
  • The European Commission is picking up the pieces after hackers wielding an AI-powered security testing tool targeted its internal IT systems, potentially exposing staff members' personal data.
  • It has been revealed that the attack, first reported by Politico, has caused more than 10 days of disruption at the EU's executive arm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Staff HR and medical reimbursement systems taken offline as officials investigate whether personal data was compromised.

The European Commission is picking up the pieces after hackers wielding an AI-powered security testing tool targeted its internal IT systems, potentially exposing staff members' personal data.

It has been revealed that the attack, first reported by Politico, has caused more than 10 days of disruption at the EU's executive arm. Among the applications temporarily taken offline were Sysper, which staff use to access payslips, submit timesheets, and request vacation time, and MyPMO, which handles medical reimbursements.

Sources indicate that both were brought back online earlier this week, though Sysper fell over again on Wednesday. The Commission's translation services were also affected.

"The European Commission has taken the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign," Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told Politico. "Individual systems were targeted and, in line with our standard practice, we have informed those concerned.".

According to Politico's sources, the Commission's cybersecurity defenders detected hackers using ARTEX, a publicly available AI-powered penetration testing framework. The incident prompted an emergency meeting of the Commission's Corporate Management Board earlier this month, and tech commissioner Henna Virkkunen briefed her fellow commissioners on Wednesday.

The Commission has yet to respond to The Register's questions about the attack, including whether the crooks got their hands on employee data or whether the applications were simply taken offline as a precaution.

The attack might not come as much of a surprise to the Commission's own security bods. CERT-EU, which looks after the cybersecurity of EU institutions, warned on November 5 that it had spotted what it believed to be ARTEX-assisted attacks against organizations under its watch.

The developer behind ARTEX pulled the project's GitHub repository in October after reports that hackers were putting the software to use. But by then, the code was out in the wild, and anyone wanting to have a crack at an organization's IT estate could get hold of one of several forks.

It has been revealed that the FBI also sounded the alarm last week [PDF], revealing that researchers had found more than 1,600 ARTEX consoles exposed to the internet. In some of the attacks detailed by the Feds, hackers went from identifying a target to obtaining privileged access in less than three hours.

“What used to take a skilled operator days or weeks of chaining is now happening in hours because frameworks like ARTEX let a single actor stand up fleets of agents that plan, probe, exploit, and move laterally with almost no further human input after the initial goal is set,” Snehal Antani, CEO of security firm Horizon3.ai, told The Register.

Antani stated the proliferation of these tools could also make life harder for investigators trying to establish who's behind an attack, as government-backed hackers and garden-variety cybercriminals increasingly draw from the same toolbox.

Commission staff at least appear to have been paid on time. According to Politico, some couldn't book time off or submit their timesheets, but salaries landed as usual. Whether the hackers managed to snoop on their payslips is something the Commission has yet to establish. ®.

#11065. Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

📅 03 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1571 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task.
  • According to recent reports, earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing.
  • It has been revealed that while the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each newly introduced agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

According to recent reports, earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

It has been revealed that while the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

According to recent reports, funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:.

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with new runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

Sources indicate that from there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the fresh one.

According to recent reports, with funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

Recent findings suggest that recall returns the original text, not a summary, and demonstrates exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Sources indicate that underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three vital properties:.

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:.

Sources indicate that the bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:.

According to recent reports, or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:.

funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

Industry observers note that A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent notes so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

It has been revealed that claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

This matters in a few different scopes:.

Recent findings suggest that published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious.

Recent findings suggest that your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

Industry observers note that funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

Recent findings suggest that funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Recent findings suggest that ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

  • Norwegian energy giant Equinor is battling a cyberattack on its IT systems, though the tech giant insists that hackers haven't disrupted its oil and gas production.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Norwegian energy giant Equinor says oil and gas production remains unaffected.

Norwegian energy giant Equinor is battling a cyberattack on its IT systems, though the tech giant insists that hackers haven't disrupted its oil and gas production.

Equinor, Europe's largest supplier of natural gas, first disclosed the attack on Tuesday evening, saying it had called in the relevant resources to deal with the intrusion and had found no indication that any data had been stolen.

In an patch on Wednesday, the firm said it had a better handle on how the attack was carried out and which of its systems had been compromised, though it stopped short of sharing either of those details.

"As this is not a virus attack, there is no risk of the attack spreading," Equinor said. The company added that it had found nothing to suggest the incident would affect employees, partners, or suppliers.

In a further enhancement on Thursday, Equinor said the attack remained ongoing but did not appear to be specifically targeting the organization. Production continued normally, with no indications that data had been stolen or altered. The incident has been reported to police.

What kind of attack Equinor is dealing with remains a mystery. The firm hasn't identified those responsible, disclosed whether it's received any demands from the hackers, or said when it expects the affected systems to be fully restored.

The Register has asked Equinor to elaborate, including whether any of its UK operations have been affected and whether the hackers managed to venture beyond its corporate IT network.

In a recent development, equinor spokesperson Ellen Maria Skjelsbæk told Norwegian news agency NTB that the company hadn't lost access to its IT systems, though staff could have trouble accessing some corporate applications and services. Email appears to be among the casualties, with Reuters reporting that the company's internal email system was down.

According to recent reports, equinor, which traded as Statoil until 2018, is still largely in the hands of the Norwegian state, which owns 67 percent of the manufacturer. The oil and gas biz employs around 25,000 people and operates in more than 20 countries.

The bulk of Equinor's oil and gas production takes place off the coast of Norway, but the firm also pumps oil and gas in the UK, US, Brazil, and Canada. It's one of the companies behind Dogger Bank, the enormous offshore wind project off England's northeast coast, and is also in the business of capturing and storing carbon dioxide.

Equinor's assurances about production will be particularly welcome in Europe, which has become increasingly reliant on Norwegian gas since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

In a recent development, the attack comes just weeks after Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) raised its cyberattack risk assessment to four on a five-point scale. The agency mentioned the number of successful cyber operations against Norwegian businesses had tripled over the preceding six months and warned of potential disruption to essential services, including water and electricity supplies.

Sources indicate that europe has already had a few nasty reminders this year of what happens when hackers get their hands on industrial equipment. Last week, the French government pinned a series of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems at more than 700 retail sites in October on a hacking unit affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The crooks turned up the temperature in supermarket fridges and freezers, ruining tens of millions of euros' worth of food and starting fires at some premises.

Nothing suggests Equinor's hackers have similar ambitions, or that they've got anywhere near the kit used to extract and transport oil and gas. Given how much of Europe depends on that kit continuing to work, a little more detail from the Norwegian energy giant wouldn't go amiss. ®.

GitHub availability report: October 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.
  • Industry observers note that the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate.
  • According to recent reports, as of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

Industry observers note that the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

According to recent reports, as of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

Recent findings suggest that we also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Industry observers note that reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in owners. More details on these and other incidents follow.

In a recent development, the East US 3 buildout is about one week behind blueprint. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Recent findings suggest that jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

In a recent development, customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

It has been revealed that A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Sources indicate that duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or concerns, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

Web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

In a recent development, during regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Industry observers note that customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Sources indicate that customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, latest commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

It has been revealed that audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

In a recent development, some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, new connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the matter.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

It has been revealed that copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 9 minutes.

Customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Challenges, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. Newly introduced requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

The pool was already running near capacity when some update requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

It has been revealed that follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance.
  • Industry observers note that structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Industry observers note that structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

According to recent reports, note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:.

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

According to recent reports, for the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Industry observers note that the IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

In a recent development, we use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:.

Recent findings suggest that after GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:.

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:.

In a recent development, the gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

To reproduce or extend this work, see the original IFStruct v1.0 blog post, the Liquid4All/ifstruct benchmark repo, and the LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0 dataset.

    Breaking: AWS PrivateLink Tunnel Endpoints Open a Whole CIDR Range to Another Account

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • InfoQ Homepage News AWS PrivateLink Tunnel Endpoints Open a Whole CIDR Range to Another Account.
    • Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.
    • Recent findings suggest that AWS has published a technical walkthrough of tunnel endpoints, a VPC endpoint type debuted in September that lets an application in one VPC reach every address in a CIDR range shared from another account, instead of one resource at a time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    InfoQ Homepage News AWS PrivateLink Tunnel Endpoints Open a Whole CIDR Range to Another Account.

    Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.

    Recent findings suggest that AWS has published a technical walkthrough of tunnel endpoints, a VPC endpoint type debuted in September that lets an application in one VPC reach every address in a CIDR range shared from another account, instead of one resource at a time. The provider shares a CIDR-type resource configuration through AWS Resource Access Manager and the consumer creates a tunnel endpoint against it. From then on, anything inside the range is reachable, including resources that did not exist when the share was made.

    According to recent reports, bruce Pinsky and Ashish Kumar of AWS frame it as a vendor-access problem, for "a vendor or service provider whose software must reach applications and resources in a customer's network." Until now, that meant a separate PrivateLink resource configuration per database or host, which breaks down when the resources are ephemeral, or the customer does not want to enumerate them. With a CIDR configuration, the customer defines a perimeter in address ranges, and "resources located outside the perimeter can't be reached by the vendor." Two further properties come with the design: the consumer and provider VPCs can use overlapping CIDR blocks, and connections "can start only from the consumer VPC, not from the provider network.".

    (Source: AWS Networking & Content Delivery blog).

    On the r/aws thread about the September launch, the first question was what this does that VPC peering does not, from a self-described veteran of AWS's advanced networking components. The answers that followed are the use cases: a peering connection exposes the whole VPC in both directions, while a tunnel endpoint shares a subset of the address space in one direction only; one commenter at a bank wrote that "peering with unregulated partners is a massive no-no, the auditors will rip you to shreds for it." Another pointed to clusters that do client-side load balancing, such as self-managed Kafka or Aerospike, which until now needed port-based routing on a Network Load Balancer and a separate port-mapping horizon for connections arriving over an interface endpoint. The same thread drew the line against VPC Lattice itself: Lattice services work at layer 7, tunnel endpoints at layer 4 without a resource configuration per target.

    Sources indicate that the unusual part is on the consumer side: the application's traffic has to arrive at the tunnel endpoint wrapped in GENEVE, the encapsulation protocol defined in RFC 8926, over UDP port 6081 and in the same Availability Zone. The endpoint strips the header, checks that the inner destination falls inside the shared range, rewrites the source to a resource gateway address, and forwards a plain packet into the provider VPC. Linux can do the wrapping in the kernel. The walkthrough creates an ip link add ... type geneve id 0 device inside its own network namespace with a default route through it, which sends the provider's ranges into the tunnel and leaves the instance's other traffic alone. On the far side, the resources see the resource gateway as the client, so the post advises security groups that reference the gateway's security group or subnet rather than a single address.

    The documentation lists the constraints. Inner traffic must be TCP, with UDP permitted only for DNS, so ICMP and ping do not work, and IP fragments are dropped. Private DNS names are not supported on tunnel endpoints. The endpoint's subnets must sit in Availability Zones that overlap with the resource gateway's, or the association indicates as inaccessible. A resource gateway's DNS setting cannot be changed after creation. And the access logs identify the consumer's endpoint but carry no field for the inner source address, so a provider can attribute traffic to a vendor and not to a workload behind that vendor's endpoint. The post also warns that sharing 0.0.0.0/0 grants access to everything the provider VPC can route to, including networks behind VPC peering, Direct Connect or a Site-to-Site VPN, and recommends sharing the narrowest ranges that work.

    According to recent reports, both points have been tested in practice. Ryo Suzuki of the Japanese consultancy Classmethod connected two VPCs that both use 10.0.0.0/16 and got HTTP through, but only by running a GENEVE relay as root on the client, by routing a /32 per destination host, or by putting an HAProxy or NAT instance in front, each of which adds a hop or a single point of failure; his conclusion was that "route management according to the number of destinations is required." In a second experiment, he shared 0.0.0.0/0 from a VPC with a NAT gateway and reached the internet from a VPC with no gateway at all, which confirmed AWS's warning from the other side; he judged it workable as a temporary path and "difficult to use in a permanent production setup.".

    Industry observers note that pricing is an hourly charge per tunnel endpoint plus a per-GB charge for data processed, under PrivateLink pricing, with the provider side billed per GB through the resource gateway under VPC Lattice pricing, and the feature is available in 28 regions. Terraform support followed from the community: a contributor request opened two days after launch was implemented by another contributor and shipped in version 6.71.0 of the AWS provider, as a Tunnel endpoint type on aws_vpc_endpoint and a cidr_resource block on the Lattice resource configuration.
